23258-journal-of-jasper-danckaerts-1679-:
The Journal of Jasper Danckaerts records a Dutch journey across America in 1679 and 1680, in an edition issued in 1913. Its editors explain their text with care. The translation is substantially Mr. Murphy's, as printed in his edition of 1867, and Murphy was an excellent Dutch scholar.

Careful checks were made between that translation and the original manuscript. The Long Island Historical Society, which owns the manuscript, allowed the editors to examine it. Readers get both a first-hand early colonial travel record and a model of how such records are edited, checked, and brought back into print.
acosta-natural-moral-history-markham-vol:
José de Acosta, a Spanish Jesuit who spent years in Peru, published his Historia natural y moral de las Indias in 1590. Volume one here is Clements R Markham's Hakluyt Society edition of 1880, built on Edward Grimston's English translation of 1604. Acosta set out to describe the New World whole: its skies, lands, plants, and peoples.

His natural history reasons about winds, climates, and species with a scholar's care and a traveler's eyes. His moral history turns to the customs and beliefs of the native peoples. Acosta even framed an early theory of how humans first reached the Americas. The work became the first broad natural history and ethnography of the New World.

Volume two completes Markham's 1880 edition of José de Acosta's Natural and Moral History of the Indies. The Spanish work of 1590, in Grimston's English of 1604, joined two surveys in one: the nature of the Americas and the life of their peoples. Acosta wrote from long residence in Peru and wide reading of reports.

The second volume carries his account of native religion, government, and custom to its close. He treats the peoples of Mexico and Peru as nations with laws, rites, and histories of their own. That respect, rare in his century, gives the book lasting worth. With volume one, it forms the first systematic survey of the New World.
arxiv-2511-20280:
Liu, Zhao, Wen, Dai, and Huang coach video generators to respect real physics. Their 2025 paper refines generated videos through guided self-correction. Modern video models produce gorgeous but physically wrong clips. Objects float, collide wrongly, or melt through each other. Prompt quality strongly steers what models can do.

Their framework loops a vision-language critic over drafts. The critic spots physical inconsistencies in each attempt. A multimodal chain-of-thought turns complaints into better prompts. Regeneration then fixes the flagged errors progressively. No training is needed for the generator itself. The loop plugs into many video models as-is. Tests ran on the PhyIQ physics benchmark. Scores rose from 56.31 to 62.38 overall. That is a gain of about six points. Language models supply the physics-aware guidance throughout. Prompt design emerges as a capability trigger. World-model ambitions need exactly this grounding. The authors frame it as early exploration.
arxiv-2511-20380:
Ibnyahya and Reiss redesign the filters that shape artificial room echo. Their 2025 paper makes attenuation filters for feedback delay networks trainable. Such networks fake the late reflections of real spaces. Each delay line needs a filter taming its decay. Different pitches should fade at different rates.

Graphic equalizer designs stack many filters per line. The new design uses parametric equalizer sections instead. Each section is a second-order filter block. Frequency, gain, and quality factor are its knobs. Those knobs are shared across all delay lines. Only gain adjusts to each line's length. Parameter counts drop sharply as a result. The whole design stays differentiable end to end. Gradient-based training can fit target decay curves directly. Fitting uses supervised learning on smooth targets. Accuracy matches the state of the art reported. Computing cost falls significantly at the same time.
arxiv-2511-21080:
Yeswanth Ravichandran, Duoduo Liao, and Charan Teja Kurakula automate in 2025 the hunt for hidden damage inside concrete bridge decks. The context is stark: about 7.5 percent of America's 617,000 bridges are structurally deficient, with a repair backlog near 125 billion dollars. Their framework uses impact-echo testing, tapping the deck and listening to resonances. Fourier analysis extracts each point's dominant peak frequency, and the values are interpolated into spatial maps of the deck.

Unsupervised k-means clustering flags low-frequency, defect-prone zones, checked against ground-truth masks from laboratory slabs with seeded defects. Ordered peak-frequency sequences from validated zones then feed a stacked LSTM network. It classifies four defect types, shallow and deep delamination, voids, and honeycombing, at 73 percent overall accuracy. Field tests on an in-service deck showed laboratory-trained models generalising despite coupling and noise differences, a step toward network-scale, repeatable bridge monitoring.
arxiv-2511-21180:
Computer scientist Shuhan Xia and five coauthors present CAHS-Attack in 2025, a method for breaking the safeguards of Stable Diffusion, a popular program that turns text prompts into images. Earlier attacks needed the model's internal gradients, meaning its built-in correction signals, or relied on hand-written trick prompts. CAHS-Attack instead works from outside, as a black-box attack, judging tries only by the images that come back.

The search pairs Monte Carlo tree search, a method that explores options through many trial simulations, with a genetic algorithm that breeds the most promising starting prompts. A CLIP-aware score, based on the model's own text encoder, keeps the most disruptive result at each step. In tests on short and long prompts, it beat rival attacks including QF-Attack and PGD. The authors trace the weakness to the CLIP text encoder itself, a risk shared by many image generators.
arxiv-2511-21880:
Bahini and colleagues dissect the fine structure of a giant vibration of the magnesium-24 nucleus, a strongly deformed nucleus. The vibration, the isoscalar giant monopole resonance, is a collective breathing mode whose details reveal how stiff nuclear matter is. In deformed nuclei it mixes with a quadrupole vibration, producing extra structure at lower energies. The team used alpha-particle scattering data from iThemba LABS in South Africa, covering excitation energies from 9 to 25 MeV.

They analysed the data with wavelet transforms, which pick out characteristic energy spacings, against QRPA theory with two Skyrme models. The model with low nuclear incompressibility, 202 MeV, matched the data best across the full range studied. Instead of isolated spacings, they found a continuous range of scales from 200 to 1,000 keV, confirming Landau damping, the spreading into simpler motions, as the main decay route.
arxiv-2512-00080:
The MARWIN robot checks radiation levels inside the long tunnels of the European XFEL accelerator. André Dehne, Juri Zach, and Peer Stelldinger evaluate whether deep visual stereo odometry could guide it, in a 2025 study. The tunnels are long and look nearly the same everywhere, so standard ways of tracking position struggle there.

MARWIN now finds its place with lidar edge detection and wheel and lidar odometry. It also uses periodic QR code checks and fuzzy control of its distance to the wall. The authors weigh a camera-based depth method against that setup. Their work speaks to anyone building robots that must navigate plain, repetitive spaces where landmarks are rare.
arxiv-2512-00480:
Fetching a record from a public database can reveal exactly what you were looking for. Liang Feng Zhang presents a unified framework for information-theoretic private information retrieval in 2025. These protocols let a user retrieve any entry without revealing which entry it was.

Private retrieval protects readers of sensitive material, from medical guidance to legal records, against profiling by servers. A unified construction aims to organize many known protocols under one design logic. Such frameworks help engineers choose protocols with proven privacy rather than ad hoc promises, as these tools move from theory into real services. Information-theoretic privacy means security that holds even against unlimited computing power.
arxiv-2512-00880:
Haijian Shao, Wei Liu, Xing Deng, Qi Liu, and Yingtao Jiang propose a quantum-inspired method for neural operators in a 2025 paper. Multimodal AI on home-grade hardware faces tight limits: mixed data types, real-time demands, and repeated operator blocks that waste capacity. Neural operators are the building blocks that transform data inside such models.

Their framework describes each operator by its singular value spectrum, a fingerprint of how it stretches data, placed on a geometric sphere. That view lets them test when two operators are equivalent and prune ones that repeat work. Leaner models could run better on modest devices.
arxiv-2512-01080:
Benhour Amirian, Ashley Dale, Sergei Kalinin, and Jason Hattrick-Simpers set out what trustworthy AI for materials discovery should mean in a 2025 paper. Artificial intelligence and machine learning now speed up the hunt for new materials, including in autonomous laboratories that run experiments themselves. Speed is worth little if scientists cannot trust the models.

The authors define a framework with named criteria, including whether methods are generalizable, interpretable, fair, transparent, explainable, robust, and stable. They tie evaluation to simple summary scores. A shared trust framework could help labs decide which machine learning claims to build on.
arxiv-2512-01680:
Mihai Prunescu builds arithmetic closed forms for famed prime families. Mersenne primes, Fermat primes, and twin-prime pairs each have long open tales. Sophie Germain primes join the set here. Closed forms that list them are rare objects in number theory.

Prunescu gives forms that generate each family, with repeats allowed. He also gives forms that count each family up to a bound. Counting forms turn existence hunts into sums that can be studied. The work is a formal build, not a proof of how many such primes exist in total. Counting forms double as membership tests, since a prime family count that jumps at a point marks that point as a family member.
arxiv-2512-01880:
Chess engines are built to find the best move, but people rarely play the best move. A 2025 paper by Daren Zhong, Dingcheng Huang, and Clayton Greenberg takes the human side instead, trying to predict which move a person will actually choose, given their skill level.

Their tool is a family of n-gram language models, one trained for each skill group, that learn the patterns in how players at that level continue a game. Because beginners and experts make different kinds of choices, separate models capture habits a single model would blur. The work offers a window into human decision-making, not just machine strength.
arxiv-2512-01980:
Shrinking a neural network by low-rank approximation is like surgery: cutting the model down costs accuracy, and fine-tuning afterward is the rehab that wins it back. Haoran Qin and four co-authors propose in 2025 flipping the order, preparing the network before compression so the cut does less damage.

Methods based on singular value decomposition, including Fisher-weighted and activation-aware variants, have become standard compression tools. The authors' preparation step, nicknamed Prehab, shapes the network in advance so its important structure survives decomposition. If preparation pays off, smaller models could keep more of their skill, easing deployment on limited hardware.
arxiv-2512-02280:
Modern AI perceives, speaks, and reasons impressively, yet it cannot reliably watch itself, catch its own errors, or govern its behavior as conditions change. Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Sindhuja Penchala, and Shahram Rahimi survey in 2025 the gap between today's systems and cognitive autonomy, and what bridging it would take.

Self-monitoring, self-correction, and self-regulation in dynamic settings are the missing capacities the authors emphasize. Perception and language advances alone do not supply them. The paper frames the research agenda for autonomous systems that could be trusted in open environments, where no human can pre-script every response.
arxiv-2512-02680:
Keiichi Maeda and co-authors study an unusual stellar explosion, the supernova called SN Ic 2022esa. Some stripped star explosions show late narrow lines from oxygen rich material around the star. Those lines suggest the blast wave is hitting nearby gas shed before the explosion.

The team reads 2022esa as the death of a massive Wolf-Rayet star in a binary system. Its companion may later explode as well, leaving a pair of black holes. Odd supernovae like this one help trace how massive pairs live, die, and seed the black hole mergers that gravitational wave detectors hear. Each odd burst of this class adds a clue to how pairs of big stars live out their last years.
arxiv-2512-02880:
R. Grau and A. Moralejo mine old MAGIC telescope data to bound the faint glow filling the universe. The extragalactic background light is all light emitted across cosmic history, from ultraviolet to infrared. Stars and dust in galaxies should be its main source.

Gamma rays from distant objects fade as they cross that glow, leaving a measurable imprint. Archival MAGIC observations turn that fading into constraints on the background level. Tighter bounds test models of star formation history and help correct gamma ray spectra for other studies. Old data is free data. A fresh read of it can fence in the glow of all past stars with no new scope time spent.
arxiv-2512-02980:
Elise Bailly-Rioufreyt and a large team generate entangled light from pairs of semiconductor nanowires. Quantum entanglement powers secure communication and enhanced sensing. For decades, polarization entangled photons came mainly from bulk crystals using down conversion, a method that blocks scaling and chip integration.

Orthogonal gallium arsenide nanowires offer a compact alternative source. Their near infrared photon pairs are tunable, the title notes. Chip scale entangled sources would let quantum networks shrink from optical tables into devices, a step toward practical quantum links in cities. Small sources that pair up clean can be set in rows on a chip. Rows of them are what a real net needs to span a town with links.
arxiv-2512-03080:
Language models need a good way to read molecules. Mingxu Zhang, Dazhong Shen, and Ying Sun present a new atom-level tokenizer in this 2025 work. A tokenizer cuts input into small pieces the model can handle, here one atom at a time.

Their tool, AtomDisc, uses molecule graphs that show how atoms connect. Those links shape how atoms act and what a molecule does. The authors say the tool lifts model results and reveals links between structure and traits. Better molecule reading could speed drug and materials research done with AI help. Chemists may value how atom-level pieces keep local bonds clear to the model.
arxiv-2512-03880:
Spongy trabecular bone gets its strength from a delicate internal lattice, and doctors would like to predict that strength from scans. John Rick Manzanares, Richard Leslie Abel, and Paweł Dłotko test a topological approach in a 2025 quantitative biology preprint. Their concern is that such summaries of bone structure should not depend on an arbitrary choice of sideways coordinate frame.

The team built a frame-invariant method. They compared its strength predictions with signed distance persistent homology and conventional shape measurements. The test set held two dozen human bone cores. Prediction errors from those models ran close to or below standard morphometry, though intervals overlapped. Equal-removal experiments found localised removal weakened cores more, despite a smaller change of that kind. Frame invariance, the authors conclude, cleans up the approach, and the component-based scores deserve testing on larger external datasets.
arxiv-2512-04180:
Chains of Majorana fermions, particles that are their own antiparticles, host phase transitions theorists prize as laboratories. Hekai Zhao and Philip W. Phillips analyse a family of interacting Majorana chains in a 2025 preprint. Each shows a tricritical point between an Ising critical phase and a supersymmetric gapped phase. The chains split into even and odd personalities depending on the interaction's range.

Even-range chains develop competing order and resist numerical treatment, while odd-range chains possess a solvable point where entanglement vanishes. The authors introduce a swirling twist. It rewraps each chain into a two-dimensional model of half the width. A helical boundary condition stitches the end of one row to the start of the next. In that picture, the one-dimensional transition becomes a finite-size transition of the two-dimensional system. Finite-size scaling predicts how the critical coupling moves with range.
arxiv-2512-04580:
Huifeng Zhu, Shijie Li, Qinfeng Li, and co-authors introduce CryptoTensors, a file format that keeps large language models secret while they travel and deploy. Firms now tune models on private data from health, law, and finance. Those tuned weights count as personal assets or trade secrets. Yet standard model formats ship weights in the open, with no access control built in. Their 2025 arXiv paper fills that gap with a lightweight secure format.

CryptoTensors wraps model weights with protection designed for sharing and deployment. It avoids the heavy cost of full encryption schemes and the lock-in of private servers. The design also fits trusted hardware, so models can run inside guarded enclaves. Owners gain control over who can load a model and where. As tuned models grow more valuable, such formats help hospitals, banks, and law firms share tools without leaking the crown jewels inside them.
arxiv-2512-04780:
Apurva Seth works out when tensor products of one algebra family keep a stability trait no matter what they pair with. The family is the diagonal AH-algebras, built as limits of matrix-like blocks joined by diagonal maps. They sit at the heart of work sorting C-star algebras. K-stability asks whether an algebra's K-theory behaves well under stabilization. His 2025 arXiv paper studies products of such an algebra with arbitrary partners.

The main result is a clean test: the product stays K-stable for every partner exactly when the block sizes in the building system grow without bound. Uses follow at once. Villadsen algebras of the first kind that lack Z-stability still pass the test when paired with anything. Any simple, unital, endless diagonal AH-algebra meets the growth rule alone. Such results tell which K-theory counts survive pairing, a daily question in the field.
arxiv-2512-05080:
Ian Dunn, Liv Toft, Tyler Katz, and four co-authors present OMTRA, a single generative model for structure-based drug design. Designing a drug molecule that fits a chosen pocket on a protein involves many related jobs. They include inventing new candidates, docking them into the pocket, and searching by shape. Each job usually gets its own tool. The authors argue these jobs share one structure, so one model should be able to perform them all.

OMTRA is built on flow matching, a generative technique, and moves flexibly between the tasks, including some with no counterpart in standard workflows. To train it, the team assembled a vast dataset of molecular shapes alongside protein-ligand data. The system reaches top performance on inventing pocket-fitting molecules and on docking, though the authors note the benefits of huge pretraining and multi-task training are modest. Code, models, and data are released openly.
arxiv-2512-05180:
Zijian Zhang and a very large team of co-authors report two gravitationally lensed Little Red Dots, the puzzling compact objects the Webb telescope has been finding in the early universe. Most vary little over days to years, keeping their nature, probably feeding black holes, unsettled. These two sit behind a galaxy cluster, and one of them, RX1, is imaged four times, with the light paths differing by well over a century.

Comparing the four images is like watching one object at four epochs at once. RX1 changes in colour and brightness between them by a large margin, in a pattern matching temperature swings of a glowing surface. That suggests long-term pulsation, like a Cepheid star's, but from a vastly larger, more massive envelope. The authors propose Little Red Dots are a distinct class of active nucleus wrapped in such an envelope.
arxiv-2512-05280:
Laura Estridge and Joel Franklin introduce the CUBE, a virtual reality immersion built to make electromagnetic fields visible. Fields are abstract and hard to picture. The radiation fields covered in upper-level physics courses are the least familiar of all: students meet them as equations long before they can imagine them. The CUBE puts the student inside the field instead, letting them stand within the patterns that textbooks can only draw.

The note explains the pedagogical thinking behind the software's features: why particular views and interactions were chosen, and what each is meant to make intuitive. It then gives a brief overview of the CUBE in use. As a short introduction rather than a manual, the paper's purpose is to put the tool on record for other instructors. It is a worked example of virtual reality aimed at a specific, stubborn visualization problem in physics teaching.
arxiv-2512-05380:
Xinyue Yin and Sibo Zheng ask whether a future CERN experiment could catch the mediator of a two-step dark matter origin story. In sequential freeze-in, dark matter is produced so feebly that it normally leaves no trace in detectors. Adding a second field changes the picture: a dark photon mediator, produced out of equilibrium, feeds the dark matter, and the mediator might be visible at the proposed SHiP experiment.

Requiring the dark photon to stay out of equilibrium while the final dark matter abundance matches observation pins the model's parameters into a narrow corridor. The authors then compute what SHiP's proton beam would produce through bremsstrahlung over years of running. The projected sensitivity excludes most of the surviving corridor at high confidence, leaving only a sliver, where the mixing is weakest, for other experiments. A nearly invisible scenario becomes, on paper, almost fully testable.
arxiv-2512-05580:
Aurprita Mahmood and five co-authors test whether branching reasoning beats linear reasoning for mathematics in Bengali, a low-resource language. Math word problems demand language understanding and multi-step calculation together; chain-of-thought prompting helps, but its line of reasoning propagates early errors. The authors run a comparison on a set of problems from the SOMADHAN dataset. They evaluate several large language models under plain prompting, chain-of-thought, and tree-of-thoughts, which explores several reasoning branches before committing.

Chain-of-thought lifts accuracy over plain prompting, and tree-of-thoughts adds a gain, reaching the best result with the largest model. The advantage concentrates in medium and large models; small ones benefit less from the branching. The study establishes tree-of-thoughts as a strategy for problem solving in Bengali and, more broadly, evidence that structured reasoning transfers to languages where training resources are thin.
arxiv-2512-05680:
Alexander Mattick and four co-authors address how phones keep a fast wireless link while moving through 5G and 6G networks. Modern antenna arrays form narrow beams, each aimed a different way from a fixed codebook. Picking the best beam, again and again, is tricky when reflections and blockages keep changing the picture. Their 2025 paper frames the search differently, as a game played under partial information.

The codebook itself becomes the world of the game. At each step the method holds a belief about where the unseen best beam is, probes a candidate, and updates the belief. A meta-learning layer of multi-armed bandits learns how to search well across many such games. Because nothing is memorized about fixed paths, the method copes with new routes and changed surroundings. In tests it beat earlier approaches by orders of magnitude, a large margin.
arxiv-2512-05880:
Simon Guiroy, Mats Richter, Sarath Chandar, and Christopher Pal tackle a quiet decision that shapes many applied AI projects. Which checkpoint of a big pretrained vision model should you fine tune for a new task? When target data is scarce and unlabeled, validation collapses. Their selection method needs only a few unlabeled examples from the target task itself. It rests on a new measure called Neural Coherence.

Coherence profiles a model's activation statistics on source and target data. Rankings by coherence pick starting points that go on to generalize better. In experiments with ImageNet pretrained models aimed at food photographs, plant images, and wildlife data, the method improved results over established baselines across the board. The team further shows coherence can select training data, not just models. A model's internal orderliness, read cheaply, predicts its future on unfamiliar ground.
arxiv-2512-05980:
A large international team from the COSINUS collaboration and Duke University reports careful calibration work behind one of dark matter's longest running arguments. Sodium iodide crystals doped with thallium are the detectors of DAMA/LIBRA, the experiment that claims an annually modulating dark matter signal no one else sees. Reading them hinges on the quenching factor: a recoiling nucleus makes less light than an electron of the same energy. The team measured that factor for sodium recoils, varying both recoil energy and the crystal's thallium concentration.

Five ultrapure crystals were exposed to a neutron beam in North Carolina. A dependence on thallium content appeared under one calibration scheme, using an americium source, but vanished under another, using a low energy barium line. Calibration is where discovery claims stand or fall. If the light to energy translation shifts, so does the claim's meaning. Such measurements corner the truth slowly.
arxiv-2512-06080:
Tzofi Klinghoffer and seven co-authors teach lidar to see around corners by listening to light that bounced twice. Ordinary lidar times light reflecting straight back. Two bounce light secretly encodes occluded geometry and mirrors. Earlier work lit one point at a time. This team tackles the practical case: many laser spots lit at once, their bounced contributions tangled together with shadows and specular reflections.

So the method is learned. About one hundred thousand simulated transients trained a light transport prior. From one measurement the system then reconstructs hidden and mirrored geometry. Code and data are public. Robots gain safety by sensing what occlusion hides.
arxiv-2512-06380:
Xiao Zhan, Guangzhi Sun, Jose Such, and Phil Woodland raise a privacy risk in voice assistants: they hear everyone in the room, not just the person talking to them. A bystander's words can be picked up, stored, and later revealed, yet past tests never measured whether a model can listen to one speaker and refuse to spill what another said nearby.

The team builds SH-Bench, a test set of mixed speaker audio, both real and made up, with tens of thousands of questions. A new score weighs both grasp of the main speaker and guarding of the bystander. Top models, open and closed alike, leaked bystander detail freely; strong hearing did not mean safe hearing. The authors then fine tune models to refuse bystander questions, and that training lifted privacy sharply while keeping the main speaker clear. The work sets a bar for voice tools used in shared spaces.
arxiv-2512-06680:
Quentin Ehret opens the study of a hybrid algebraic structure in the trickiest arithmetic setting, where two plus two can equal zero. Poisson superalgebras blend a commutative product with a Lie bracket, graded by a parity that adds signs, and they encode the algebra behind classical and quantum mechanics. In characteristic two, where the sign rules collapse, much of the usual theory must be rebuilt from scratch.

Ehret works through the basics in this setting: how such algebras act on spaces, how two can be joined into a semidirect product, and the cohomology that classifies their deformations. He defines their universal enveloping algebras, the associative homes where they can be computed with. A companion structure, Lie Rinehart superalgebras, turns out to share the same enveloping algebra, a tidy bridge between the two. Worked examples and a first look at pre Poisson superalgebras round out the foundations.
arxiv-2512-06980:
J Allagan, G Morgan, and D Sinclair count ways to split graphs into groups, extending two classic counting sequences into the world of networks. Bell numbers count the ways a set can be divided into blocks, and Stirling numbers refine that count by block number. The authors work out exact formulas for several families: complete multipartite graphs, complete bipartite graphs with a perfect matching removed, and Mycielskian graphs built from trees.

For multipartite graphs they give a simpler proof that the count factors into a product over the parts. Star graphs under the Mycielski construction yield neat closed forms at key values. Computer checks tie these graph counts to known sequences in the standard online encyclopedia of integer sequences, several of them newly identified. The formulas extend from stars to arbitrary trees, giving counters a ready toolkit for these network families.
arxiv-2512-07080:
Madison D Griffin and co-authors read the life stories of Chesapeake Bay oysters out of two decades of shell measurements. Virginia's reefs look age-truncated, with old oysters scarce, a pattern blamed on overfishing, disease outbreaks, habitat decline, and climate change. Yet hints of resilience exist, and a huge state archive of shell lengths, gathered across hundreds of reefs from the early two thousands onward, had never been mined for lifespans.

The team fits mixture models to each reef's yearly shell lengths, teasing apart the overlapping size bands of different age groups. A linking algorithm then follows each band through time, forbidding the impossible step of shells shrinking, to form true cohorts. Only a subset of reefs had data thick enough for the treatment.
arxiv-2512-07180:
Nawshad Ahmed Evan and Md Raihan Uddin deploy decoys inside a working production network and report what happens. A honeypot is a fake resource, built to look valuable, that lures attackers away from real systems; a honeynet strings several decoys into a believable environment. With company services increasingly dependent on the internet, such traps both divert intruders and record their methods for study.

The authors describe setting the honeynet into live network infrastructure, where the decoy must pass as a genuine production resource. Attackers who take the bait can be observed safely while their tools and habits are analyzed, rather than merely blocked at the wall. The demonstration covers how the trap is presented, how intruders are misled inside the simulated environment, and what their behavior reveals.
arxiv-2512-07280:
Hendrik Reiter and a large consortium of co-authors move process mining out of the data center and into the machines where work actually happens. Process mining reconstructs how an organization really operates from event logs, but it traditionally gathers those logs centrally. Industrial internet-of-things systems instead sprawl across edge devices and clouds, with tight limits on energy, bandwidth, and privacy. Their framework, ContinuumConductor, decides step by step where each mining task belongs.

For every stage of the pipeline, from preprocessing through correlation to discovery. The authors weigh decentralizing against centralizing and propose explicit decision criteria, aiming at mining that is private, responsive, and light on resources. The framework is demonstrated on a live use case, optimizing processes in inland ports, where machinery, vehicles, and control systems all generate events at the edge.
arxiv-2512-07680:
P. A. Wigner and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 robotics paper on a crawler for tree canopies. Studying or sampling high branches is hard for people and drones alike. Their machine, AMBER, is built to be dropped in by air and then climb.

The crawler grips branches with tracks lined in compliant microspines. A rotary gripper with two tracks and an elastic tail helps it hold on. Branches of varied curve and tilt are its home terrain. In experiments it keeps its grip through steep rolls and climbs. It moves along horizontal branches at a steady pace. Its tracks can also yaw slightly, adding steering on rough bark. Power use is strikingly low next to a hovering drone's appetite. That thrift suits long sensing and sampling missions in the canopy. Full integration with a delivery drone remains future work. The deployment itself is shown at a feasibility level for now.
arxiv-2512-07780:
Jenny Gonzalez-Jara and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on the faint outskirts of galaxies. A stellar halo is the sparse cloud of old stars around a galaxy's bright body. Its mass and metal content follow a relation astronomers call the MZhR.

The team asks when that relation appears and when each halo settles onto it. They use the CIELO simulations, following central galaxies across most of cosmic time. Halos are traced in an outer shell. A new tool, the halo cardiogram, charts each halo's assembly history. From it they define a stability time for the halo's metal content. Simulated halos already trace the relation in the young universe. The slope matches today's surprisingly early. At fixed halo mass, metals grow steadily as satellites accrete and enrich the halo. One dominant contributor can lock the metal content once it fully disrupts.
arxiv-2512-07980:
Xiaoyang Huang, Zohar Komargodski, Andrew Lucas, and two co-authors wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper. Order usually melts as temperature climbs without limit. Entropy, the champion of disorder, can paradoxically favor order instead.

In some systems, generic high-energy states are the ordered ones. Symmetry then breaks spontaneously at arbitrarily high temperatures. The authors present minimal models where that entropic order appears. Their leading example replaces ordinary Ising spins with non-negative integers. An arithmetic Ising model, plus its quantum analogue, carries the argument. A large-flavor expansion and numerical simulations do the heavy lifting. Both classical and quantum versions order in their hot phase. Classical gas models join the menagerie with the same trick. Their interactions drive the gas into a crystal when heated. Simple ingredients, it turns out, suffice for heat-born order. Thermodynamics textbooks may need a stranger chapter.
arxiv-2512-08580:
Peijun Tang, Shangjin Xie, Binyan Sun, and colleagues, robotics researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their model, Lumo 1, aims at robots that reason before they act, the way people do. Internet scale training gave AI systems broad reasoning, but grounding that reasoning in physical action remains an open problem. Lumo 1 unifies the two in one vision language action model, mind and hand together.

Training proceeds in three stages. The model first studies curated data to strengthen planning and spatial understanding. It then trains jointly on robot data from many body types. Finally it learns actions with explicit reasoning traces on a nimble two armed mobile robot, and reinforcement learning tightens the match between word and deed. In real world tests, Lumo 1 beat strong baselines across many hard tasks, generalizing to new objects and rooms, and excelled at long tasks.
arxiv-2512-08880:
Adrian Parra Rodriguez and coauthors introduce a driven dissipative model that acts as a topological amplifier and converts signal frequency. The system is a single harmonic oscillator whose frequency and decay rate are both modulated in time. That modulation creates a synthetic lattice in frequency space, with an effective electric field gradient across it.

Using Floquet methods and a doubled form for non Hermitian systems, the authors show the linear response carries a local winding number. When that number is nontrivial, amplification proceeds in one direction along the synthetic dimension, shifting input signals to new frequencies. The mode structure matches a continuum theory with Dirac cones and topological zero modes. The design is simple and fits current quantum technology, such as superconducting circuits. The work offers a feasible route to non Hermitian topological amplification without a large physical lattice.
arxiv-2512-09280:
Arthur Ramos and three co-authors present Metatheory, a library for the Lean 4 proof assistant aimed at the foundations of programming languages. Proof assistants check mathematics mechanically, but each new project usually rebuilds basic results from scratch. Two classic goals in language theory are confluence, where different reduction orders reach the same result, and strong normalization, where reductions always end.

The library proves confluence of abstract rewriting systems through three classical techniques: the diamond property, Newman's lemma, and the Hindley-Rosen lemma. Those tools are then applied in six case studies, including the untyped lambda calculus, combinatory logic, term rewriting, and the simply typed lambda calculus with products and sums. The authors also supply the substitution machinery for de Bruijn indices and prove strong normalization by logical relations. Every theorem is fully mechanized, with no axioms or unfinished steps left in the code.
arxiv-2512-09380:
Ishan Swamy and Deobrat Singh ask whether a cosmic string attached to a black hole could give itself away. Cosmic strings are hypothetical defects from the early universe. A string through a rotating black hole drains its spin and changes its mass. For an accreting black hole in an X-ray binary, spin is measured through the innermost stable circular orbit, the closest orbit matter can hold before falling in.

That orbit's position depends on spin and mass, so it moves as the string slows the spin-up. Near maximum spin, small spin changes shift the orbit sharply, ejecting material for prograde motion or dropping it in for retrograde motion. Accretion still spins the hole up more slowly when a string is present, even at high feeding rates. A hole tied to a large string never reaches the transition, and that absence could serve as evidence for the string.
arxiv-2512-09980:
Mattéo Blamart and colleagues ask whether cosmic strings can explain why the early universe holds more bright galaxies than expected. The James Webb Space Telescope found abundant bright galaxies at high redshift, straining galaxy formation models. Cosmic strings are hypothetical line like defects left from a phase transition in the universe's first moments. The team built strings into a semi analytic galaxy formation code, letting them predict the ultraviolet luminosity function, the census of galaxy brightness, across many settings.

With strings included, the predicted abundance rises enough to match the measured luminosity functions from Webb and Hubble. It holds across a wide span of cosmic time, with star formation physics unchanged. The authors map how string effects trade off against standard parameters. They also set a new upper bound on string tension, tighter than limits from the cosmic microwave background, while noting dependence on modeling choices.
arxiv-2512-10180:
Pracheta Harlikar, Abdel-Hameed A. Badawy, and Prasanna Date build a low cost neuromorphic processor on a reconfigurable chip. Neuromorphic hardware mimics brain style spiking computation and promises very low power, real time inference. Progress is slowed by scarce flexible, open platforms for experimentation. Their processor, implemented on a Xilinx Zynq FPGA, supports all to all configurable connectivity between neurons. It uses the leaky integrate and fire neuron model, with tunable threshold, synaptic weights, and refractory period. A serial interface to a host computer allows runtime reconfiguration, with no need to rebuild the hardware design.

The team validated the design on standard benchmarks, the Iris classification task and MNIST digit recognition. Post synthesis results highlight energy efficiency and scalability. The project's significance is accessibility: a research grade spiking platform that is cheap, adaptable, and slated for open source release.
arxiv-2512-10280:
Venkata Tanuja Madireddy presents a graph neural network system for spotting attacks hiding in cloud identity logs. Identity and access management records who did what, with which role, in which session. Attackers moving through a cloud often look statistically normal line by line; the malice is in the pattern across entries. Rule and signature systems miss such novel behavior. Madireddy's framework models the audit trail as a heterogeneous, evolving graph of users, roles, sessions, and actions. A graph network with attention based aggregation learns the latent patterns of normal interaction, and embeddings update continually as the environment changes.

On synthesized and real identity datasets, the system achieved higher detection precision and recall than sequence based and plain graph baselines, while scaling across multi tenant clouds. The targeted threats are the quiet kind: insider misuse, privilege escalation, and lateral movement between accounts.
arxiv-2512-10580:
Albert Benveniste and co-authors fix a rough edge in the modelling of hybrid systems, the kind that switch between discrete modes, each with its own differential-algebraic equations. Languages like Modelica let engineers build such models from first principles and reuse parts. But at a mode change the physics can jump impulsively, and general tools lack a firm mathematical account of how to restart.

Users have often had to smooth the jumps by hand. The authors give hot restarts a precise mathematical meaning and build a combined structural and impulse analysis that generates the restart automatically, impulses included. Their algorithm runs at compile time, and when a mode change is not specified well enough to restart safely, it says so and returns diagnostics explaining the gap to the user. The paper runs to fifty-three pages.
arxiv-2512-10680:
José Halloy and co-authors reframe sustainability as a physics problem before it is a technology problem. Much public debate leans on efficiency and clean gadgets, they argue, while ignoring hard limits set by how energy and matter interact. Earth is closed for materials but open to energy, fed by sunlight that arrives spread thin over the surface.

Inside those limits, a fossil-fuelled industrial system cannot last, and its replacements are hungry for land, materials, and power in their own right. Long-term survival would mean favouring carbon-based chemistry over purified metals, running at low power density, and keeping material throughput low. The authors call for life-compatible technology built on circular biogeochemical processes, and expect a shift toward a degrowth steady state to follow, the two changes reinforcing each other.
arxiv-2512-10980:
Akhmadillo Mamirov studies why large GPU clusters waste so much computing power while training and running AI systems. Real clusters often sit near half use because jobs fragment the available machines and static rules assign work poorly. He reviews these problems and proposes three dynamic schedulers that balance several goals at once.

The schedulers favour urgent work, fill gaps with jobs that fit, and group similar jobs together for better efficiency. In a controlled simulation with many mixed AI jobs, all three beat simple first-come and shortest-job rules on use, speed, fairness, and waiting. The best version sharply cut starvation, where jobs wait far too long. The results offer a practical base for production scheduling.
arxiv-2512-11480:
Weijian Ma, Shizhao Sun, Ruiyu Wang, and Jiang Bian present CADMorph, a system that edits a computer aided design by changing its shape while keeping its construction recipe valid. A CAD model is both a parametric sequence of steps and the geometry that sequence produces. Designers often want a new shape, which forces synchronised edits to the steps, with three demands: keep the structure, keep edits meaningful, and match the target shape.

CADMorph loops through planning, generation, and verification using two pretrained models. Attention maps from a shape predicting diffusion model pinpoint which segments must change. A masked prediction model fills those segments with valid edits. The shape model then embeds each candidate and picks the closest to the target. Both models train without edited example triplets, dodging a data bottleneck. The system beat a top commercial model and specialised baselines.
arxiv-2601-06680:
Tomasz Kania and Jerzy Kakol study amenability constants for Banach algebra sums in 2026. Their subject is Johnson amenability for unconditional direct sums. A family of Banach algebras is summed over an index set.

A Banach sequence lattice on that index set defines the sum's norm. The E-sum collects the algebras with sizes controlled by that lattice. Amenability measures how well an algebra supports averaging and derivations. Constants quantify that amenability rather than merely asserting it exists. For infinite sums, the constants can blow up or stay tame. Their analysis tracks that behavior across unconditional sums of algebras. Functional analysts get precise control over a basic construction. Such sums appear wherever systems combine many independent algebraic parts.
arxiv-2601-07080:
Research by Mohammad Farhat and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with magma ocean waves and thermal variability on lava worlds. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Lava worlds are rocky planets with dayside skins made molten by stellar irradiation. Tidal heating on these shortest-period planets is more than skin deep.

The authors show how orbital eccentricities of just. A few percent (within current observed bounds and maintained secularly by exterior companions) can create deep magma oceans. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07480:
Yi-Long Luo and Jing-Xin Nie prove that mixture gas equations keep a well-defined notion of solution for large data. Their 2026 preprint studies renormalized solutions to Boltzmann systems for mixtures of monatomic and polyatomic gases. The work follows the DiPerna-Lions approach to these kinetic equations. Distribution functions describe each species. For polyatomic species, the function also carries a continuous internal energy variable.

Renormalized solutions made the Boltzmann equation tractable when classical solutions may not exist. Extending that theory to mixtures with internal energy widens its reach. Real gases in engineering and atmospheric science are mixtures, not single species. The Cauchy problem studied here starts from initial data and asks for solutions for all later times. The paper serves analysts working on kinetic theory. It strengthens the foundation under gas mixture simulations.
arxiv-2601-07880:
Gal Engelberg and colleagues benchmark AI agents on basic questions about identity security. Identity Security Posture Management is a core challenge for firms running cloud and software services. Simple visibility questions ask what identities exist and whether their configuration is hygienic. Answering them requires interpreting complex identity data. Agentic AI systems are a growing candidate for that work. Their 2026 preprint introduces a benchmark for this visibility task.

A benchmark gives vendors and buyers a shared yardstick. Without one, claims about agent competence in security operations stay untested. Identity data is messy, spread across many systems with overlapping accounts. The benchmark focuses on visibility, the foundation for any later remediation. Security teams evaluating AI agents are the readers. The paper helps them ask whether an agent truly sees their identity landscape.
arxiv-2601-08080: Ariel Chitan, Sarah Gallagher, and Shahram Abbassi simulate a pair of supermassive black holes over 250 years. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies OJ287, a bright and nearby candidate binary at redshift 0.3. New facilities may soon catch light and gravitational wave signals from such pairs. Long runs are needed to track how accretion drives changes in brightness over time. The simulation follows that slow, accretion-driven variability across two and a half centuries. It gives observers a long baseline for a system often watched for outbursts.
arxiv-2601-08280: Angshul Majumdar argues that greedy selection suffices for finding useful actions in agentic language models. The 2026 arXiv paper notes that modern agent systems face extremely large action spaces. Tool-augmented models may hold thousands of available APIs or retrieval operations. Empirical evidence suggests only a small subset of actions truly moves performance in a given deployment. Sparse action discovery aims to find that subset cheaply. If greedy search finds it, agents could skip costly exploration and run leaner in production settings.
arxiv-2601-08980:
M. Sanchez-Garcia and a large team map star birth in near bright galaxies that shine strong in heat rays. Such galaxies are oft two galaxies in a crash. The team looks at gas cloud scale, near a span of a few score parsecs. They use a set of near bright cases at all crash stages, from lone to late merge.

They track how gas traits link to star birth rate in each cloud zone. Crash stage may bend those links as gas is squeezed and torn. A reader in galaxy work gets a cloud scale view across a full crash path. It can show when a crash helps stars form, and when it starts to tear clouds apart.
arxiv-2601-09080:
Yufei Li, Zeguang Liu, and Kehe Zhu link a deep zero ask in function work to a famed guess in time and rate work. The zero ask is by Hedenmalm. It asks where a class of smooth functions can be forced to be zero, and what that says of the whole class. The guess is the HRT conjecture, a long open claim on shifts of a function in time and rate.

The team shows the two are kin in a direct way. That kin lets them prove yes for the zero ask and for like asks near it. A reader in pure math gets a bridge that pays at once. A hard guess in one field can lend its strength to a deep ask in a next.
arxiv-2601-09380:
Haohao Shi and five co-authors ask how large LED lighting systems should be serviced. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a semi-physical model of how LED installations wear out over time. Two failure modes drive the decay: slow package degradation and sudden driver outages.

What counts as failure here is not a dead lamp but light levels that break set rules across space and time. The authors use a gamma-process model for the gradual decay. Around it they build a simulation-based plan for opportunistic maintenance, fixing parts when crews are already on site. The goal is compliant light at lower service cost.
arxiv-2601-09580:
A. Ballester-Bolinches, R. Esteban-Romero, L. A. Kurdachenko, and V. Pérez-Calabuig continue a study of highly symmetric algebraic structures called braces. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at Dedekind left braces, where every subbrace is an ideal. Braces blend two group operations and link to solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation.

The authors focus on Dedekind braces whose additive group is non-periodic. A prior paper began the classification; this one pushes it further. Knowing when all substructures are ideals reveals how rigid the brace must be. Such rigidity results help organize the growing zoo of brace examples.
arxiv-2601-09780:
T. J. L. C. Bakx and a large team listen for oxygen light from dusty galaxies in the early universe. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports [O III] 88-micron observations of four Herschel-selected dusty star-forming galaxies. The galaxies sit at redshifts 2.9 to 4 and shine with extreme infrared luminosity.

The Atacama Compact Array took the spectra in its Bands 9 and 10. The oxygen line traces hot, ionized gas inside these hidden star factories. Dust blocks their visible light, so far-infrared lines are a prime window. The measurements test how fast such galaxies formed stars when the universe was young.
arxiv-2601-10280:
Antonio Celentano, David Krejčiřík, and Vladimir Lotoreichik tune a bound state in a curved plane. The plane is hyperbolic, where lines bend out. They cut a bounded shape out of it. On the cut edge, a Robin rule ties the value to its slope.

They ask when a bound state sits below the main band. The main band starts at one fourth. With a convex cut shape, such states exist just when the Robin term sits below a set point. That point is at or below zero and rests on the shape. The work sorts when the edge can trap a wave.
arxiv-2601-10380:
Shrigyan Brahmachari, Shuchen Zhu, Iman Marvian, and Yu Tong learn the rule of a quantum rig at the best rate. Each rig is ruled by its Hamiltonian. To know it is key for sensors and chip checks. The best learn rate is named the Heisenberg limit. Past plans hit it with a cost.

Some plans need joint moves on many qubits, which are noise prone. Some need fields that grow as the goal gets fine. The team give a plan with fixed single qubit fields. It hits the top rate with no such growth. That makes it fit for the chips of today.
arxiv-2601-10580:
Wessel Poelman and Miryam de Lhoneux study how we judge language models that work in more than one language. Scores such as perplexity and bits-per-character are easy to use for one language. The authors argue that these scores rest on hidden assumptions once many languages are involved. Their 2026 arXiv preprint looks at what these measures really capture.

The paper asks what form and meaning each score reflects when text is compared across languages. A score that looks fair in one language may treat another language in a skewed way. The authors work through those assumptions one by one. Readers who build or test multilingual models get a clear warning about what the common scores can and cannot show.
arxiv-2601-10780:
Nursultan Daupayev, Christian Engel, Ricky Bendyk, and Sören Hirsch design an adaptive algorithm for environmental microsensors. Steady sensing matters for jobs like anomaly detection in building structures. But collecting data at a fixed rate wastes energy and piles up redundant readings. Deleting data to save space costs quality instead.

Their algorithm adapts how the sensor samples, so it gathers more when conditions change and less when they are flat. Smarter timing cuts energy use and storage load at the source. The work targets long-lived sensor networks that must run for years on small batteries. It shows how a little on-device judgment can stretch both power and data value.
arxiv-2601-11080:
Stephan G. Heinemann, Jens Pomoell, and Manuela Temmer analyze the magnetic shape of observed coronal holes. Coronal holes are dark patches where the Sun's field opens into space and the solar wind escapes. Potential Field Source Surface models map that field and feed solar wind forecasts. Yet the models often fail to match the holes actually observed.

The team studies 702 coronal holes seen between 2010 and 2019. They compute matching field extrapolations and compare topology and loop statistics with quiet Sun regions. Where model and data part ways, forecasters learn their error bars. Better coronal maps mean better warnings for the space weather that can disturb satellites and power grids.
arxiv-2601-11380:
B. Sicardy and L. Dettwiller study central flashes in stellar occultations. Their 2026 preprint works out what shapes those flashes. An occultation is when a solar system body blocks a star. At the center of the shadow, light can flash bright.

The flash comes from air around the body bending starlight. The team catalogs diffraction effects on that flash. They treat stars as points and light as monochromatic waves. Cases cover clear spherical air shells of unlike forms. They also add corrections for stars with real size. A star's disk blurs the flash in set ways. The catalog helps read real flashes from moons and planets.
arxiv-2601-11480:
Riya Baruah and four coauthors probe heat and work in a quantum resonator. Their 2026 preprint deals with a driven resonator system. A heat engine needs a working fluid to turn heat into work. At the nanoscale, that fluid can be a quantum system.

Quantum behavior there is non-classical in key ways. A quantum resonator is a flexible such working fluid. It allows precise control of the system's state. It also couples cleanly to thermal reservoirs on both sides. Fluctuations of heat and work are the focus here. At small scales, those fluctuations can rival the means. The study maps them for driven resonator engines.
arxiv-2601-11780: Members of the ATLAS team report a test of top quark pair output near its birth threshold. They use proton-proton crashes at 13 TeV at the Large Hadron Collider. They look at end states with two charged leptons and many jets, near a pair mass of about 345 GeV. Near the threshold, the pair can act in ways that boost the count. The title reports a rise in the rate near that point. Such a rise tests how quarks bind for a brief time.
arxiv-2601-11880:
Yingxiao Zhang, Jiaxin Duan, Junfu Zhang, and Ke Feng make fake treasury futures data with a diffusion transformer. Such models have done well at fake stock and order flow data. Their skill on treasury futures was less clear.

Treasury futures data have low volume, links to the wider market, and grouped links among their fields. The team's model, named TF-CoDiT in the work, is built for a set state or class. Good fake data can aid tests of trade and risk tools. It can stand in where real data are scarce or private.
arxiv-2601-11980:
A team of physicists gauge neutrons made by cosmic rays in large liquid scintillator detectors. Muons from cosmic rays make neutrons as they pass through matter. Those neutrons form a key background for rare event hunts, such as dark matter and double beta decay searches.

They match real neutron yields and counts to sims. The sims use the GEANT4 toolkit with three sets of physics rules. Data from the Daya Bay reactor neutrino work anchor the tests. Sound background models help rare event hunks set true limits.  The yield checks span more than one detector data set.
arxiv-2601-12580:
Sofiya Zaichyk presents a formal framework for coordination among many AI agents with no central boss. The framework is called Semantic Fusion. Agents work over scoped views of a shared memory. Each agent can propose structured updates to that memory. Global coherence must hold even though control is spread out.

The framework keeps coherence through local checks and refresh steps. Checks use a shared ontology, a formal map of concepts and relations. There is no centralized control and no explicit message passing. That design aims for systems that scale without a single point of failure. It speaks to distributed algorithms, temporal logic, and probabilistic computation at once.
arxiv-2601-12680:
Zheng Fang and six co authors work on teaching language models to use tools well. Tool learning lets a model pick and combine external tools for complex real world tasks. With tools, a model goes beyond pure language and can act in specialized ways. The challenge is to make that skill generalize to new tools and tasks.

Their system is called MetaToolAgent, built on meta learning. Meta learning trains a model to adapt fast to fresh problems. Applied to tools, it should let a model learn new tools from few examples. Generalizable tool use is a key step toward agents that work in open settings. The work speaks to the fast growing agent research community.
arxiv-2601-13180:
Shreesha Rao D. S and co-authors take rare lab marks of a special glass fibre. The fibre is made of ZBLAN glass with a small oval core. It keeps the lean of light waves fixed as they pass. Such fibres draw work for light work in the mid infrared band.

Two marks are key to model fast pulse flow in them. One is group birefringence, the split in speed by wave lean. The other is group velocity dispersion, how pulse speed shifts with hue. Lab data for both marks were scarce. The team fills that gap. Their marks help staff who build supercontinuum sources and fast fibre lasers in that band plan with real numbers, not guesses.
arxiv-2601-13380:
Chaoxin Wang and co-authors give hands on guides to semi supervised object detection. The task trains a detector with few marked pics and many unmarked ones. That mix fits fields where marks cost a lot, such as scans or field pics.

Past work in the area grew fast, with many tricks that are hard to sort. The team shares what works in real use and where gains are thin. They weigh how pseudo marks for the unmarked set are made and kept clean. For vision teams with thin mark funds, sound guides can save weeks of blind tests. The piece is a field note set, not a new model claim.
arxiv-2601-13480:
Matthias Y. He and Eric B. Ford build one model to match two marks in the Kepler planet census. Kepler showed that planet sizes split in two crowds. A gap, called the radius valley, parts super Earths from sub Neptunes. Kepler also showed that worlds in one system tend to match in size, a peas in a pod mark.

A good growth model must yield both marks at once. Their model is a hybrid. It joins clumped multi planet forms with orbits set by a stability bound based on angular momentum deficit. By match of both marks, the model ties size growth to orbit calm in one tale.
arxiv-2601-13580:
Ahmad Al-Zuraiqi moves trained transformer layers as organs from one model to a next. His frame is called Neural Organ Transplantation. In stock fine tune, taught weights are tied tight to one model and its train data. They cannot be reused with ease in a next model.

His swap cuts a run of layers from a taught model as a donor organ. That run is taught on its own on field data. It is saved as a lone checkpoint file. It can then be set in a fit host model, with no need for the first train data. For teams that adapt models per field, reusable layer organs cut cost and time.
arxiv-2601-13780:
Antoine Siraudin and Christopher Morris build a faster way to generate new graphs with AI in 2026. Graph diffusion models make state-of-the-art graphs, from molecules to social nets. Their cost grows with the square of the node count. Much of that cost is spent modeling edges that are not there, in sparse graphs.

The pair compress graphs into a low-dimensional latent space first. Diffusion then runs in that small space, not on the full graph. Laplacian autoencoders do the compression and rebuild steps. Latent diffusion has cut costs in images, and may do the same for graphs.
arxiv-2601-13980:
Rishin Madan and co-authors study the geometry of flux surfaces with quasi-poloidal symmetry in 2026. Such magnetic fields aim to confine plasma in fusion devices. Quasi-poloidal fields bring prized traits: no radial drift of guiding centres, and zero Pfirsch-Schlüter current. They also damp poloidal flows less, which can cut anomalous transport.

Lower transport means heat stays in the plasma longer. Possible stability benefits add to the draw of this symmetry. The team examines the shape of the flux surfaces that carry it. Sound geometry is a base step toward stellarators with this design.
arxiv-2601-14180:
Yichao Liu, Zongru Shao, Yueyang Teng, and Junwen Guo denoise low-dose CT scans without paired clean data in 2026. Self-supervised learning has been increasingly investigated for low-dose CT denoising. Paired normal-dose data are often difficult to collect for training. Many blind-spot methods suffer training inefficiencies and suboptimal performance.

Restricted receptive fields limit what those methods can see in a scan. Their progressive J-invariant self-supervised learning targets those flaws. J-invariance keeps the model from cheating by peeking at the pixel it predicts. Cleaner low-dose scans could cut radiation exposure for patients.
arxiv-2601-14480:
Egemen Erbayat and five co-authors set shared ground rules for network design in this 2026 paper. Mobile networks are moving toward 5G and 6G architectures. Passive optical networks offer a critical solution for cost-effective fronthaul transport, the links that carry data from antennas inward. Many optimization strategies compete in this space.

The literature lacks standardized evaluation models, so objective comparison of those strategies is hard. The team proposes a unified benchmarking framework. It standardizes cost catalogs and deployment scenarios for PON-based fronthaul design. Readers get a common yardstick, so future design claims can be checked against the same facts.
arxiv-2601-15080:
Ka Kit Kelvin Ho, Vladislav Yu. Shishkov, and a large team report cooling a quantum fluid with light-like control. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a Bose-Einstein condensate of exciton-polaritons. These hybrid light-matter particles form the condensate far from equilibrium.

The team observes stimulated cooling of that condensate. It falls from near room temperature all the way down to about 20 kelvin in the test. They map the condensate in energy and momentum space. Careful interferometric tests then set the true condensate apart from the hot particles that sit in excited states.
arxiv-2601-15180:
Pedro Ângelo, Atsushi Igarashi, Yuito Murase, and Vasco T. Vasconcelos add staged code generation to a language for message passing. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with session types, which state the shape of a conversation between programs. Metaprogramming lets a program write code in stages.

The authors build on contextual modal type theory with multi-level contexts. Contextual values can close a term over a set of variables. Those values can be boxed and sent inside messages. The work shows how staged generation and session-typed messaging can live side by side in one language.
arxiv-2601-15280:
Chloe Qianhui Zhao, Jie Cao, Jionghao Lin, and Kenneth R. Koedinger let an AI tutor give feedback and compare it with a teacher's. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with feedback that is timely, targeted, and multimodal. Such feedback helps students fix errors fast and stay motivated.

Making that feedback at scale is the hard part. The authors build a real-time AI system for it. It joins written explanations with media: the most apt slide page, plus streaming AI audio narration. Their title reports the outcome: learning matched educator feedback, and student perceptions were better.
arxiv-2601-15380:
Elon Litman and Gabe Guo rethink the attention step inside transformer models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with how attention weighs the parts of an input. Seen through entropic optimal transport, standard attention solves a transport problem with a hidden assumption.

That assumption is an implicit uniform prior. The authors replace it with a learnable, continuous prior. Their mechanism is called Goat, short for a generalized optimal transport attention with trainable priors. It aims to encode each patch's context better. The design promises attention that adapts to the data instead of treating all routes alike.
arxiv-2601-15680:
M. P. Thejitha, James A. Sellers, and S. N. Fathima count colored partitions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their counting function tracks multicolored partitions of a number. Even parts and odd parts get different color allowances. Even parts may appear in one of r colors. Odd parts may appear in one of s colors. Both r and s are fixed, at least one each.

Parity restrictions drive the paper, per its title. Splitting parts by even and odd is a classic move in partition theory. Adding colors multiplies the structures to count. Such problems often yield generating functions with elegant forms. They also connect to q-series and modular forms. The authors work in that tradition, asking what arithmetic traits the counts display.
arxiv-2601-15780:
Pascal Benschop, Justin Dauwels, and Jan van Gemert test vision-language models on synthetic video in a 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial reasoning in these models stays fragile. It breaks when meaning hinges on subtle timing or geometry. The authors build a synthetic benchmark to probe two skills. One is situational awareness: telling a harmful interaction from a benign one. The other is spatial awareness: tracking who does what to whom.

Relative positions and motion also fall under the second skill. Synthetic video gives full control over those cues. Each factor can be varied while others stay fixed. That control exposes exactly where models fail. Real video cannot isolate causes so cleanly. For safety uses like monitoring, knowing a model's blind spots is essential.
arxiv-2601-15880:
Dennis Dobler, Alina Schenk, and Matthias Schmid build a regression method for comparing treatments in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their effect measure is the relative treatment effect. It compares outcome variables from two samples. It reads as a probability: how likely one sample's outcome beats the other's. It also links to the area under the ROC curve. The measure has been used for ordinal outcomes and for censored time-to-event data.

Their approach uses pseudo-observations in a two-sample regression. Pseudo-observations let standard regression tools handle the effect. That makes adjusting for covariates more straightforward. Clinicians like probability-scale effects because they are easy to explain. A method that puts such effects into regression form widens their use in trials and studies.
arxiv-2601-15980:
Martina Formichetti and four co-authors infer wall roughness from sparse data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Surface roughness shapes turbulent boundary layers. It acts mainly through the roughness function and the equivalent sand-grain height. Finding that height directly needs detailed velocity and wall-shear data. Such measurements are often impractical in real facilities. Roughness therefore often goes unmeasured where it matters.

The authors build a data-driven framework for the inference. Sparse experimental data go in; rough wall properties come out. The title calls the process assimilating rough features. Wind tunnels, pipelines, and aircraft surfaces all live with roughness effects. A tool that reads roughness from little data helps engineers predict drag and heat transfer without costly full surveys.
arxiv-2601-16680:
Zhenduo Wen and Amin Gohari study how to pack data with a kind of care. A pack tool is stable if small tweaks stay small. Change a few marks in the source, and the code should shift just a bit. Their 2026 preprint sets out this trait and tests known tools. A famed tool, random binning, fails the test flat.

In random binning, near twins can land in far bins. That leap breaks the care trait at once. The authors build the base math for stable packs. Such packs could guard streams where inputs shift by bits. They may also help codes that must shrug off small noise.
arxiv-2601-16880:
Bethan Evans and Jared Tanner work out the least nudge that flips a deep net's call. Small weight shifts can tilt a call in a set aim. Their 2026 preprint finds exact forms for that least shift. One-layer forms fall out in full. The team names what sets the shift's size.

They then set those forms next to broad multi-layer bounds. The two gauges land of the same rough size. That match says the broad bounds lose little truth. The work also feeds low-rank backdoor attack work. Such attacks flip calls with faint, cheap nudges. Sharp least-nudge math helps guard nets from such tricks.
arxiv-2601-17180:
Inés Gonzalez-Pepe and a team of four co-authors speed brain scan nets by use of junk marks. Scan nets grow vast, and their cost stays a pain. Much of their work runs on noise-drowned marks. Those marks sway the net's calls by next to nil. Their 2026 preprint sorts such marks in two grades. Safe junk can be skipped with no loss.

Bold junk skips trade a hair of truth for speed. The tool in view is the U-Net, a scan workhorse. Fast scans aid wards with long wait lists. Lean nets also cut the power bill of AI care.
arxiv-2601-17280:
David Condrey tests a claimed way to spot AI-written text. The claim rests on keystroke timing. A score from gaps between key presses is said to split human typing from AI text. Condrey shows that defense can be fooled in two plain ways. In one attack, a person just retypes AI text by hand.

That copy-type attack gives the timing signal a human shape. A second attack class forges timing in a like way. If both work, timing alone cannot prove who wrote a text. The study warns schools and firms not to trust such checks. False claims of AI use can harm real people, so proof must be strong.
arxiv-2601-17380:
Detelina Kamburova gives new tests for when a space is Hausdorff. Hausdorff spaces keep points apart with disjoint open sets. The paper works with first countable T1 spaces, a broad and common class. Kamburova defines two forms of contractive orbit for set-valued maps. One form uses the space's own topology. The other uses a generalized distance.

She ties those orbits to fixed point theorems. Fixed points are where a map sends a point to itself. Such theorems drive proofs across analysis and topology. New characterizations give topologists fresh ways to check a key trait. They also link separation traits to map behavior. That link can shorten proofs that now take long detours.
arxiv-2601-17480:
Marton Szep and five co-authors study a privacy leak in fine-tuned language models. Fine-tuning on sensitive data can make models memorize it. Names and other personal facts can then leak out. The team looks at a less studied path. They test facts that appear only in model inputs, not in the target outputs.

Input-only facts are easy to overlook in safety checks. If models store them, chat logs and forms are at risk. The study maps how bad that exposure can be. Its lessons guide data handling for health and legal tools. Teams learn what to strip before training starts. Privacy law sets a high bar here, and leaks can breach it.
arxiv-2601-17580:
Joshua Viszlai and four co-authors present PropHunt, a tool to optimize quantum syndrome measurement circuits. Fault-tolerant quantum computing rests on error correction codes. Codes run parity checks on data qubits again and again. Those checks are syndrome measurement circuits. Their design sets the code's logical error rate. Small design flaws cost dearly at scale.

PropHunt automates the search for better circuits. Hand design cannot scan the full space of layouts. Automated optimization can find leaner, safer checks. Each saved gate cuts noise in the full machine. The work targets a bottleneck in quantum scale-up. Better syndrome circuits bring useful quantum machines closer.
arxiv-2601-17680:
Shota Takashiro and four co-authors generalize Mixture of Experts to infinitely many experts. Standard MoE picks a few feed-forward networks per token. That gives a good trade of cost and quality. In standard designs, each expert stands alone. Experts combine in a discrete space. As expert counts grow, training each one well gets hard.

Their infinite form rethinks that structure. A continuous view of experts could scale more smoothly. Language models lean on MoE for cheap capacity growth. A better expert frame could cut training waste. The work asks what experts should be at the limit. It may reshape how large sparse models are built.
arxiv-2601-17780:
Andrea Medini works on a question in set theory about special kinds of filters. His 2026 preprint deals with P-filters that are non-meager, terms from the study of sets and size. Filters are rules for calling some sets large. The work also touches Miller measurability, a property tied to a classic forcing notion. A question posed by Hrušák frames part of the study.

The main result links a group of filters to a bound on a cardinal number. If a product of such filters has a strong sameness property, then the count of filters stays below a known cardinal. Each filter in the group must also be of the non-meager P kind. Results of this sort help map how set-theoretic claims hang together.
arxiv-2601-17880:
Muhammad Umar Salman, Mohammad Areeb Qazi, and Mohammed Talha Alam present Quran-MD, a data set of the Qur'an built for language and speech research. Their 2026 preprint describes the set at a fine grain. Each verse comes with its Arabic text, an English translation, and a phonetic rendering. The set also adds audio and language detail at both verse and word level.

Such layers let one resource serve many kinds of study. Text models, speech tools, and language teaching aids can all draw on it. Word-level links help where exact form matters, as it does in sacred text. The authors frame the set as broad and fine-grained at once. It fills a gap for multilingual, multimodal work on this text.
arxiv-2601-18580:
Vincenzo De Paola and three colleagues give a fresh twist to the way smart agents learn by trial. In the plain way, many twin agents run the same task to feed one learner fast. All twins act in the same style, so the learner sees a thin range of tries. That thin range can trap the learner in a poor style of play.

Their plan, named K-Myriad, runs a crowd of agents that are not twins. Each agent tries the task in its own style, with no training at that stage. The mix of styles gives the learner a wide first view of the task. A wide start could help the learner find strong styles that a thin start would miss. The trick may serve games, robots, and any task where the first tries shape all that comes next.
arxiv-2601-18680:
Marine Demarty and three colleagues build a fair test for when a noisy quantum tool could beat a plain one at a hard search. Such a win is the prize of the field, but it is hard to claim with care. A test must weigh the task, the way the tool is built, and the noise in the kit, all at once. One past test does weigh all three, and it gives a sharp read on where a win could lie.

Noise can be cut by tricks, but the tricks shift the test. The team fold the cost of those tricks into the test from the start. That way a claim of a win must clear the bar with its fix costs paid. A fair bar helps labs pick tasks where a real win is in reach. A fair bar also stops hype.
arxiv-2601-19280:
Kishan Panaganti and five co-authors train language models to reason well on every group, not just on average. Group distributionally robust optimization guards the worst off group in the data, rather than the mean case. The team drives reinforcement learning for reasoning with that guard in place.

Post training gains in reasoning often come from tweaking loss functions and alignment choices. A worst group lens asks whether those gains hold for the hardest slice of problems. Reasoning that stays strong on its weakest ground is the kind users can rely on when a hard query lands.
arxiv-2601-19580:
Cuong Le and five colleagues build vision systems that recover human motion in three dimensions. Filming a person and rebuilding their pose over time is a core task in computer vision.
