A solemn warning to Germany is the subject of Grew's cable of February 6, 1945. The French Embassy had presented a formal note in Washington on February 3. France intended to warn the German government against maltreatment of, or reprisals against, French prisoners of war and deportees. Such acts would violate international law.

The French believed the warning would carry more weight, and might save thousands of lives, if issued by the United Nations as a whole. Paris sought clarification on one point: would the warning cover all United Nations nationals, not only French ones? Grew sent the matter on in case it rose at the conference. Left there, he would take it up in Washington.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d80:
Harriman was told to carry the President's words to Stalin in person. Secretary of State Stettinius sent the instruction on 5 December 1944, marked for the ambassador's urgent and personal attention. The cable, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, opens the final push to settle Security Council voting.

Roosevelt's message says the Big Three meeting is still unsettled, so the voting question cannot wait. Agreement on it must come before a general United Nations conference can be called. Harriman is to discuss the matter with Stalin on the President's behalf, and the same approach is being made to Churchill. The cable then quotes the draft voting provision itself, beginning with one vote for each Council member.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d180:
Under Secretary Grew forwarded the revised British agenda to the President in a memorandum dated July 3, 1945. The short covering memo is document 180 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It follows the trail of the original British list, sent May 30, and the Department's comments of June 14.

The British Embassy has now handed over a revised list of suggested topics, with comments, drawn up in a form fit to be shown to the Soviet government. Many problems on the first list have since been solved, as the Department expected. The new list runs mostly parallel to the Department's own draft agenda. The principal difference, Grew notes, is that it contains no topic on the Far East, an omission the Department pointed out to the embassy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d280:
Ambassador Kirk reported a standstill over the British move into Styria in a telegram from Caserta on July 3, 1945. The message is document 280 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Allied headquarters had directed the British Eighth Army to arrange with the local Soviet commander for a withdrawal from southern Austria.

On July 1 the British Fifth Corps commander met the Russians at Soviet Fourth Army headquarters and delivered the Eighth Army's letter. The Soviet commander said he had received no orders to withdraw and would hold his position until he did. A written reply the next day was cordial: the letter would go promptly to Marshal Koniev, but Soviet forces in Styria could not move without his orders. The episode mirrors the delays the Americans met over Berlin and Austria alike.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d380:
American and British reparations men met at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945, and a delegation memorandum records the session. Sir Walter Monckton led the British group; Pauley, Clayton, and others spoke for the United States. Clayton read the American paper's sections on war booty, labor services, restitution, and territorial cessions.

On war booty the British agreed in principle, but counseled against pressing the point. An agreed definition, they argued, would bind the West while not restricting the Russians. Pauley disagreed, saying the negotiations would drag on without end unless agreement was reached. The memo captures allied tactics, not just allied aims, on the eve of Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d480:
British second thoughts on Allied Force Headquarters come in a memorandum by the British Chiefs of Staff representatives dated July 12, 1945. London has given further thought, it reports, to the dissolution of the headquarters and the organization that would follow it. The supreme commander, Mediterranean, and the commanders-in-chief, Middle East, have sent in their comments on the original proposals.

When those comments are considered, the British chiefs will put forward further draft proposals for the American chiefs. Meanwhile they agree to dispatching the message enclosed with the American paper, with one amendment. A substituted paragraph promises that the Combined Chiefs will send direction for the headquarters' future following the Terminal conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d580:
Japan's foreign minister, Shigenori Togo, wired his ambassador in Moscow, Naotake Sato, on July 11, 1945. The very secret cable, read here in translation, is document 580 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. U.S. officials held a copy within days of its sending.

Togo says Japan's state at home and abroad is very grave. Even ending the war, he admits, is now weighed in private. Tokyo's talks with Moscow aim not just at closer ties, but at sounding out Soviet help to end the war. He hints Japan could give up fishing rights won in 1905 to please the Soviets. He orders Sato to see Molotov at once and learn Soviet thinking. Yet Sato must not let Moscow sense that Japan hopes to use it to end the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d680:
A top secret briefing paper on the Montreux Convention was dated June 27, 1945. It is document 680 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The 1936 pact set the rules for warships and trade ships passing the Turkish Straits.

The paper notes that Moscow aired its discontent at Yalta without stating its wishes. The Big Three agreed Russia would present them later for talks among foreign ministers. Washington has since told London it stands ready to discuss the Straits at the heads-of-government meeting. The paper remarks on an oddity in that stance. The United States never signed the Montreux Convention, yet Britain and Russia have drawn it fully into the question. Turkey, the state most affected, has not been consulted at all. U.S. interests are named as free commerce and a Straits regime that best promotes peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d80:
General John Deane, head of the U.S. military mission in Moscow, reported a Soviet refusal to Eisenhower on June 20, 1945. His urgent telegram is document 80 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The Americans wanted General Parks's survey party admitted to Berlin at once; Soviet General Antonov would not move the date.

Antonov told Deane the question was being decided between the two governments, and he could not change his earlier decision to hold the survey until Zhukov returned around June 28 or 29. Deane notes that Harriman had raised the matter with the Foreign Office twice already, on June 15 and again the night before. They would keep trying. The exchange is an early taste of the slow Soviet bargaining style that marked the conference itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1080:
Foy Kohler, an assistant chief of Near Eastern affairs, recorded this conversation in Washington on July 25, 1945. The Greek ambassador had called to read a telegram from Athens. It quotes a Yugoslav note of July 23 demanding an end to terror against people of Yugoslav origin in Aegean Macedonia. Property was to be restored and reparations paid.

Athens calls the note a planned blow at Greek security and refuses to answer it. Greece has never recognized a Yugoslav minority, the telegram insists, and foreign meddling cannot be admitted. The refugees in Yugoslavia are branded collaborators or fugitive ELAS men. Greece will take no action, the ambassador adds, until it hears the American and British views.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1180:
The Secretary of State wrote to the President on 30 June 1945, more than two weeks before Potsdam opened. Papers from the run-up set the agenda and framed the choices Truman would face in Germany. The war in Europe had been over for less than two months.

Pre-summit messages did quiet, vital work. They sorted the questions, marked the hard ones, and lined up the facts the president would need. This letter belongs to that groundwork. It shows the peace being planned while the guns in Europe were barely cold. The summit's story starts here, not at the opening gavel.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1280:
General Deane, who commanded the United States Military Mission to the Soviet Union, wrote this memorandum on 24 July 1945. Deane's mission in Moscow was the American army's post inside the Soviet capital. He dealt with Soviet officers daily and knew their ways at first hand.

His memoranda carried that hard-won knowledge to the summit's staff. Few Americans had watched Soviet conduct as closely, or with as much friction, as Deane. A paper from his hand gave the team the Moscow mission's view. It is the soldier-envoy's voice in the record, blunt from experience.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1380:
W. Averell Brown, a special assistant to the secretary of state, wrote to both President Truman and Secretary Byrnes on 2 August 1945. That was the day the Potsdam Conference issued its closing papers. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A paper addressed to the president and the secretary together sits high in the pile. Brown wrote as the talks ended, when the results had to be summed up and carried home. Readers can place his memorandum at the hinge between the conference and what followed. First came the return to Washington and the reports to Congress and the press. Then came the hard work of making the Potsdam choices stick, in a world still at war with Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-80:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the plenary session of July 23, 1945, compress the day's foreign ministers' report into a page. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov read the report aloud, and Cohen tracked its points in order.

The economic subcommittee was told to study the Soviet reparations plans. On German economic principles, Russia withdrew her amendment to paragraph 13. She asked instead that paragraph 18 be deleted for further study by the Control Council, and no agreement was reached. The Council of Foreign Ministers proposal was approved with wording changes. On trusteeships, the Italian colonies' disposition was assigned to that council. Tangier produced a clean decision amid the disputes. It would return to its international status, with a four-power conference, France included, to meet in the near future.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d780:
Erhardt reported again on Austrian affairs on July 23, 1945, in document 780. The political adviser wrote to the Acting Secretary of State from his post among the occupiers. Austria's zones and its future government were live questions. His report joined the second Potsdam volume.

Follow-up reports show a problem refusing to sit still. Erhardt updated Washington as facts on the ground changed. Readers see occupation politics at working level: parties, officers, and rumors. The document adds ground truth to the summit's air. It reminds us that Potsdam's lines on maps had to be walked by men like Erhardt.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d880:
Willard Thorp, deputy to the Assistant Secretary of State for economic affairs, cabled William Clayton at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. Thorp reports a Washington meeting with British officials on German supply problems. The talks backed a zonal approach to buying and financing imports for occupied Germany.

Thorp quotes the British telegram that reported the American plan. Zone needs would be coordinated through CRAB, a joint supply body, using shared standards for food and industry. Shortfalls in one zone would be met from surpluses in others where possible. Import programs would go to the Combined Boards together, with equal priority for each zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d980:
Edwin Pauley and Isador Lubin sent this report on German reparations to the President on September 20, 1945. The printed text is an extract. It reviews their work from February to September 1945. Part V, shown here, covers the tripartite conference at Berlin, from July 16 to August 2.

Pauley reached Berlin from Moscow on July 14 with his senior staff. Talks with William Clayton's team shaped how to lay the reparations problem before the Big Three. The American proposals went into an annex on reparations. It held the seven agreed principles, the disputed first charge clause, and the agreed division of shares. It also offered definitions of restitution, war booty, and reparations.
gaius-institutes-muirhead-1880:
James Muirhead published his translation of The Institutes of Gaius in 1880. Gaius, a Roman law teacher, wrote the Institutes around 160 CE as a textbook for students. The text was lost for centuries and recovered in 1816 from a scraped parchment in Verona.

Gaius sorted all law under persons, things, and actions, a scheme that law teaching used for a thousand years. His plain style and clear order made Roman law learnable, and Justinian's own Institutes copied his plan. Muirhead, a Scottish professor of law, added notes for English students. The translation gives modern readers the Roman law school's own starting point, in the form that taught lawyers for a millennium.
gao-gaoreports-b-295780: AVL Books.Com shelved a March 2005 protest at GAO, and the ruling writes the last chapter. The bookseller's claims were read cover to cover. The story ended at the gavel. The final chapter closed. The gavel came down. The book was closed.
gao-gaoreports-b-297280: Alluviam took its December 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299880: Kemron Environmental Services took its 2007 cleanup-contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The firm said the agency's award was flawed; the call tests the claims against bid law. For the firms that scrub the nation's toxic messes, the ruling shows how GAO judges the contest for dirty work.
gao-gaoreports-b-310780: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Federal Vacancies Reform Act of 1998 - Assistant Attorney General for the Office of Legal Counsel, US Department of Justice. The June 13, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests.
gao-gaoreports-b-310980: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Fedcar Company, Ltd. Decided March 25, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-380: Shielding buildings from wildfire got a GAO tech look in 2005, and the assessment covers structures and fire communications. The review tests the firefighting toolkit. The towns in the path deserved the science. The assessment was delivered. The towns in the path deserved the science.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-480: Defense tech transition needed stronger management in 2005, and GAO's report says the process for new programs required strengthening. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the war gadgets deserved doing right. The process had to be strengthened. The war gadgets deserved doing right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-380: WIC infant formula costs needed containing in 2006, and GAO's report says the food agency could take more steps to hold down prices. The findings target the spending. The report warns that the babies' formula dollars deserved guarding. The costs had to be contained.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-580: Customs' trade computer was progressing in 2006, and GAO's report says progress had been made on the automated system, though long-standing issues remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the border's digital gate needed finishing. The system had to work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-780: The EPA's soot science was starting to move in 2006, and GAO's report says the agency had begun addressing the Academies' recommendations on health benefits. The findings track the start. The report warns that the particle math mattered for lungs. The work had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-80: Older workers needed better planning help in 2006, and GAO's report says Labor could help employers and employees plan for the future. The findings prescribe the aid. The report warns that the gray workforce deserved guidance. The planning had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-880: Medicare's hospital payment plan looked promising in 2006, and GAO's report says the proposed approach to inpatient payments appeared sound. The findings give the early nod. The report cautions that the new math still needed watching. The promise had to be proven.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-980: The Pentagon's travel booking system was a mess in 2006, and GAO's report says the claimed savings were doubtful and challenges remained. The findings doubt the math. The report warns that the troops' travel should not be a travel nightmare. The system had to work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-280: Nursing-home asset games were rarer than feared in 2007 — GAO's report says few people shed assets before applying for long-term care. The findings calm the panic with data. The report's take: the loophole was much smaller than the outrage.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-380: The Army's future-combat dream had a fox in the henhouse in 2007 — GAO's report says the lead contractor's dual role raised oversight alarms. The findings question the referee-player setup. The report warns that the biggest weapons bet in history needed independent eyes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-480: Guarding the sewers against terror had a price tag in 2007 — GAO's report totals the cost of vulnerability studies and risk plans for wastewater plants. The findings price the protection. The report's lesson: even the drains need defending in the age of fear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-680: Profiling the jobless needed a manual in 2007 — GAO's report says the worker-sorting initiative wanted more guidance and a real evaluation of results. The findings question the sorting science behind the labels. The report asks whether the algorithm helped workers or just labeled them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-780: The Pentagon could not say how hard it worked its people in 2007 — GAO's report finds the deployment-tempo data unreliable and the quality checks missing. The findings expose a blind spot on troop burnout. The report demands honest numbers on the human cost of the war rhythm.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-80: Phone competition needed better watching in 2007, and GAO's report says the FCC had to improve its monitoring of dedicated access markets. The findings target the blind spots. The report warns that the lines businesses rented needed a real referee. The market needed measuring.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-180: The Government Accountability Office dug into homeland Security: First Responders' Ability to Detect and Model Hazardous Releases in Urban Areas Is Significantly Limited in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-280: GAO published its findings on information Security: Securities and Exchange Commission Needs to Continue to Improve Its Program in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-380: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at no Child Left Behind Act: Education Actions Could Improve the Targeting of School Improvement Funds to Schools Most in Need of Assistance. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-480: GAO published its findings on global HIV/AIDS: A More Country-Based Approach Could Improve Allocation of PEPFAR Funding in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-680: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at international Food Security: Insufficient Efforts by Host Governments and Donors Threaten Progress to Halve Hunger in Sub-Saharan Africa by 2015. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-80: The Government Accountability Office dug into economic Sanctions: Agencies Face Competing Priorities in Enforcing the US Embargo on Cuba in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
geheimnisse-einiger-philosophen-und-adep: Geheimnisse einiger Philosophen und Adepten, 1780. The philosophers' secrets. This book preserves that alchemy. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. It retains its place in time. The paper lived through the years.
grimm-teutonic-mythology-stallybrass-188:
Jacob Grimm, best known for the tales he gathered with his brother, built this vast study of German myth over many years. James Steven Stallybrass turned it into English in four parts from 1880 to 1888. Grimm worked from old poems, laws, and folk speech. He spent years in the work, and the notes grew to a vast heap.

The study traces gods, heroes, beasts, and rites across the old German world. Rune lore runs through it, tied to names, charms, and carved signs. Nearly all later work on German myth starts here, and its notes still guide those who study the north.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol3-1880:
Hering's Guiding Symptoms reached its third volume in 1880, one more shelf of the ten-volume materia medica. The editorial team working from Constantine Hering's notes kept his system intact. Remedies appear in alphabetical order across the set, each with its full train of symptoms.

Mind, head, eyes, and the rest of the body each get their own sections within an entry. Odd and striking signs, the ones homeopaths call characteristic, stand out by their marks. Readers use the set as a court of appeal when smaller remedy books disagree, and Volume III does its share of that settling.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol4-1880:
By its fourth volume, from 1880, Hering's Guiding Symptoms had settled into the shape prescribers relied on. Each remedy entry moves through the body in a fixed order, so a reader always knows where to look. Marks of differing weight point to the signs worth trusting most.

Constantine Hering died the year the volume appeared, leaving his notes to students who kept the work going. What they printed came from provings, tests in which healthy people took a drug and noted each change. Volume IV shows the method at full stretch, a vast card index of symptoms bound as a book.
hershon-talmudic-miscellany-1880:
Paul Isaac Hershon was a Polish Jewish scholar who settled in London and translated rabbinic texts for English readers. His Talmudic Miscellany, published in 1880, gathers a thousand and one extracts from the Talmud, the Midrashim, and the Kabbalah. The book appeared in Trubner's Oriental Series.

Hershon orders his extracts by theme: prayer, ethics, folklore, law, and the sayings of famous rabbis. A gentile reader could browse rabbinic wisdom here without Hebrew or a guide through the vast originals. The miscellany became a classic of its series and a quiet bridge between Jewish and Christian readers.
hodgkin-italy-invaders-vol-1-1880:
Thomas Hodgkin published Italy and Her Invaders, Volume 1, in 1880. Hodgkin tells the story of the barbarian invasions of Italy from the Italian side. This volume covers the Visigoths, Alaric's sack of Rome in 410, and the Vandals. The fall of the Western Empire unfolds through Italian eyes.

Hodgkin writes with deep learning and humane sympathy for all sides. He studies church, law, and daily life beside battles and kings. The full work grew to eight volumes over many years. It became the English classic of the invasions period. Readers who want the end of Rome told fully and fairly start with Hodgkin. His patience rewards theirs.
how-to-educate-the-feelings-or-affection: How to Educate the Feelings, 1880. The affections' education. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
institutes-of-vishnu-jolly-1880:
Julius Jolly translated the Institutes of Vishnu for the Sacred Books of the East in 1880. The text frames its law as the god Vishnu's own teaching. Vishnu instructs the goddess Earth in the duties of humankind.

Civil and criminal justice, penances, and caste duties fill the code. The duties of life's four stages receive systematic treatment. Kingship, ordeals, and inheritance law appear in practical detail. Jolly was a leading authority on Hindu law of his era. His translation presents one of Hinduism's most important legal scriptures. Religion and jurisprudence meet in a single ancient code here. The frame story makes dry law feel like sacred instruction.
james-washington-square-1880:
Henry James published Washington Square in 1880, building it from an anecdote a friend had told him at dinner. James set it in the New York of his childhood, in a house on Washington Square like his grandmother's. He considered it one of his most perfectly made works.

Catherine Sloper is a plain, shy heiress with a large fortune and a brilliant, cold father. When the handsome fortune hunter Morris Townsend courts her, Dr. Sloper forbids the match and threatens to disinherit her. Catherine must choose between obedience and the only love offered her. The tragedy unfolds in drawing rooms, almost in whispers. James called the story's design flawless, and its quiet ending still stings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mantle-of-the-l:
Mantle of the Law, the cover of a Torah scroll, is described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Its Hebrew name, mappah, comes from a Greek word for a napkin. At first a silk wrapping ran the scroll's full length, guarding the writing from dust. The Talmud already knows it: a scroll without a mantle was turned face down.

The article explains the mantle's later form and care. Shaped like a bag, it slips over the rolled scroll, open below and closed above. Two holes let the scroll's handles pass through. It must be made of new, costly material never used for anything else. Worn-out mantles are not thrown away; they go to the genizah or are sewn into a shroud. Mantles are often embroidered with the Crown of the Law and the Lion of Judah. Women frequently make and present them, sometimes with the donor's name worked in.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matriarchy-1048:
Matriarchy is a social system in which descent and property run through women alone. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs give it a compact treatment in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article asks whether ancient Israel ever lived under such a system. It collects the hints scholars had drawn from the Bible itself.

The evidence offered is suggestive rather than firm. The mothers of kings are named prominently in the Books of Kings, and the wives of the patriarchs hold unusual weight in Genesis. The tribes divide into houses of Rachel and of Leah, whose names were even read as animal names under a theory of totem worship. The article is careful to show that the whole case leans on that totem theory. It points readers to Robertson Smith's “Kinship and Marriage in Early Arabia” for the argument.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merneptah-greek:
Merneptah, fourth king of Egypt's nineteenth dynasty, stands at the center of the Exodus dating debate, and the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 states the problem plainly in an article by Emil G. Hirsch and W. Max Müller. His father Rameses II built the store cities of Exodus, so Merneptah, the successor, was taken for the Pharaoh of the Exodus itself, fixing the event in the thirteenth century B.C. Then Petrie found the Israel stele: a triumph song of Merneptah's fifth year boasting "Israel is annihilated," named among the settled peoples of Canaan.

The article lets that inscription unsettle the old certainty: Israel sounds already planted in Palestine, though scholars have read it of tribes still wandering or still enslaved. A short coda notes his twenty-five years, the Libyan wars of his first five, and his mummy, newly found at Thebes and lodged at Cairo.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moravia-10980:
Moravia, the Austrian province once part of Bohemia's kingdom, held 44,255 Jews in a population of 2,437,706 in 1900. Gotthard Deutsch writes its long history in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The first evidence is the Raffelstetten toll law. It mentions Jews coming from Moravia. The article cautions that this proves traveling merchants, slave-buyers among them, not yet settlement.

Settlement is certain by the eleventh century. Cosmas of Prague mentions Moravian Jews repeatedly. His story for 1096 sets the pattern. As Crusaders approached, the Jews tried to emigrate. Duke Bretislav confiscated their property. His logic was that money made in the country should stay in it. The article follows the province's communities from those beginnings toward the modern census.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-motal-abraham-b:
Abraham ben Jacob Motal was a Turkish rabbi of Salonica, born about 1568 and dead in 1658. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied under Samuel Hayyun and probably under Solomon Kohen. As head of the yeshiva of Salonica's old Lisbon community, he gathered many devoted pupils.

Motal's responsa and decisions were printed inside other men's books, including the Bene Shemuel and Hayyim Shabbethai's collections. Two works stand under his own name. The Torat ha-Nazir, printed in 1821, treats the tractate Nazir and the Nazarite rules. The Magen Abraham deals with divorce bills and the exact writing of names in them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-music-and-music:
Music grew up with poetry among the ancient Israelites, since every poem was also sung. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack survey the subject in this Jewish Encyclopedia article. Music served the Temple, feasts, dances, and harvest festivals. It welcomed generals home, crowned kings, and cheered the shepherd alone with his pipe.

The article follows the rise of professional Temple singers in families, with the crowd answering only Amen or Halleluiah. Choirs sang against each other, as in Nehemiah's two great choruses at Jerusalem's walls. Harmony, the authors argue, was unknown: voices and strings sounded together in unison or octaves. Without fixed strophes, Hebrew melody stayed free, earnest, and close to the speech of the words.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahman-bar-jaco:
Nahman bar Jacob, usually called simply R. Nahman, was a Babylonian amora who died in 320. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. A pupil of Mar Samuel, he was chief justice under the exilarch and head of the school of Nehardea. Marriage into the exilarch's family let him entertain scholars lavishly.

Nahman ruled that a defendant who flatly denies his guilt must take the rabbinical oath. Sure of his own worth, he said any living Messiah would have to resemble him. His sayings run earthy and direct: God let Balaam go to Balak, so shamelessness avails even before Heaven. A visiting Palestinian sage blessed him with the parable of the sheltering tree.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathanson-mende:
Mendel Levin Nathanson was a Danish merchant, editor, and economist. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Altona on Nov. 20, 1780. At eighteen he set himself up in business. He died in Copenhagen on Oct. 6, 1868.

When his banking firm failed in 1831, he turned to economics. His great work traced Danish trade and finance from 1730. He also fought for full rights for Danish Jews. He founded a Jewish boys' school in 1805. A girls' school followed in 1810, kept up by his purse. Full civic rights came by decree in 1814. He later edited the Berlingske Tidende for twenty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neustadt-phineh:
Phinehas Neustadt was a German rabbi who rose from hardship. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Borek on Sept. 23, 1823. He died at Breslau on Feb. 24, 1902. His father died before he turned two.

His mother apprenticed him to a bookbinder in childhood. Cruel treatment and hunger for study drove him away. He passed a teacher's examination at eighteen years old. Posts in Mecklenburg filled the years to 1855. Arnswalde and Kolberg then took him as rabbi. At Breslau he earned a doctorate from Jena in 1864. His thesis treated immortality in the Talmud. His Hebrew school won state recognition in 1867.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-testament-1:
The New Testament is viewed here from a Jewish standpoint. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and Kaufmann Kohler for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Church named these books near the second century's close. The name claims a new covenant replaced the old. Its root idea comes from Jeremiah's prophecy.

The entry insists Jeremiah promised renewal, not law's end. Paul's followers, though, read Jesus as that covenant's mediator. Jewish writers use the name only to identify the books. The contents fall in three parts, the entry notes. Gospels and Acts tell the story first. Paul's letters follow, then the Catholic epistles and Revelation. The Gospels arose between 80 and 150 C.E. Mark, the simplest, came first and fed the others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nola-menahem-jo:
Menahem Nola became John Paul Eusthatius at baptism. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was an Italian convert to Christianity. He was born about 1540, it is thought. He died at Rome about the year 1602.

Before baptism he taught Hebrew to Thomas Aldobrandino. That pupil was brother to Pope Clement VIII. The two often debated points of religion together. Aldobrandino likely led him to the Christian faith. He took the name Eusthatius in 1568. His Italian books then defended Christianity in print. One explained the jubilee year's gate ceremony from Scripture. Nine sermons upheld the Trinity and the Messiah's coming. The Vatican keeps his notes on Ruth and Lamentations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orsha-11780:
Orsha is a town in the province of Moghilef, Russia. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Russian tales name the town as far back as the eleventh century. In 1579 a Jew of Brest farmed its customs dues. He farmed the dues of Moghilef and other towns too.

In 1643 a Jew of Orsha helped gather the realm's taxes. By the count of 1897, the town held 13,161 souls. About 7,000 of those souls were Jews of the town. Of them, 950 worked in crafts of the hand. A count in 1880 found 837 houses in Orsha. Jews owned 431 of those houses at that count. The town held one synagogue and ten houses of prayer. Its schools gave lessons to some hundreds of Jewish young.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pamiers-11880:
Pamiers is a chief town of Ariège, in France. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish group lived there in the twelve hundreds. In 1256 the Abbot of St. Antoine gave a grant. It shielded the Jew Bonio, son of Beslinenga, there.

That shield cost Bonio a gold coin in tax each year. In 1279 the Jews of Pamiers made rules for themselves. They curbed the rich gifts they gave at births. They curbed the count of guests at their feasts too. A New Year gift to a child was capped in coin. They barred their folk from the square on the Sabbath. They barred dice and chess games among themselves as well. The abbot passed these rules and showed them good will.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedro-ii-11980:
Pedro the Second ruled Aragon from 1196 to 1213. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1204 he went to Rome for his crown. The pope himself placed it on his head.

At Rome the king swore to guard the Catholic faith. He also swore to hunt down heretics. Jews at home feared they would be driven out. They met him with a Torah scroll and kept a fast. Their fears proved groundless in the end. The king owed Jewish lenders too much to lose them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pfalzburg-12080:
Pfalzburg is a German city in the district of Metz. Gotthard Deutsch and J. Wiener wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish community has lived there since the mid-1700s. In 1770 it counted twelve families. Its cemetery opened in the year 1796.

The town built an old synagogue in 1772. A new one rose on the same site in 1857. The community kept a house with an oratory and bath. Its charity league, founded in 1803, cared for the poor. A Jewish school ran until numbers fell in 1901. One rabbi later led all France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pipe-12180:
The pipe was a flute-like instrument of the ancient world. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Egypt's monuments show flutes of many shapes. Israel likely played several kinds as well. The Mishnah counts flutes in Temple song.

The Hebrew halil was a bored tube of wood. A cane tongue and few holes made its voice. Each key needed a flute of its own. It sounded at feasts, processions, and pilgrim marches. It also wailed at funerals across the land. Even the poorest mourner would not skip it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poppers-jacob-b:
Jacob Poppers was a German rabbi born at Prague in the mid seventeenth century. The Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father, a noted Talmudist, taught him rabbinic books. Jacob grew very skilled in that learning. He died at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1740.

Poppers served as rabbi in town after town. He held posts at Coblenz, Treves, and Halberstadt. In 1718 he was called to the rabbinate of Frankfort. He stayed there for the rest of his life. His book Shab Yaakov gathers his rulings in two volumes. It came out at Frankfort in 1742. His Talmud notes were printed inside another man's work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-profiat-12380:
Profiat is a name used by Jews of Provence and northern Spain. Richard Gottheil wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In Hebrew the name is spelled in more than one way. A change of one letter is common in Romance tongues, he notes. In Provençal the name took the forms Prophegue and Profag.

In Latin papers the name shows as Profatius. Jacob ben Makir is one bearer of that form. Copernicus names him in his own work, the article says. In French the name shows as Profait. A record of 1409 names one Isaquetus Profait. The article traces the name through lands and tongues.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-huna-1:
Rabbah bar Huna was a Babylonian teacher of the third set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of Huna, head of the school at Sura. He died in the year 322. Men knew him for true piety and deep modesty. Tales of both traits stand in the Talmud.

His father urged him to hear Hisda with great care. Hisda's sharp mind would train him well, his father held. At first Rabbah held back from those talks. The themes raised there did not draw him, it seems. The entry tells how the son grew into a master. It weighs his words beside his father's great name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raschkow-lazar-:
Lazar Raschkow was a German physician and writer born in 1798. Isidore Singer and Moses Löb Bamberger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Raschkow in the province of Posen. He died on August 2, 1870.

The article says his father, the local rabbi, taught him Hebrew. He tutored at Neisse while preparing for higher school. He studied medicine at Budapest and served as an army surgeon. He had to resign over writings for Jewish emancipation. Ill health later ended his medical practice at Mad. He turned to tutoring and writing instead. Near death he wrote his own epitaph. It told the story of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-bonin:
Hugo Rosenthal-Bonin was a German author born at Berlin on October 14, 1840. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied natural science at Berlin and Paris, then traveled widely.

His travels took him through southern Europe, the United States, and Japan. Settling at Stuttgart, he edited the magazine Vom Fels zum Meer from 1889. He wrote steadily, filling book after book with tales and novels. His story collections were translated into many European languages. Titles include Der Diamant-Schleifer, Das Gold des Orion, and Die Tierbändigerin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-wilhelm-1:
Wilhelm Sachs was a German dental surgeon born at Wesenberg on September 22, 1849. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He studied at Breslau and at the Philadelphia Dental College, graduating in 1872.

Sachs practised dentistry at Vienna and Paris before settling at Breslau. In 1890 he became privat-docent in dental surgery at Breslau's university. He received the title of professor there in 1896, six years later. His book Die Pflege der Zähne, on care of the teeth, appeared in 1887. He also wrote on filling teeth and on pivot teeth for handbooks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-books-of:
Emil G. Hirsch wrote this long Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Books of Samuel. They are two books in the Prophets, the second main part of the Hebrew Bible. They follow Joshua and Judges in the standard order. Samuel and Kings began as single books. The Greek Septuagint joined all four as one history called Books of Kingdoms.

The article first traces how Jerome's Vulgate and later printed Bibles fixed the present split. It then walks through the story chapter by chapter. The first book covers Eli and the young Samuel. It moves to Samuel and Saul, then to Saul and David. Readers get the ark's capture, Saul's rise and fall, and David's victory over Goliath. The survey gives a full map of Israel's first kings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanhedrin-frenc:
Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the French Sanhedrin. Napoleon the First called that Jewish high court into being. It was meant to give legal force to answers given by the Assembly of Notables. The government had put twelve questions to the Notables. They covered marriage, divorce, usury, and Jewish loyalty to France.

Commissioner Molé told the Notables the emperor was pleased. Still, Napoleon wanted a pledge of strict loyalty to those answers. So he resolved to summon a great sanhedrin. It would turn the answers into binding decisions. It would also shape the future status of the Jews. Like the ancient court, it was to hold seventy-one members. Two-thirds were to be rabbis and one-third laymen. The Notables would elect them and alert communities across Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlesinger-sig:
Frederick T. Haneman and Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Sigmund Schlesinger. He was an Austrian writer. Schlesinger was born at Vienna in 1811. He studied at the Schottengymnasium and the University of Vienna. He took his medical degree in 1835. At seventeen he had already published a poem in the Sammler.

In 1831 Schlesinger wrote a drama on the crown prince's marriage. It played several times on the Vienna stage. Under the pen name Sigmund, he joined the Theater Zeitung that year. His Mährische Reisebriefe, letters from Moravia, appeared in 1835. He went to Dalmatia in 1837 as a physician. He served as a surgeon in the honved army in 1848 and 1849. After that, the article says, his history cannot be traced.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-see-13380:
Isidore Singer, Frederick T. Haneman, and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on the Sée family. The family comes from Alsace. Its first figure here is Abraham Adolphe Sée, a French barrister. He was born at Colmar in 1819. He died at Paris on February 26, 1905. He led the Jewish consistory at Colmar.

Camille Sée, Abraham's nephew, was a deputy and jurist. Born at Colmar in 1847, he entered the chamber in 1876. He championed laws for the schooling of girls. Measures he proposed passed the Senate in 1880. In 1881 he became a councilor of state. His book treats the lycées and colleges for girls. Eugène Léon Sée served the Third Republic as prefect in several departments. The entry traces a family deep in French public life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-zebi:
Shabbethai Zebi, son of Mordecai, was a false messiah and cabalist born at Smyrna in 1626. Kaufmann Kohler and Henry Malter wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His family came from Spain, and his father sold poultry in the Morea. Trade shifts later made the father a rich agent at Smyrna.

Young Shabbethai was trained for Talmud study under Smyrna's veteran rabbi. Dry legal debate never held his fervent, fanciful mind. Mysticism and the Cabala drew him instead. From that pull grew the Shabbethaian movement, a sect he founded. It shook Jewish communities across the world. The entry begins the full story of the man behind that upheaval.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shimei-13580:
Shimei was a Benjamite of Bahurim, of the house of Saul. Emil G. Hirsch, J. F. McLaughlin, Wilhelm Bacher, and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He tormented David during David's flight from Absalom. Shimei cursed the king and threw insults along the road.

When David returned in victory, Shimei begged for pardon. David forgave him on the spot and spared his life. On his deathbed, though, David charged Solomon to avenge the insult. Rabbinic tales sharpen Shimei's taunts against the king. They say he mocked David's Moabite descent and Bath-sheba affair. In his plea he cited Joseph, who returned good for evil. The entry shows mercy and revenge bound in one story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ii-ben-g:
Simeon II, son of Gamaliel I, led the Great Sanhedrin at Jerusalem in the last twenty years before the Temple fell. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A Pharisee leader, he joined the revolt against Rome. He even worked with Anan, a former Sadducee high priest.

Even Josephus, his foe, praised his care and energy. Simeon held that no rule should be laid on people that they could not keep. When doves for offerings grew too dear, he cut the number a woman had to bring. Prices then fell to a fourth of what they had been. His own rule praised silence and work over much talk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sinigaglia-1378:
Sinigaglia was an Italian family that took its name from that town. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The family later settled in Scandiano. Solomon Jedidiah Sinigaglia was rabbi and mohel there in 1639. He later moved to Modena, where many kin served as rabbis.

The entry traces the family member by member. Abraham Vita kept a diary covering 1722 to 1733. He also wrote notes on many Mishnah tractates. Jacob Samson Shabbethai wrote Talmudic works and responsa at Pisa and Leghorn. Moses Elijah taught in Modena for fifty years. Readers get a full map of one rabbinic family's learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-mos:
Solomon ben Moses Chelm was a Polish rabbi of the eighteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Samoscz, in the government of Lublin. He served as rabbi of Chelm, Samoscz, and Lemberg in turn. In 1771 he was called to Lemberg as chief rabbi.

In 1777 he left Lemberg, intending to reach the Holy Land. He died at Salonica shortly after arriving there in 1778. He was known as a grammarian and mathematician as well. His Merkebet ha-Mishneh held notes on Maimonides' Yad. It also held a pamphlet on Talmudic arithmetic and geometry. A revised edition appeared at Salonica in 1777 and 1778.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spaeth-johann-p:
Johann Peter Spaeth, called Moses Germanus, was a convert to Judaism. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Venice in the seventeenth century. His father, a poor shoemaker, fled to Augsburg about 1642. There Jesuits took charge of the boy's education as a Catholic.

Spaeth later lived at Vienna as a private tutor. Unhappy with Catholic dogmas, he became a Lutheran in 1680. In 1683 he returned to Catholicism and defended it in print. New doubts then drove him toward mystic sects and Hebrew study. At last he renounced Christianity and attacked it with force. He died at Amsterdam on April 27, 1701.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szold-benjamin-:
Benjamin Szold was an American rabbi born in Hungary in 1829. Cyrus Adler and Louis H. Levin wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Nemiskert on November 15. He studied under rabbis in Hungary and at Presburg. He died at Berkeley Springs in 1902.

Szold led the conservative wing of American Reform Judaism. In 1859 he took the pulpit of Baltimore's Oheb Shalom. He arrived that September, a month after his marriage. Under him the congregation grew fast. It became known for strict Sabbath observance. He served as rabbi until 1892, then as emeritus. He held the bond with his flock until death. The entry honors a Hungarian scholar rooted in one American pulpit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tedeschi-marco-:
Marco Tedeschi was an Italian rabbi and poet born in 1817. Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Piova in Piedmont. His father became rabbi at Vercelli, and Marco followed him. He died at Triest in 1870.

In 1838 Tedeschi went to Turin to study. Hillel Cantoni was his teacher there. Towns elected him rabbi one after another. Nizza-Monferrato, Saluzzo, and Asti each called him. Triest was his final pulpit and home. He won wide fame as a preacher. His main poems were printed after his death. Castiglione issued them in 1886 at Drohobycz. He also translated a French Jewish prayer book. The entry honors a preacher-poet of Italy's small towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-threshold-14380:
The threshold held a special sanctity in early times, this entry argues. Joseph Jacobs wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. The Temple threshold was a marked spot with set taboos. Special keepers guarded the thresholds of the sanctuary. Families also made sacrifices at their own thresholds.

Herodotus reports the same practice among the Egyptians. Trumbull linked the threshold to the first Passover. He read pesaḥ as a leaping over a blood-marked threshold. Dagon's temple threshold was clearly sacred to its priests. Cheyne even reread a verse in Kings as leaping between two thresholds. That meant serving both Baal and God at once. The custom survives as a folk taboo against treading on thresholds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-unger-ephraim-s:
Ephraim Solomon Unger was a German educator and mathematician at Erfurt. Isidore Singer and W. Salzberger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Coswig in 1789, he died in 1870. He studied philosophy, mathematics, and science at Erfurt University. He lectured there privately from 1810 to 1816.

With his brother David he founded a school in 1820. It taught mathematics and modern languages at first. Fourteen years later it became a real-school. The board offered him its directorship for converting. He refused, yet kept a senior teacher's post until 1862. Erfurt made him an honorary citizen for long service. Prussia's king gave him a professor's title and an order. He also won incorporation for Erfurt's Jewish congregation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-warranty-of-tit:
Warranty of title is a seller's promise about ownership rights. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. When land or slaves were sold by deed, a clause was added. The seller pledged to repay the buyer for any loss. A flawed title triggered that promise.

The custom was already ancient in Babylon and Assyria. Jewish law implied a warranty in every sale. It covered land, slaves, and goods alike. Courts treated a missing clause as a mere slip. Only a special pact could free the seller. The entry shows how buyers gained firm protection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wetzlar-14880:
Wetzlar is a Prussian city in the Coblenz district. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was once a free imperial city. Jews likely lived there in the twelve hundreds. A Wetzlar youth appears in a murder record then. Tax lists name the town's Jews in 1241.

Rulers repeatedly pledged the Jews' taxes as income. In 1265 Archbishop Werner swore to protect them from violence. Rudolph I granted their tax yield to a noble in 1277. Emperors passed the revenue from hand to hand. In 1349 Charles IV transferred the Jews conditionally to Count John. The entry shows Jews treated as a fiscal asset.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-lucien-149:
Lucien Wolf (born 1857) was an English news writer and a student of Anglo-Jewish past. Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in London, he joined The Jewish World in 1874. He rose fast and led that paper's views for near twenty years.

By age twenty he was a lead hand on a daily paper. In 1890 he joined the Daily Graphic as a foreign desk chief. He wrote long pieces on world affairs for the Fortnightly Review. Those pieces ran under the pen name Diplomaticus. In 1905 his notes on Russian funds drew world note. The finance chief of Russia felt forced to reply in print. Wolf also wrote much on the Jews of England in past times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yeshu-ah-jeshua:
Yeshuah ben Elijah ha-Levi was a scholar of Africa who saved old hymns. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. No date for his life is known to men now. His chief work was a book of the poems of Judah ha-Levi.

He gave that book a preface in the Arabic tongue. He set a head note on most of the poems there. Each note tells what the poem treats and why it was made. He drew on three sets of poems made before him. He added many more poems to that base stock. He did not vouch that Judah wrote each added piece. Two hymns in a Tripoli rite book may be his own work. Both hymns are sung on the night of Atonement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zausmer-jacob-d:
Jacob David ben Isaac Zausmer was a Polish Masorite of note. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the 1500s and the 1600s in Poland. He served as rabbi of Zausmer, a town near Cracow.

He died at a date some time before the year 1644. He wrote two works on the Masorah, the text note lore. One work clears up hard points in that lore in full. It forms a mate to a book by Elijah Levita. The second work is a note set on the Masorah text. His son brought out a new form of the works in 1644. In that book the son speaks of his sire as dead. The entry rests on three book lists of Hebrew lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zomber-bernhard:
Bernhard Zomber was a Polish scholar who taught for many years in Berlin. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Lask in 1821, he died at Berlin in 1884. He learned rabbinical literature in Poland, then studied in Germany under Joseph Shapiro and Jacob Ettinger.

Zomber later attended the universities of Würzburg and Berlin. In 1871 he became principal teacher at Berlin's Bet ha-Midrash, holding the post until his death. His books edit older works on Passover law and on Talmudic tractates, with comments of his own. He also wrote for Jewish scholarly journals, including a study of Judah ben Yakar, a commentator on the Jerusalem Talmud.
knights-of-pythias-illustrated-1880:
Knights of Pythias Illustrated, issued by publisher E A Cook in 1880, printed the ritual of the Knights of Pythias with pictures. The Knights were a fraternal order founded during the Civil War, built on the story of Damon and Pythias and their famed friendship. Cook sold such books to readers eager to see inside secret lodges.

Inside are the forms for opening a lodge, admitting members, and giving the degrees, shown step by step. Signs, grips, and emblems appear with the words said to go with them. The book served critics of secret orders, curious readers, and anyone who wanted the hidden work of the lodge in plain print.
koch-etiology-traumatic-infective-diseas:
Robert Koch was a German country doctor who became a founder of bacteriology, the study of bacteria. In 1878 he published his research on wound infections in German. W. Watson Cheyne translated it for the New Sydenham Society, and the English version appeared in 1880.

Koch injected animals and traced which bacteria caused each kind of wound infection. He showed that specific germs, including the anthrax bacillus, produce specific diseases. His careful methods for growing and staining bacteria became standard lab practice. The work helped prove the germ theory and shaped how doctors hunt disease causes today.
lanier-science-english-verse-1880:
Sidney Lanier published The Science of English Verse in 1880, built from lectures he gave at Johns Hopkins. Lanier was a Confederate veteran, a lawyer, and above all a musician: he played flute in Baltimore's Peabody orchestra. He brought a trained ear to a field ruled by counting syllables.

Lanier argues that verse is a kind of music and should be scanned in bars, like a score. Rhythm, pitch, and tone-color in speech get separate, careful treatment, with examples from Shakespeare onward. He treats bad verse as bad music and good verse as sound organized by law. The book is the first systematic American prosody, and working poets still consult it. Lanier died the next year, at thirty-nine.
legge-religions-of-china-1880:
James Legge, the Scottish missionary and Oxford professor who translated the Chinese classics, published The Religions of China in 1880. The book gives his comparative account of the faiths he had lived among for thirty years in Hong Kong. Legge writes as both scholar and former missionary.

He treats Confucianism as a moral and ancestral system, Taoism as a teaching decayed into magic, and Buddhism as an import that reshaped China. His judgments favor Confucius, whose works he had spent his life translating. The book shows Victorian sinology at its most learned and most confident. Readers can watch a fine scholar wrestle with faiths not his own.
life-of-johnson-volume-3-1776-1780:
Volume Three of Boswell's Johnson spans March 1776 to October 1780. Appendices treat George Psalmanazar and Johnson's love of travelling. Others cover lord mayor elections and the inmates of Johnson's house. Boswell's own academy secretary letters close the apparatus.

The narrative opens leaving Ashbourne and changing horses at Derby. Doctor Butter there rages over a lost Scotch militia bill. Johnson violently opposes the bill and delights in its defeat. Boswell notes how loosely Johnson used the epithet scoundrel. Boswell's academy secretary acceptance letters appear among the appendices. Derby's Dr. Butter shared Johnson's indignation over the militia bill.
malleus-maleficarum-latin-1580:
The Malleus Maleficarum, the Hammer of Witches, is the most infamous book of the witch-hunt era, tied to the inquisitor Heinrich Kramer. This text is the Latin edition printed at Frankfurt in 1580. The three parts of the Hammer appear with added tracts by Basin, Molitor, Gerson, and Murner on kindred subjects.

The Hammer defines witchcraft, argues its reality, and instructs judges in procedure. Its authority shadowed trials for two centuries. The library's English version is the Summers translation; this is the Latin source behind it. Reading the original shows the terse, legal Latin that carried the doctrine across Europe. No serious study of the persecution can skip it.
marsh-odontornithes-1880:
Othniel Charles Marsh, a Yale professor and fossil hunter, published Odontornithes in 1880. The monograph describes extinct birds with teeth, found in the chalk beds of Kansas. Marsh was Cope's great rival in the race for fossils.

The toothed birds, like Hesperornis and Ichthyornis, mixed bird traits with reptile traits. Their jaws held real teeth, and their bones told of swimming and flight long ago. For Darwin's supporters, they were gold: a clear link between reptiles and birds. Darwin himself praised Marsh's finds as strong support for evolution. Full measures and plates record the Kansas finds in detail.
mela-de-chorographia-latin-1880:
Pomponius Mela wrote the first geography in Latin to survive, in the first century of the Empire. De Chorographia, in Carl Frick's 1880 school text, gives Mela's three books on the world. Frick's edition prints the spare Latin in a clean, worked form.

Mela walks the coasts of the known world, land by land, naming seas, towns, tribes, and wonders. His earth is a ring of lands around a great sea, edged by strange peoples. The book is short, brisk, and full of the color of its age. It opens the Latin line of writing about the earth.
nasa-tm-19710070126-flutter-investigatio:
Robert W Miller and Margery E Hannah reported this flutter study as Technical Memorandum X-325. Half span delta surfaces with leading edge sweep from sixty to eighty degrees faced helium flow at Mach 7.0. Tests ran in the Langley hypersonic aeroelasticity tunnel. Flutter is a dangerous shaking where airflow feeds a surface's own vibration. At hypersonic speeds, very little data then existed.

Each sweep angle flew with wedge and double wedge airfoil sections. Two hinge positions were tried for the pitching motion. Wedge models proved more stable than double wedge ones. A hinge at or near the center of gravity also beat a forward hinge. Sweep angle itself mattered little. One simple piston theory analysis matched the tests best.
openalex-w1972186280:
David Keith, Jon Paul Rodríguez, and many co-authors wrote this paper. It appeared in PLoS ONE in the year 2013. The IUCN Red List assesses risk for species worldwide. No standard global system assessed ecosystems in that way. Planners need such risk knowledge to slow decline, they write.

Their work lays scientific foundations for an ecosystem Red List. It extends extinction-risk thinking from species to ecosystems. Shared criteria would let teams compare ecosystem health globally. Services for future human use depend on that health. The framework guides which ecosystems need action first. It became a base for later IUCN work.
openalex-w2169748580:
Susan Howard, Daša Cerar, and Michael Anderson led this 2009 study in Emerging Infectious Diseases. They checked how often the mold Aspergillus fumigatus shrugs off azole drugs. Azoles are the main pills used against aspergillosis. Drug failure had been rare, and the team tied it to cases where care failed.

In a Manchester set of over five hundred samples, one in twenty beat itraconazole. That rate had clearly risen since 2004. Most of those samples also beat the other two main azoles. Nearly every patient behind them had taken azoles before. Many of their cases got worse or failed to improve on the drugs. The study marks this as a growing threat in care.
openalex-w2177259980:
Jared Decker, Stephanie McKay, Megan Rolf, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Genetics in 2014. They charted ancestry, divergence, and mixing in domesticated cattle worldwide. Breed histories were poorly known, above all for African, Asian, and American herds, despite cattle's deep impact on human societies.

The team genotyped over fifteen hundred animals from one hundred thirty-four breeds at tens of thousands of DNA markers. Every method and subset told the same broad story. Three major groups stood out: Asian indicine, Eurasian taurine, and African taurine cattle. Their patterns of spread trace how herds dispersed geographically alongside the people who raised and traded them.
openalex-w2528608880:
Vanessa Wong, Stephen G. Baker, and Thomas R. Connor, with the International Typhoid Consortium, published this 2016 paper in Nature Communications. It concerns Salmonella Typhi, the bacterium that causes human typhoid fever. Typhi strains differ very little in their DNA, which makes telling one isolate from another hard. Earlier typing schemes based on a small gene set could only sort strains into broad groups.

The team used whole-genome data from almost two thousand isolates collected in sixty-three countries. That data revealed hundreds of thousands of small DNA differences across the core genome. From them the authors built a global framework for the Typhi population. Their new scheme uses sixty-eight marker differences to classify strains in fine detail. It also confirmed the spread of the drug-resistant H58 family, including into Africa. Better typing helps track outbreaks and guide typhoid surveillance worldwide.
openalex-w3010547780:
Francesco Rubino, Rebecca Puhl, David Cummings, and colleagues issued this consensus statement in Nature Medicine in 2020. It calls for an end to the stigma faced by people with obesity. A broad group of international experts, including patient representatives, signed the statement.

People with obesity meet bias at work, at school, and in health care itself. Research shows weight stigma harms body and mind, and that shamed patients often receive worse care. The authors argue that this damage to health and to basic rights is unacceptable in modern societies. Their statement aims to inform doctors, policymakers, and the public, and to replace blame with care grounded in science.
openalex-w3045619980:
Sean Gordon, Bruno Contreras-Moreira, Joshua Levy, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2020. It traces how a doubled genome evolves, using pan-genomic analysis of the grass Brachypodium hybridum and its two parent species. All flowering plants descend from an ancient genome doubling.

After doubling, genomes slowly shed spare copies and drift back toward a working single set, a process still underway. Many of today's crops, from wheat to potato, are fairly recent doubled species. By comparing the hybrid grass with both parents, the team could watch that shedding and reshaping in detail. The changes proved gradual rather than sudden. The work clarifies how doubled genomes settle over time, a question central to plant breeding.
openalex-w3191864380:
Míkel Izquierdo, Reshma Merchant, John Morley, and colleagues present expert consensus guidelines on exercise for older adults. The guidelines appeared in The Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging in 2021. Ageing steadily weakens muscle and fitness, and a seated lifestyle speeds the loss. The panel asked how much structured exercise can slow that decline and protect daily independence.

Exercise, the panel finds, softens age-related losses in muscle and aerobic capacity. It also helps prevent heart disease, stroke, diabetes, weak bones, and obesity, and lifts mood and quality of life. Programmes improved the signs of frailty and sharpened thinking in trials. The guidelines treat exercise like a medicine, dosed on evidence for a chosen goal.
openalex-w4206564180:
Osval Antonio Montesinos-López, Abelardo Montesinos-López, and José Crossa wrote this book chapter on overfitting in prediction models, published in 2022. It forms chapter four of a Springer volume on statistical machine learning. Overfitting happens when a model learns training data too well, noise included. Such a model then performs badly on new, unseen data.

The chapter sets overfitting beside its opposite, underfitting, where a model is too simple to capture real patterns. Diagrams compare a too-simple line, a balanced curve, and a curve chasing every point. The authors then cover tuning, the careful adjustment of model settings, and honest evaluation of prediction performance. These habits decide whether a model is useful or merely lucky on old data.
openalex-w4321438780:
Jordi Mitjà, Andrea Alemany, Michael Marks, and colleagues describe mpox in people with advanced HIV infection, in The Lancet in 2023. Mpox spread across many countries in 2022. People with HIV made up roughly two fifths to half of reported cases. Most had well-controlled HIV and fared much like other patients. Clinicians worried, though, about those whose HIV was far advanced and immune systems deeply weakened.

This global case series gathers such patients from many centres to describe their illness and outcomes. Early reports had suggested worse disease and higher death rates in this group. A shared series lets doctors compare symptoms, complications, and survival on a common footing. The work guides care for the patients at greatest risk from mpox.
openalex-w7204176380: Stray dogs and cats have overrun two universities in Teresina, Piaui, and this study takes stock. The authors diagnose the scale of the abandoned-animal population at UFPI and UESPI, mapping the environmental, health, and ethical fallout. Part environmental audit, part animal-welfare plea, it asks what institutions owe the creatures on their grounds.
openalex-w7207702580: High blood pressure and diabetes weigh heavily on health systems, and local clinics need better ways to treat them. This review looks at light-hard technologies, a term for practical tools and set methods, for managing these long-term illnesses in frontline care. The authors hunt for new ideas that raise the quality and speed of treatment. Written for clinic managers and doctors, it seeks realistic upgrades to daily care.
openalex-w7212027280:
Everaldo dos Santos Mendes leads a team on school inclusion in Brazil, and on who must carry it. Inclusion work, they argue, is too often dumped on the classroom teacher alone. Their study sorts duties among four levels: the teacher, the school, the school network, and the state. It rests on past research and on the laws that frame the field.

The authors split mere access from real inclusion. They track diversity in body, senses, mind, race, faith, language, and place. Curriculum and grading, they note, can help or harm. Their main offer is a shared-duty matrix. It matches five needs for inclusion with the level that owns each task. Families and students run through the whole plan. The aim is to move the talk from urging teachers to try harder, to naming who owes what.
openalex-w7212236180:
Fernando Eblen Vignoli Reis, Felipe Borges de Souza Martins, and Leonardo Gerhardt Lopes review trials on exercise for long-term low back pain. The pain is the world's top cause of years lived with limits. The team searched three databases in 2026 for strict trials with at least one hundred adults in each. Work from 2021 on met the bar. Of more than two hundred finds, a small set of trials made the final cut.

Most of those trials showed less pain or more ease in daily acts with exercise. Set by plain care, by talks alone, or by no care, exercise won out each time. One type of drill did not beat the rest by much. The authors back exercise as a first-line, safe path. The best plan, they add, is the one that fits the person's life and taste, so it lasts.
openalex-w7214017480:
Yane Gama da Silva and Cristiana de Cerqueira Silva Santana discuss environmental schooling under the climate crisis. Their 2026 library article treats the crisis as an expression of a wider social and environmental crisis. Historical, social, economic, and political contradictions of capitalism frame the argument.

Climate change cannot be read as the sum of single acts alone, they argue. It grows from historically built relations between society and nature, marked by exploitation and capital accumulation. Critical environmental schooling is offered as a political and teaching project. It aims to form citizens who grasp structural causes, join processes, and build fairer, sustainable societies oriented to human emancipation.
openalex-w7214626280:
Carla Rocha Pordeus and Maria de Fátima Nóbrega Barbosa proposed, in a 2026 article, a model for judging public policies that harvest rainwater in semi-arid regions. Dry regions depend on catching scarce rain, yet existing evaluation models, they found, lean heavily on technical and operational points. Their critical review of national and international literature on water governance and sustainability aimed to widen that lens.

Their framework has six dimensions, covering legal rules, institutions and governance, social and economic life, environment and technique, and culture and sustainability, each with indicators and ways to check them. The model is aligned with global sustainable development goals. Used well, the authors argue, it gives governments an interdisciplinary tool to plan, run, monitor, and improve rainwater policies, strengthening water security where rain cannot be taken for granted.
openalex-w7215981280:
Alessandra Rodrigues Araújo, Roberta dos Santos Avelino, and Cássio Eduardo Soares Miranda reviewed, in 2026, dental care for pregnant women in Brazilian primary care. Their review covered studies from 2015 to 2025 across five databases and kept only five, which they sorted by objective, design, evidence level, and findings. Two linked themes emerged: clinical and pharmacological guidelines for treating pregnant patients, and the challenges and barriers in professionals' own views.

Dental care during pregnancy matters for maternal and child health, the review confirms, yet gaps persist in clinical safety and professional attitudes. Those weaknesses connect to missing training for this care and care protocols in the network. The authors press for further education and uniform guidelines so pregnant women receive full, safe care instead of being turned away out of insecurity.
openalex-w7218701680:
Luiz Carlos Fanaia de Almeida and Diogo Marcelo Delben Ferreira de Lima studied, in a 2026 article, changes in land management in Mato Grosso, Brazil, between 2019 and 2025. Their focus is the state land institute, Intermat, its state system, and the land products it offers on a public digital platform. Those products are property titles, certificates, registrations of court decisions, consent letters, georeferenced registers, thematic maps, and public information.

The system has raised citizen service, integrated land information, and brought geotechnology into land governance, the authors find. The products show both public government performance and challenges that remain for an effective, open system. Despite real innovation in land policy, they conclude, the system still needs work to deliver territorial ordering, citizen services, and sustainable development. The study is a close look at how a land-rich state puts who owns what online.
openalex-w7220664480:
Renata Galvão de Lima wrote a 2026 qualitative article on a project called Move for Life at a federal institute in Brazil's Pernambuco hinterland, asking whether it counts as non-formal education. The project offers bodily practices to its community, usually framed as health promotion and quality of life at work. Her documentary study reads it against writing in three fields: non-formal education, professional and technological education, and integral human formation.

The project shows participation, interaction, autonomy, and bodily practices, elements that can favor learning processes beyond formal school spaces. Its teaching dimension, however, depends on teaching intent and on work that enables reflection, taking part, and collective construction. The project has real potential, she concludes, to be a space of non-formal learning joining bodily practice, work, and integral human formation, rather than just a wellness benefit with teaching side effects.
openalex-w7221186480:
Alexandre José de Oliveira Fernandes and three co-authors evaluated the Active Prevention Group of the Pará Military Police in a 2026 study. The group works to stop crime before it starts. Instead of only reacting, it builds citizenship and community strength. It also tackles the social roots of violence in high-risk areas.

The team combined books, documents, and a closed questionnaire. Military police officers answered it. Most views of the group's community approach were favorable. Officers valued the closer tie between police and residents. They also saw room to expand the work. Training, planning, and structure still need improvement. The group holds real promise, the authors conclude. Staffing, links across agencies, and regular review must grow with it.
phrenology-and-its-uses-embracing-the-ch: Phrenology and Its Uses, 1880. The pursuits and health. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
plos-pbio-0000080:
Prabhat S. Kunwar, Michelle Starz-Gaiano, Roland J. Bainton, and others studied germ cell movement in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2003. Germ cells form far from the gonad, the organ where they must end up. They cross a sheet of gut cells to get there, guided by signals.

The team found that a receptor called Tre1 steers that crossing. Tre1 belongs to a large family of receptors that sense cues outside the cell. Without its guidance, germ cells fail to pass through the gut wall as they should. The work shows how a single signal can direct a key step in building the reproductive system. That step is shared, in broad form, by many animals.
plos-pbio-0020280:
Vitali Matyash, Eugeni V. Entchev, Fanny Mende, and their team studied worm dormancy in PLOS Biology in 2004. When food runs out, young C. elegans worms can enter diapause, a paused state called the dauer stage. They can wait there for months until times improve.

A hormone made from sterols, the fat family that includes cholesterol, controls entry into that pause. The study shows the hormone works by switching on a chain of genes in sequence. Naming the hormone signal fills a long-standing gap in worm biology. It also links this worm's survival trick to steroid hormones in other animals, including humans, where similar signals time growth and reproduction.
plos-pbio-0020380:
Damien Devos, Svetlana Dokudovskaya, Frank Alber, and a large team compared two cell structures in PLOS Biology in 2004. Coated vesicles are small sacs that ferry cargo between cell compartments. Nuclear pore complexes are the gates through the nucleus membrane. The two look different, yet their parts share a common architecture.
