Shared shape suggests a shared origin deep in evolution, when early cells were building inner compartments. The authors lay out the structural kinship piece by piece. That kind of deep link helps explain how complex cells arose from simpler ones. It also predicts that lessons from one structure, like how its coat bends a membrane, will apply to the other.
plos-pone-0000080:
Zhihua Jiang, Jennifer J. Michal, Galen A. Williams, and their team checked two obesity drug targets in PLOS ONE in 2006. The targets are a hormone called UCN3 and its receptor CRHR2, which help control appetite and stress responses. The team compared the genes across species to judge whether animal results might apply to people.

Drug targets that behave the same in test animals and in humans are far more likely to pay off. Cross-species checks like this one sort promising targets from traps early. The appetite system is full of targets that worked in mice and failed in people. A careful filter at the gene level saves years of wasted effort and guides safer trials.
plos-pone-0000180:
James O. Lloyd-Smith published this statistics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Outbreak data are often highly overdispersed: most cases cause few infections, while a few cause many. The negative binomial distribution captures that spread through a dispersion parameter, and the author presents a way to estimate it by maximum likelihood.

Getting that parameter right changes how superspreading is measured and how outbreaks are modeled. The method is aimed at infectious disease data, where overdispersion is the rule. It gives epidemiologists a more reliable handle on one of the key numbers describing how a disease spreads.
plos-pone-0000280:
Saman K. Hashmi, Maria B. Afridi, Kanza Abbas, and colleagues published this public health study from Pakistan in PLOS ONE in 2007. It examines factors associated with adherence to anti-hypertensive treatment, whether patients with high blood pressure actually keep taking their medicines. Poor adherence is one of the main reasons blood pressure stays uncontrolled.

High blood pressure is silent, so patients often stop pills they feel no benefit from. The authors identify what helps or hinders sticking with treatment in this setting. Findings like these guide clinics in supporting patients, since an untaken drug cannot prevent a stroke.
plos-pone-0000380:
Yu-Tsueng Liu and Dennis A. Carson presented a new laboratory approach in PLOS ONE in 2007 for finding breakpoints in cancer genomes. A breakpoint is a spot where a chromosome has broken and rejoined, an error that can drive cancer growth. Tumor samples are usually mixed with normal cells, and that normal DNA hides the breaks.

The method aims to pinpoint breakpoints even when normal DNA is present in the sample. Finding exact break locations matters because they often reveal fused genes or lost control regions that push a cell toward cancer. A cleaner way to locate them could sharpen diagnosis and help match patients to treatments aimed at their tumor's specific errors.
plos-pone-0000480:
Luisa Bernardinelli and colleagues tested a gene's link to multiple sclerosis in a distinctive population, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is ACCN1, which makes an ion channel that senses acid in tissue. The study population lived in central east Sardinia, an island whose long-isolated communities are prized for genetic studies.

Multiple sclerosis, where the immune system strips insulation from nerves, clusters on Sardinia at unusually high rates. Isolated populations concentrate genetic signals, so an association found there can reveal risk factors hidden elsewhere. The team reported an association between ACCN1 and the disease in this population, adding a candidate to the list of MS risk genes.
plos-pone-0000580:
Thomas P. Gosden and Erik I. Svensson studied a mating system where females come in several forms, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Female sexual polymorphism means females of one species have distinct types, often differing in color. The team measured the fecundity consequences of male mating harassment in the wild: how persistent male attention affects each type's egg production.

Harassment is a real cost of being common and attractive; rare female types may escape it, which helps keep several types in the population. Measuring egg output in the wild ties that theory to fitness. The study is a neat test of frequency-dependent selection maintaining variety.
plos-pone-0000680:
Denis G. Pelli and Katharine A. Tillman separated three routes to recognizing words, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Object recognition research has long debated two routes: seeing the whole at once, or assembling parts. Context offers a third route, since an object can be guessed from its surroundings. Words are objects too, and how we recognize them is the core question of reading research.

Their title claims a triple dissociation, evidence that parts, wholes, and context each contribute separately. Do fast readers lean on letters, word shapes, or context most? A clean separation of the three helps explain skilled reading, and it may clarify what breaks down in reading disorders.
plos-pone-0000780:
Robert A. Kleps, Terrell C. Myers, Romuald N. Lipcius and colleagues used a physics tool to find a chemistry difference between the sexes of a marine invertebrate. Hormone levels are generally accepted as the main cause of sexual dimorphism, the differing forms of males and females. Levels of small metabolites also differ between men and women, in circulating amino acids, lipids, and carbohydrates, and within brain tissue.

Their method was phosphorus-31 nuclear magnetic resonance, which detects phosphorus-bearing compounds. The title reports a sex-specific metabolite identified this way. A molecule found in one sex only hints that development's chemistry differs beyond hormones, in creatures far simpler than humans.
plos-pone-0000880:
Sunhwan Jo, Taehoon Kim and Wonpil Im presented an automated builder and database for protein and membrane systems, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Computer simulations of membrane proteins can reveal how they work at the atomic level. Setting up a fair test system, though, is much harder than placing a normal protein in water.

Their tool builds a realistic protein set into a membrane for molecular dynamics simulations, the physics based movies of atoms in motion. A shared database of ready systems saves each lab from starting over. Tools like this quietly speed up drug and basic research on the proteins that sit in cell membranes.
plos-pone-0000980:
Freddie-Jeanne Richard, David Tarpy and Christina Grozinger measured how mating quantity reshapes honey bee queen physiology, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mating changes female insects deeply, and in honey bee queens the changes are permanent. Queens mate with many males in a brief window early in life, then begin laying eggs.

The team varied insemination quantity and tracked what changed inside the queen. Knowing which shifts follow mating itself, and which follow the amount, helps explain queen health and colony performance. Beekeepers depend on queens that stay productive for seasons. The study breaks a once in a lifetime event into parts that can be tested.
plos-pone-0001080:
Jason Barbour, Mariana Sauer, Elizabeth Sharp and colleagues studied people carrying both HIV and herpes simplex virus 2, in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV is often acquired while other infections are already present. HSV-2, a common sexually transmitted virus, is one of the most frequent of those companions.

The team examined how HSV-2 status at the time of HIV acquisition affects the later clinical course and CD4 T cell patterns. Their title reports elevated CD4 counts in co-infected adults early in HIV infection, a direction that needs care in reading. Co-infection studies warn against treating HIV's course as set by HIV alone.
plos-pone-0001180:
Wheezing in infancy has been linked to lungs that work less well later in childhood. Christophe Delacourt and colleagues followed a group of asthmatic infants to test that link, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on bronchial hyperresponsiveness, the tendency of airways to narrow too easily.

The team prospectively investigated how hyperresponsiveness relates to progressive impairment of lung function, following the children until age nine. Their study connects a measurable airway trait in infancy to lung performance years later. Such links help doctors judge which wheezy infants need the closest watch.
plos-pone-0001280:
In pond-dwelling Daphnia magna, genotypes differ in how well they compete and in how often they get infected. Florian Altermatt and Dieter Ebert tested whether those two traits go together in natural populations, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The cost of resistance hypothesis predicts that resistant genotypes pay for their resistance with lower fitness when uninfected.

The authors report, as their title states, that genotype-specific competitive ability does not correlate with infection in the natural populations studied. That null result still teaches: a popular theory prediction failed in the field. It pushes theory toward the mess of real populations.
plos-pone-0001380:
Richard Haber and Warren Browner wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study on low phosphate in the blood of malaria patients. Low phosphate shows up in 40 to 60 percent of acute malaria cases. It also shows up in other states marked by high fever. The pair asked whether fever itself might be the cause.

They looked back at records for all adults found to have malaria in their data set. By weighing fever against other traits, they tested the link in a direct way. Sorting out this cause matters for care, since low phosphate can weaken muscles and breathing. The study gives doctors a clearer guide for when to check and treat it.
plos-pone-0001480:
Tihana Jovanic and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on an enzyme that starts gene changes in immune cells. The enzyme sparks changes in antibody genes by altering one DNA letter. Those changes come in two phases, one tied to DNA copying. The team placed the enzyme in a non immune cell line to test its reach.

They found it can spark both kinds of change in test DNA rings that do not copy. That widens the view of how this enzyme can act. Since stray action by it can help cause cancers, sharp maps of its reach matter. The work refines a key step in how antibodies are honed.
plos-pone-0001580:
Nicolas Mathevon and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on birdsong in the rain forest. How song form is shaped by the place it must travel through is a key test of communication theory. Forest air bends sound, so forest birds should sing in ways that carry well there. The team studied a tropical bird's song in its own forest.

They tracked how the song's parts carry data as they move through the trees. Some cues fade fast while others hold up over range. That split shows which parts a mate or rival can truly use at a distance. It refines the rules for how habitats sculpt animal signals.
plos-pone-0001680:
Thomas Steiner and co-authors tuned a glowing protein's folding with a swapped building block, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Green fluorescent protein, GFP, glows under light and is a standard lab marker. Its folding and stability depend in part on proline. That amino acid's bonds can flip between two shapes, and its ring can pucker two ways.

The team replaced proline with fluoroproline, a fluorine-bearing version, to steer those shapes. The full text gives the protein variants, their glow, and their stability measurements. The study shows how one careful swap in a protein's parts list can retune its behavior. Synthetic biology can apply that method to enzymes and materials well beyond GFP.
plos-pone-0001780:
Lee R. Berger, Steven E. Churchill, Bonita De Klerk, and their co-authors reported small-bodied human fossils from Palau in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Surface collection and test excavation in limestone caves in Palau's rock islands, in Micronesia, produced fossil assemblages of small-bodied Homo sapiens. Some features looked primitive, of a kind thought to mark early members of the genus Homo.

The full text describes the bones, their cave context, and the size estimates. Small island humans recall the Flores 'hobbit' finds, and island dwarfing is a known response to isolation and scarce food. The Palau material lets researchers test how fast body size shrinks on islands, and it drew wide debate on how the bones should be interpreted.
plos-pone-0001880:
Dario Greco and colleagues took a broad look at what makes each human tissue distinct in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A liver cell and a skin cell hold the same genes, yet each turns on its own set. Some genes run in all tissues for basic house tasks, while others run in just one or a few tissues.

By pooling gene activity data from many past studies, the team sorted genes into house-wide and tissue-tied groups. They then used those maps to judge how tissues relate to each other in health and in disease. Such maps help labs spot when a tissue has drifted from its true self, a hallmark of many ills.
plos-pone-0001980:
Ron Kerkhoven and co-authors warned of a hidden bias in gene chip studies, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Microarrays read the activity of thousands of genes at once, but samples often must be amplified first. One common method, based on the T7 primer, adds short stretches of six to ten letters to the start of each copied message.

Across more than six thousand arrays, the team found that probes matching those added stretches gave falsely high signals. As the title states, the primer is a source of bias and of variety between platforms. Labs that know the trap can clean old data and design better chips.
plos-pone-0002080:
Ming Li and co-authors found a two-part signal system a pig bacterium needs to cause severe disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Streptococcus suis serotype 2 has evolved into a highly infectious form. It caused two large outbreaks of human disease in China, marked by a toxic shock-like syndrome. How it causes such illness was still being worked out.

The system, called SalK/SalR, is a two-component signal pathway that senses the world and switches genes on. As the title states, it is essential for the full virulence of this invasive strain. Break that sensor, and a drug might disarm the bacterium without killing it outright.
plos-pone-0002180:
Semir Zeki, Oliver Hulme, and Barrie Roulston scanned the brains of people watching regular and irregular visual patterns, for a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The brain is quick to notice when a steady rhythm in what we see is broken. The team set out to find the neural systems that detect predictable timing and departures from it.

Using functional MRI, they watched brain activity while subjects viewed displays whose timing was either regular or irregular. The scans located the areas that respond to each kind of pattern. Knowing where the brain tracks regularity helps explain how we spot the odd event in a stream of sights.
plos-pone-0002280:
Maha Saeed and co-authors looked for surface proteins on the sexual stage of the malaria parasite, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The blood stages of Plasmodium falciparum display many varied, strongly immunogenic proteins on the red cells they infect. Far fewer studies had examined the gametocyte, the stage that mosquitoes pick up to spread malaria.

Using flow cytometry, the team probed the surface of red cells carrying gametocytes for parasite antigens. Finding such proteins matters because antibodies against them could block transmission to mosquitoes. Transmission-blocking targets are a distinct and hopeful front in malaria vaccine research.
plos-pone-0002380:
Led by Overney, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Leila S. Overney, Olaf Blanke, Michael H. Herzog, and others. Its subject is enhanced Temporal but Not Attentional Processing in Expert Tennis Players. In tennis, as in many disciplines of sport, fine spatio-temporal resolution is required to reach optimal performance.

While many studies on tennis have focused on anticipatory skills or decision making, fewer have studied the underlying visual perception abilities. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002480:
Research by Finkelstein and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Myra Finkelstein, Victoria Bakker, Daniel F. Doak, and others. Its subject is evaluating the Potential Effectiveness of Compensatory Mitigation Strategies for Marine Bycatch. Conservationists are continually seeking new strategies to reverse population declines and safeguard against species extinctions.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002580:
Xiang and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Jinhua Xiang, James H. McLinden, Qing Chang, and others. Its subject is characterization of a Peptide Domain within the GB Virus C NS5A Phosphoprotein that Inhibits HIV Replication. GBV-C infection is linked to prolonged survival in HIV-infected people and GBV-C inhibits HIV replication in co-infection models.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002680:
Research from Naila O. Alieva and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers diversity and evolution of coral fluorescent proteins. The catalog record names Naila O. Alieva first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. GFP-like fluorescent proteins (FPs) are the key color determinants in reef-building corals (class Anthozoa. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002780:
Work by Jennifer Winter and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was comparative 3'UTR analysis allows identification of regulatory clusters that drive eph/ephrin expression in cancer cell lines. Authorship is credited in the record to Jennifer Winter and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Eph receptors are the largest family of receptor tyrosine kinases. The authors add a further point. Together with their ligands, the ephrins, they fulfill multiple biological functions. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002880:
Jian Liang, Wenjun Song, Gail Tromp and co-authors surveyed a whole gene family in PLOS ONE in 2008. The family makes CCCH zinc finger proteins, named for the pattern of atoms that grips zinc in each protein. Earlier work had cast some members as brakes on macrophage activation, the process that arms a key immune cell.

The authors combined a genome-wide survey with tests of gene activity to judge the family's role when macrophages switch on. That gives a fuller view than studying one gene at a time. Immunologists get a map of which family members may help calm or shape inflammation.
plos-pone-0002980:
Norbert Dahmen, Nina Manderscheid, Jana Helfrich and co-authors measured the fat signal visfatin in narcolepsy patients in 2008. Narcolepsy is a severe sleep disorder with excess daytime sleepiness, sudden muscle weakness called cataplexy, and a tendency toward obesity. Its main cause is loss of hypocretin-producing neurons, likely by immune attack.

Peripheral visfatin levels were elevated in patients, as the title states. Published in PLOS ONE, the finding connects a sleep disorder with a metabolic signal. It may help explain the weight gain so common in narcolepsy and guide further metabolic study of the condition.
plos-pone-0003080:
Ian Fiske, Emilio Bruna and Benjamin Bolker asked how sample size warps population growth estimates in 2008. Matrix models are widely used to study population dynamics and demography. How the number of sampled individuals influences the estimated growth rate, called lambda, was an important but overlooked issue.

Even unbiased estimates of birth and death rates can combine into biased growth estimates at small samples. Published in PLOS ONE, the analysis warns ecologists that small field samples flatter or sink a population's outlook by chance. Study design for rare species needs that correction. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003180:
John Richards, Beth McNally, Xianfeng Fang and colleagues study how tumour growth affects immune cell production in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Chronic tumour growth is well known to inactivate T cells and NK cells in function. It was less clear whether lymphopoiesis, the making of new lymphoid cells, is also affected. While analysing tumour effects on NK cell development, the team observed a broader pattern.

The title reports that tumour growth decreases NK and B cells as well as common lymphoid progenitors. Readers see cancer suppressing immunity at the source, not just in mature cells. That finding may help explain why immune responses weaken as tumours progress.
plos-pone-0003280:
Darren W. Logan and co-authors study scent signals in mouse urine in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Each species has its own chemical signals, pheromones, that guide acts like fighting, mating and care of young. Most of these cues are still unknown, and few mammal pheromones have been pinned down. The team focus on major urinary proteins, a scent carrier in rodents.

The title reports that these proteins stay species-specific through parallel evolution: lineages changed in like ways on their own. Readers see strong pressure for private scent channels in mammals. Such proteins may be how mice tell kin and rivals from strangers.
plos-pone-0003380:
Stefano Volinia and co-authors hunted for hidden cancer genes in this 2008 paper. Some cancer genes act only when both copies of the gene are lost. Single tests miss such genes, since one working copy can hide the damage. The team combined several kinds of gene damage into one genome-wide search.

They joined data on changed amino acids, broken reading frames, and deleted genes. Looking at the combined signals across more than twenty thousand genes flagged new suspects. The method aims at cancer genes that act in a recessive way. Its list gives other labs fresh targets to test in tumors.
plos-pone-0003480:
Lutz Bornmann, Gerlind Wallon, and Anna Ledin graded grant peer review in this 2008 study. Peer review claims to pick the best science and the best scientists. They tested that claim on two European Molecular Biology Organization programmes. Both pick fellows and young investigators by committee.

The authors checked whether chosen applicants really proved best later. Their analysis probed the selection process programme by programme. Findings like these matter to every funder using expert panels. If review misses top talent, the whole funding system needs repair. Funders across Europe use panels like these for most of their awards.
plos-pone-0003580:
José N. Boada and co-authors proposed a simple drug scoring method in this 2008 paper. Several math models exist to weigh a drug's risks against benefits. Their use in practice has stayed rather limited. The team's aim was a model anyone could apply easily.

Their method, called NEAR, stands for net efficacy adjusted for risk. It builds on the share of patients who respond to treatment. One clear number may help doctors balance benefit and harm. Simple tools stand a better chance of reaching daily prescribing. Doctors weigh such trade-offs daily, often with no clear rule to guide them.
plos-pone-0003680:
Vikram Mehraj, Juanita Hatcher, Saeed Akhtar, and colleagues published this public health study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Intestinal parasites cause illness worldwide, above all where poverty and poor hygiene prevail. The team surveyed children in an urban slum of Karachi, Pakistan.

They measured how common parasitic infection was among the children. They also recorded which household and living factors went with higher risk. The results point prevention toward clean water, hygiene, and the crowded conditions that let parasites spread from child to child in poor districts. Such surveys guide where aid and clean water should go first.
plos-pone-0003780:
Alessandro Esposito, Teresa Tiffert, Jakob M. A. Mauritz, and colleagues published this malaria imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. While growing inside a red blood cell, Plasmodium falciparum eats up to eighty percent of the cell's hemoglobin. That is far more than the parasite needs for food. A model proposed a reason tied to cell balance.

The authors used FRET imaging to measure hemoglobin concentration inside infected red cells. Their readings test the model of how the parasite manages its host cell's contents. The work probes why malaria consumes its host's cargo so far beyond its own needs.
plos-pone-0003880:
Alexandre Leroux and Luis A. Rokeach examined a channel that moves proteins in cells in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns the translocon, a pore in the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum. New proteins pass through it to enter the secretory path. The pore has three main parts, named Sec61 alpha, beta, and gamma in mammals.

Unlike the other parts, the beta part can be lost without stopping transport. The authors tested whether beta parts from unlike species can swap and still work. They found that only its membrane-spanning part is needed for that swap. The result narrows which piece of beta matters most for the pore.
plos-pone-0003980:
Kevin A. Judge and Vanessa L. Bonanno looked for weapons on male field crickets in 2008. Fighting crickets are classic models for male aggression research. They are also famous from cricket fights in Chinese culture. Yet field crickets were not known to carry male weapons.

Their PLOS ONE article reports sexually dimorphic weaponry in a fighting cricket. Males carry structures that females lack, shaped for combat. Such weapons evolve where males fight over mates. Finding them in a model group reopens questions about cricket contests. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004080:
Imma Raurell, Montserrat Codina, David Casagolda, and co-authors studied a protein mutated in inherited Alzheimer's in 2008. Presenilin1 is part of the gamma-secretase complex that cuts proteins. Mutations in it cause familial Alzheimer's disease. Presenilin1 is made as one piece, then split into two linked parts.

Their PLOS ONE article separates the protein's effects on beta-catenin signaling. Some effects need gamma-secretase activity and some do not. Beta-catenin with Tcf-4 switches genes on in that pathway. Untangling the effects clarifies what Alzheimer's mutations disturb beyond cutting. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check. Each claim in it can be checked in the full text that sits with this record.
plos-pone-0004180:
Xiaoxing Huang and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Vaccines given through mucosal surfaces, such as the nose or mouth, can block viruses where they first enter the body. The team compared two vaccinia-based vectors head to head: MVA, a well-known weakened strain, and MVTT, a novel version that can still copy itself.

They measured the neutralising antibody levels each vector produced after mucosal vaccination. They report that MVTT was superior to MVA, inducing higher levels of these virus-blocking antibodies. The comparison informs the design of vaccines delivered without needles.
plos-pone-0004280:
Daniel Wolfe, Anne Buboltz, and Eric Harvill published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Recognising bacterial lipopolysaccharide through Toll-like receptor 4 is a key step in building protection against several Gram-negative germs. B. pertussis causes whooping cough itself. Two Bordetella species, close relatives of the whooping cough germ, trigger robust TLR4 responses that immunity requires.

The team show that Bordetella parapertussis stimulates TLR4 inefficiently, and that this weakness lets it avoid host immunity. A quiet knock at the immune system's door, it seems, lets this pathogen slip inside. Weak sensing, in this case, is the pathogen's best disguise.
plos-pone-0004380:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome, called ARDS, is a severe lung failure. It can follow infection or injury and often needs intensive care. Zhaoxi Wang, Feng Chen, Rihong Zhai, and co-authors searched blood for early warning signs. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper began with gene activity measured across the whole blood genome.

That scan flagged a gene for elafin, a protein that blocks the enzyme neutrophil elastase. Elafin output fell during the early phase of ARDS. Blood tests then showed elafin levels dropping fast as well. An imbalance between the enzyme and its blocker tracked with ARDS taking hold. Such a marker could help doctors spot the syndrome sooner.
plos-pone-0004480:
Weakened malaria parasites that cannot complete their life cycle still teach the immune system to protect, compare Kota Arun Kumar, Peter Baxter, Alice Tarun, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Shots using sporozoites, the parasite stage injected by mosquitoes, weakened by radiation give full protection in mice and people. Parasites weakened by gene deletion arrest their growth in a like way.

The genes removed are called uis3 and uis4. The team asked whether the protection from these gene-deleted parasites rests on the same mechanisms as the radiation version. Shared protective mechanisms would be good news for vaccine design. It would mean more than one way of weakening the parasite leads to the same strong defense, making a sporozoite vaccine easier to build and trust.
plos-pone-0004580:
A protein that helps hold cells together can feed into a growth pathway when those joins break, show Yoonseok Kam and Vito Quaranta in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is beta-catenin. It is an essential part of two systems: adherens junctions, which glue cells to each other, and the Wnt signaling pathway, which tells cells to grow and divide.

A connection between the two beta-catenin pools had been suggested but never conclusively shown. The authors present evidence that when adherens junctions dissociate, the freed beta-catenin feeds into the Wnt pathway. That link matters for cancer, where cells break their joins to spread. It suggests losing adhesion can directly switch on growth signals, not merely loosen the cell.
plos-pone-0004680:
Antonio Garcia-España and colleagues traced how introns changed over time in one gene family, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Introns are the parts of genes that are cut out before a protein is made. Large scans can show broad trends in intron gain and loss, but fine detail needs a closer look.

The team used a family of membrane proteins whose form and job are well known. By mapping introns across species in that family, they could test ideas about gain and loss. Close cases like this check if broad claims hold up. They also show how gene shape shifts over long spans of time.
plos-pone-0004780:
Andi Gusti and colleagues showed that an Arabidopsis F-box protein is essential for the second pollen division, in PLOS ONE in 2009. In fungi and animals, SCF type ligases drive cell cycle steps by destroying brake proteins. One key checkpoint is the move from rest phase into DNA copying, where brakes must fall on schedule.

The team report that the plant protein FBL17 plays the matching role in pollen. Without it, pollen cannot complete its second mitosis. The finding ties plant reproduction to a conserved cycle machine. It matters for seed set and crop yield. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0004880:
Frédéric Hoerndli and colleagues showed a conserved function of C. elegans CASY-1 calsyntenin in associative learning, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genome wide link studies in humans enabled unbiased discovery of genes linked with memory performance. Such studies cannot test cause directly. Polymorphisms in Calsyntenin 2 were candidates requiring causal tests in model organisms with conserved genes and measurable learning behaviors.

Worm CASY-1 mutants learn links poorly. Function is conserved across vast evolution. Simple models validate human genetics findings. Memory steps share ancient components. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are. The worm is small and cheap to keep, so tests can run fast. Genes first found in people can thus be checked in weeks, not years.
plos-pone-0004980:
The human genome still hides unnamed genes. Evolution can point to some of them. Ming-Wei Kuo and colleagues tested one prediction in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used zebrafish as their model organism. The candidate was a novel gene called puf-A. It had been predicted from evolutionary analysis of human DNA.

Testing showed puf-A is a real, working gene. It is involved in the development of eyes. It also matters for primordial germ cells, the earliest forerunners of eggs and sperm. The study proves a computer-predicted gene is vital. It is a win for evolution-guided gene hunting, which can find genes that standard annotation misses.
plos-pone-0005080:
In rich countries, TB is often seen as curable with little lasting harm. Thaddeus Miller and colleagues challenged that view in PLOS ONE in 2009. They measured health quality lost to tuberculosis. The measure was quality-adjusted life years, for patients and for society. Most survivors carry chronic lung damage, earlier research showed.

The toll proved larger than assumed. Personal losses persist after the cure. Societal losses add up across cases. Death from TB is rare in developed countries, yet the disease still steals healthy years. The numbers give policymakers a truer price tag. They support stronger investment in prevention and follow-up care.
plos-pone-0005180:
Fibromyalgia causes wide pain and low mood, and its cause is still not known. One idea blames a fault in the body's own opioid system, the built-in pain control network. Younger and colleagues tested that idea in PLOS ONE in 2009 with women with and without the condition.

The team gave participants naltrexone, a drug that blocks opioid signals, and tracked pain and mood. As the title states, they found no sign that the opioid system drives the illness. A clear negative result like this matters, because it steers the search for causes toward other systems.
plos-pone-0005280:
In families with a single-gene disorder, affected relatives share the chromosome stretch that carries the fault. Jiang and colleagues presented a mapping method built on that sharing in PLOS ONE in 2009, using dense SNP genotype data.

Their homozygosity haplotype analysis looks for the shared interval around the disease mutation. Dense modern genotype data make the shared stretch easier to spot than before. A sharper method speeds the hunt for disease genes in families, a step toward diagnosis and counseling. Small towns and rare diseases gain most from this method, since a few families with the same rare fault can lead a team straight to the gene at fault.
plos-pone-0005380:
Orientation selectivity lets visual cortex neurons respond to edges at set angles, a basis of shape perception. How that selectivity is built in early life, and how long it stays changeable, were open questions. Tanaka and colleagues defined the sensitive period in cats in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team identified a postnatal critical period for orientation plasticity in the cat visual cortex. During that window, experience can reshape orientation tuning; after it, tuning hardens. Timing the window guides research on lazy eye and other early vision problems. Young cats are a classic model for the young brain, since their sight grows up in weeks. Not years, and what holds in them has oft held in the young of our own kind too.
plos-pone-0005480:
Szabolcs Lengyel and co-authors studied ants and flowering plants in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Flowering plants spread fast in the age of the dinosaurs and after, reshaping life on land. Animals helped by carrying pollen and seeds from place to place.

The team asked how much ants, as seed carriers, shaped that spread. They compared plant groups whose seeds ants carry with the family trees of those plants. Their evidence links ant carriage to faster splitting into new species. That gives small, ground-level ants a large role in the history of the world's flora.
plos-pone-0005580:
Oriana Losito and co-authors presented a lab method for studying rare cell signals in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Inositol pyrophosphates are signalling molecules inside cells that add a special tag to proteins. They likely affect many cell jobs, but they are hard to measure with common tools.

Their method uses gel separation to tell these molecules apart and track them. A ready way to see them opens the field to more labs. With better measurement, workers can learn what these signals do in energy use, growth, and stress responses. The molecules also flag how active a cell is, so measuring them well could serve many studies at once.
plos-pone-0005680:
Charlotte Faurie, Andrew Russell, and Virpi Lummaa tested birth-order effects in old Finnish records in 2009. Parents have limited time and food, so brothers and sisters compete for care. Some studies claim middle children get less and fare worse in life.

The team used data from Finns who lived before modern industry to test that claim fairly. In such a setting, family size and child deaths follow a natural pattern, free of modern birth control. Their checks ask whether middleborns truly end up less fit than first or last borns. The work helps sort real birth-order effects from mere family-size effects.
plos-pone-0005780:
Jamal Stie, Gillian Bruni, and Deborah Fox showed in 2009 how a fungus grabs a human protein to break into tissues. Cryptococcus neoformans causes serious illness in people with weak immunity. It enters through the lungs and can reach the brain.

On its surface, the fungus binds plasminogen, a blood protein that, once active, dissolves the webs between cells. Riding that enzyme lets the fungus invade the matrix that holds tissues together. Blocking the grab could slow its spread in the body. The study names a surface interaction that drug or vaccine work might target.
plos-pone-0005880:
Jin-Ming Tee and co-authors balanced two signal systems in 2009 to steer how muscle fibers grow in zebrafish. Muscle development gone wrong causes wasting conditions, and fiber type, slow or fast, shapes strength and endurance. Wnt signaling and myostatin, a growth brake, both act on the process.

Using genetic and chemical tools, the team showed tight regulation of Wnt and beta-catenin is essential for fiber growth and upkeep, in interplay with myostatin. The balance offers two levers for muscle research rather than one. It may inform treatments for muscle loss that target signaling instead of bulk protein alone.
plos-pone-0005980:
Small RNAs can switch genes off, and some of them travel. Rebecca Schwab, Alexis Maizel, Virginia Ruiz-Ferrer and colleagues showed that reach in the plant Arabidopsis in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies tasiRNAs, a class of small RNA found only in plants, made when another small RNA cuts a longer message.

These homegrown tasiRNAs affect gene control in cells beyond the ones that made them, a pattern called a non-cell-autonomous effect. A signal that moves can coordinate a whole tissue, not just one cell. The work adds a mobile layer to plant gene control and helps explain how plants pattern leaves and other parts so evenly.
plos-pone-0006080:
A diabetes drug came under a cloud when pooled trials linked it to heart attacks. Colin Dormuth, Malcolm Maclure, Greg Carney and colleagues checked that signal in everyday care in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper estimates the link between rosiglitazone and acute myocardial infarction in real-world patients who had previously been prescribed metformin.

Trial pools had suggested a rise in risk of roughly forty percent, a signal strong enough to demand a real-world test. Patients already on metformin form a group where the drug was often added next. The study shows how safety questions move from trials to practice, and it gives prescribers evidence drawn from people like their own patients.
plos-pone-0006180:
Damage to the sciatic nerve, the large nerve running down the leg, can take away movement and feeling. Wenjie Sun and colleagues tested a repair aid in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The aid was human nerve growth factor tied to laminin, a protein in tissue scaffolding. Growth factor helps nerves regrow, but free doses wash away fast.

Binding the factor to laminin holds it where the injury needs it. The team reports better regrowth of the nerve with this anchored form. The idea points toward treatments that keep helpful proteins in place longer. For patients with nerve injuries, steadier local repair could mean better recovery of strength and feeling.
plos-pone-0006280:
Anthrax toxin drills a pore through cell membranes to deliver its killing parts. Jie Wang and colleagues examined phenylalanine building blocks in the pore's stem in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The pore is built by the toxin's protective antigen part, which rearranges inside the cell's sorting compartments.

The study maps what those phenylalanine residues do as the pore forms and works. Certain residues prove key to the stem's function. Each weak point in pore assembly is a possible drug target. Blocking the pore would stop the toxin before its enzymes enter the cell.
plos-pone-0006380:
A tumor suppressor locus called INK4a helps push worn-out cells into retirement. Goedele Maertens and colleagues found several distinct Polycomb complexes sitting on that locus in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Misexpression of Polycomb repressive complex parts strongly influences when cells enter senescence, through control of INK4a.

Using tandem affinity purification, the team identified complexes containing CBX7 and CBX8 that regulate and co-localise on the locus. Multiple complexes sharing one address suggests layered control. That control decides whether cells keep dividing or stop. Cancer often breaks exactly this switch.
plos-pone-0006480:
Christian Quaia, Howard Ying, and Lance Optican tested a theory of eye muscle mechanics in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team had studied passive eye muscles in living monkeys under anesthesia and paralysis in depth. Eye muscles are not simple springs; they resist stretch in complex, time-dependent ways. Rheological measurements, which track that behavior, are hard to interpret.

Here they test the quasi-linear theory, a model for such viscoelastic tissues. A good model lets researchers predict muscle force during eye movements. That prediction feeds larger models of how the brain steers gaze. The study is part two of their work on passive eye muscle properties.
plos-pone-0006580:
Joong Kyu Kim, Mark Klinger, Jonathan Benjamin, and colleagues studied regulatory T cell maintenance in PLOS ONE in 2009. Signaling through the T cell antigen receptor is important for homeostasis of naive and memory CD4 T cells. The significance of that signaling in regulatory T cells was their focus. Regulatory cells keep the immune system from attacking the body.

They examined impact of the TCR signal on regulatory T cell homeostasis, function, and trafficking. A cell that must sense its target to survive is tightly coupled to its job. Their findings inform efforts to boost or suppress these cells in autoimmunity and transplantation.
plos-pone-0006680:
Tamás Nepusz, Andrea Petróczi, and Declan P. Naughton built a network tool for food safety monitoring in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their starting point was the Beijing Declaration on food safety and security. More than fifty countries signed that agreement. It called for full programs to watch over food safety for their citizens. At the time, no complete global monitoring system existed.

The authors used network analysis to organize food safety information across countries. Their tool highlights patterns that single reports can miss. In their analysis, China stood out as a country needing attention. A shared monitoring view could help governments spot risks earlier. It could also guide where inspection and reporting need strengthening.
plos-pone-0006780:
Teresa Simonetti and her team raised mice in rich, busy homes from birth in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early life experience shapes how sense circuits grow. Much less was known about how it shapes motor areas. The striatum steers both movement and thought. Its wiring grows in the first weeks of life.

The rich homes sped up growth of a motor control area in the mice. Skills grew faster and the cells looked more mature too. So experience speeds motor growth, not just the senses. Early homes may set the pace of motor learning for life. The work counts for care of infants who start life with too little to explore.
plos-pone-0006880:
Guisheng Song and Li Wang traced how a nuclear receptor switches on a small RNA in PLOS ONE in 2009. MicroRNAs fine-tune many cell functions in mammals. How microRNA genes themselves get transcribed was poorly known. The receptor studied is SHP, short for small heterodimer partner. Profiling showed a marked change in one microRNA, miR-206.

SHP activates miR-206 expression through a cascade of two inhibitions. Inhibiting an inhibitor amounts to switching the gene on. A dual inhibitory cascade gives the cell fine control. The mechanism is a neat piece of regulatory logic. It also adds miR-206 control to SHP's metabolic roles.
plos-pone-0006980:
Lang Rao, Xiubo Zhao, Fang Pan, and colleagues studied an enzyme from a salt-loving microbe in PLOS ONE in 2009. Halophiles are extremophiles that thrive where salt levels are very high. How their enzymes keep working in such brine was little understood. The team examined one such enzyme, a halophilic esterase.

They measured how the enzyme behaves and acts in strong salt solutions. Most proteins fall apart or clump under those conditions. Learning how this one stays soluble and active has practical value. Salt-tough enzymes could serve industry in processes where ordinary enzymes fail.
plos-pone-0007080:
Noriko Okamoto, Chitchai Chantangsi, Aleš Horák, and colleagues described a new microbe in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many photosynthetic groups carry plastids gained from red algae long ago. A hypothesis called Chromalveolata grouped them as sharing one such gain. Tests of that idea need better family trees of these organisms.

The team named a new genus and species, the katablepharid Roombia truncata. Their molecular phylogeny also supported a new high-level taxon, Hacrobia. Naming and placing one small predator reshapes the map of early eukaryote history. Trees like this test grand ideas about how complex cells evolved.
plos-pone-0007180: Dimitrios Kapogiannis, Aron K. Barbey, Michael Su, and colleagues explored links between brain anatomy and religiosity in PLOS ONE in 2009. Religiosity varies widely from person to person. The authors ask whether that variation tracks with measurable differences in brain structure. Their study treats religious tendency as a trait that can be compared across people. It uses neuroanatomical measures to place questions about belief within brain research.
plos-pone-0007280:
Tomasz Jaworski, Ilse Dewachter, Benoit Lechat, and colleagues tested the tau protein's role in Alzheimer disease in mice in 2009. In Alzheimer disease, tau damage is often considered secondary to amyloid. That ranking stayed unclear, because transgenic mouse models could not settle their relative contributions to brain damage.

The authors deliver tau using a virus vector, called AAV-tau, in normal mice. They report pyramidal neuron degeneration driven by cell-cycle re-entry. Notably, this happens without neurofibrillary tangle formation. Their result separates tau-driven neuron loss from tangle formation, two features often assumed to move together.
plos-pone-0007380: Jill Koshiol, Melissa Rotunno, Dario Consonni, and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on lung disease and cancer risk. Their subject is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term lung condition that makes breathing hard. They examine whether having that disease alters the risk of lung cancer. The study design is a population-based case-control study. It compares people with lung cancer against controls from the same population.
plos-pone-0007480:
Colton Linnertz and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the genetics behind Parkinson's disease. Variation around a gene called SNCA is repeatedly linked to Parkinson's risk. That gene makes alpha-synuclein, a protein that piles up in patients' brains. Evidence suggests the amount of the protein matters, not just its form. The team asked whether DNA differences change how much message the gene produces.

They measured SNCA message levels across several human brain tissues. Genetic variation in the region did track with differences in expression. That connects inherited spelling differences to dosage differences in the brain. Dosage, in turn, is a plausible driver of disease risk. The findings support the idea that too much of a normal protein can be harmful. They also sharpen the search for how Parkinson's begins.
plos-pone-0007580:
Dhruv Grover and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on hydrogen peroxide as more than a disinfectant. Inside the body, peroxide also acts as a signal tied to the cell's redox state. Daily locomotor rhythms are among the outputs of the biological clock. Several redox-active compounds were known to interact with clock machinery. The team exposed fruit flies to hydrogen peroxide and tracked their activity and behavior.

Peroxide stimulated the flies' activity and altered their behavior. The effect links redox chemistry to the rhythms the clock controls. A signal molecule made during normal metabolism can thus move behavior. That closes a loop between the cell's chemical state and the animal's day. The finding may help explain how metabolism talks back to the clock. It gives circadian research a simple chemical lever to work with.
plos-pone-0007680:
Robert Steele and Catherine Dana published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It traces a gene sperm need to fuse with an egg. The gene, called HAP2 or GCS1, first appeared in the shared ancestor of plants, animals and protists. Simple organisms such as Chlamydomonas and Plasmodium need it to reproduce.

The authors traced the gene's history across the animal family tree, the group named metazoans. They found a copy in a genome they searched and mapped where the gene was kept or lost. The story shows how one old gene came to serve sex in many forms of life.
plos-pone-0007780:
Kenta Nakamura and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines how human pluripotent stem cell colonies form and organize. Making such colonies from adult cells involves a dramatic change in shape and layout. The finished colonies look just like those of embryonic stem cells.

The team focused on signals from receptors called GPCRs that work through Gi proteins. They found this signaling controls both colony formation and colony organization. Knowing which signals steer colony growth helps labs grow stem cells more reliably. Reliable growth is a basic need for future cell therapies.
plos-pone-0007880:
Rakhee Sachdeva and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests three DNA vaccine designs against visceral leishmaniasis in mice. The disease, also called kala-azar, is a major worldwide health problem. It is caused by a parasite and can kill if untreated.

Genetic vaccines can deliver strings of T cell targets in series, an approach called polytope. The team compared a single antigen vaccine, gp63, with polytope designs. One design added a heat shock protein, HSP70. They measured both immune response and protection. The comparison helps vaccine builders choose formats for parasite diseases.
plos-pone-0007980:
Todd Brusko and colleagues studied a receptor part that helps steer immune cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The part is CD25, a piece of the receptor for IL-2, a signal that tells T cells to grow. Gene hunts had linked the CD25 region to immune diseases, type 1 diabetes among them.

The team asked how steady CD25 sits on the cell surface and what that steadiness does to cell action. Both guard cells and attack cells of the immune system feel the effect. Their results help explain how small shifts in this one part can tilt the whole immune balance.
plos-pone-0008080:
Amalia Trousson and colleagues traced a harmful talk between two chemical families in brain support cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. One family is oxysterols, worn forms of cholesterol tied to brain diseases like multiple sclerosis. The other is glucocorticoids, the body's stress hormones.

Together, the two families changed how the cells handle a fat-cutting enzyme. They also raised the odds of death in oligodendrocytes. Those are the cells that wrap nerves in insulation. Losing those wrappers slows nerve signals. The harmful pairing names a step where treatment might break the chain.
plos-pone-0008180:
Deepti Joshi and colleagues examined breast cancer in rural Indian women in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women worldwide. Known risk factors explain only a small share of cases. One debated idea is that a virus helps trigger some tumors. Epstein-Barr virus is a leading candidate in that debate.

The authors tested whether Epstein-Barr infection is linked with breast cancer in their study group. Finding or ruling out such a link matters for how doctors think about causes. It could also shape future work on prevention. The study adds data from a population that research often overlooks.
plos-pone-0008280:
Karla P. Figueroa and colleagues studied a gene in severely obese children in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Expanding a repeat in the ATXN2 gene causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 2. That is a neurodegenerative disease affecting coordination. Unlike similar repeats, the SCA2 repeat is not highly variable. The team asked whether normal variation in this gene relates to obesity.

They examined genetic variance in ATXN2 in children with severe early onset obesity. A gene known for brain degeneration might also influence body weight. Finding such a link would connect two fields of medicine. The study tests that possibility directly in children.
plos-pone-0008380:
Kenta Nakamura and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about mice with weak lymph vessels. Lymph vessels drain fluid from flesh. When they fail, limbs swell, the skin gets sore and raw, and tissue can break down in time. The team asked if a drug that calms sore tissue could help this state. They gave the mice a pain drug called ketoprofen, of the NSAID class.

The drug eased the lymph vessel failure in the mice. Calming the sore tissue thus helped the vessels do their job once more. Care for swollen limbs might gain from this kind of drug. The work gives a fresh lead for a state that has few good cures.
plos-pone-0008480:
Jinong Feng and co-authors link a gene to fibromyalgia in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Fibromyalgia causes chronic, widespread pain in muscles and joints. It affects about two in a hundred people, most of them women. Both genes and environment play a part. Patients and their parents show high blood levels of a signal called IL-1beta. The team study the MEFV gene in these patients.

They find missense changes in MEFV are tied to the syndrome. Missense changes swap one building block in a protein. Those changes also track with higher IL-1beta levels. The link gives a gene clue for a disorder long hard to explain.
plos-pone-0008580:
John Simes and co-authors present a trial method in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In long-term clinical trials, patients often take other active treatments. Uptake of those drugs may differ between trial arms. That difference can mask the true benefit or harm of the tested treatment. Past methods to adjust for such contamination often broke randomization. Breaking it undermines the trial's core strength. The authors propose a novel method to adjust efficacy estimates.

Their method allows for uptake of other treatments while preserving randomization. Preserving it keeps comparisons fair between arms. More accurate estimates help patients and doctors judge a drug's real effect. The method serves any long trial where outside treatments are common.
plos-pone-0008680:
Paul Holland and Thomas Hollis examined a repair enzyme from the gut germ Escherichia coli. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, called AlkB, fixes a kind of chemical damage to DNA. Extra methyl groups stuck on DNA letters can kill a cell. AlkB removes two such lesions and leaves others alone.

The pair combined shape studies with targeted changes to the enzyme. Changing single building blocks showed which parts choose the target. They also probed how AlkB searches DNA for damage. The results explain the pickiness of a repair worker found in many living things, humans included.
plos-pone-0008780:
Richard Carr, Ruth Sittl, Johannes Fleckenstein, and colleagues found a surprise effect of GABA on human nerves. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. GABA is the brain's main calming signal chemical. Some skin sensory fibers respond to chemical irritants and pain triggers. Those thin fibers lack the insulation called myelin. Textbooks would predict GABA should quiet them, not excite them.

In a subset of these unmyelinated axons, GABA raised electrical excitability instead. More excitable fibers could mean more pain or itch signaling. The flip side of a famous signal matters for pain research. It may also explain odd drug effects on sensation.
plos-pone-0008880:
João Zilhão, Simon Davis, Cidália Duarte, and colleagues dated early human remains at a cave in western Portugal. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neandertals lingered in Iberia long after vanishing elsewhere in Europe. Modern humans arrived there later than in regions farther east. Pego do Diabo, near Loures, holds layers from that transition. Pinning ages to those layers tests when modern anatomy reached Europe's far west.

Dating placed the modern human presence and its tools in sequence with late Neandertal layers. The overlap period can now be measured in millennia. A firm date reshapes stories of Europe's last Neandertals. It also anchors the spread of modern humans across the continent.
plos-pone-0008980:
Ana Cachaço and co-authors studied how radiation harms mouse bone marrow, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancer patients treated with radiation or strong drugs sometimes develop damaged marrow later. The marrow then kills off too many of its own cells and blood counts fall. That condition, secondary myelodysplastic syndrome, is growing more common as more patients survive cancer.

The team focused on TNF-alpha, an inflammatory signal, in the marrow's support tissue. After irradiation, this signal shaped how marrow cells died and how the tissue reacted. Adjusting TNF-alpha changed the damage pattern in the marrow environment. The finding may help protect blood production in patients who need radiation.
plos-pone-0009080:
Annett Schirmer tested whether the tone of a voice rewrites how words feel in memory, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Words carry an emotional charge of their own, pleasant or unpleasant. Speakers also colour words with prosody, the melody and mood of speech. The study asked which signal wins when word and voice disagree.

Volunteers heard words spoken in matching or mismatched tones of voice. Later they took a recognition test based only on memory. The voice's tone shifted how the words had been stored in memory. It tilted the felt emotion of the words themselves, this study showed.
plos-pone-0009180:
Hyun Jin Kim and colleagues published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject is PDC109, a protein found in bull semen. The protein is built from two similar blocks joined by a flexible linker. It helps sperm bind to the wall of the cow's oviduct, the tube where eggs travel.

Binding happens through fats on the sperm cell surface called phosphorylcholines. The team studied how PDC109 changes shape as it moves and how it grabs onto those fats. Shape changes matter because a stiff or loose form can bind weakly or strongly. The work adds detail to how sperm are stored in the oviduct before fertilization.
plos-pone-0009280:
Christopher Langendorf and co-authors published this protein structure study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It examines an enzyme called succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase, or SSADH. In mammals this enzyme helps break down GABA, the brain's main calming signal. People born lacking it build up GABA and a related chemical, with serious effects.

The team solved the enzyme's three-dimensional structure from the bacterium Escherichia coli using X-ray methods. The structure shows how the enzyme grips its helper molecule, NADP+. Seeing that grip in atomic detail explains how the enzyme does its chemistry. It also offers clues for understanding the human form and its failures.
plos-pone-0009380:
Xin Sun and co-authors published this nerve injury study in PLOS ONE in 2010. After injury to the brain or spinal cord, inflammation adds to the damage. Harm spreads beyond the first wound and recovery shrinks. Myelin, the insulation stripped from injured axons, was the team's suspect.

In a mouse system, myelin switched on three signaling pathways: FAK, Akt, and NF-kappaB. It also provoked an inflammatory response that depended on a receptor called CR3. Debris that was supposed to be inert turns out to shout for inflammation. That finding suggests calming the response to myelin could limit secondary damage after CNS injury.
plos-pone-0009480:
Geng Chen, Garrett League, and Sang-Chul Nam studied a protein in fruit fly eyes in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein is spastin. Faults in its gene are the most common cause of a human disease that stiffens and weakens the legs. In flies, the team looked at the light sensing cells of the eye as they develop.

A fault in spastin shifted parts of those cells out of place as their tips grew. Light sensing rods in the eye need exact layout to work. The work shows what spastin does inside a growing cell. That helps explain why its loss harms nerve cells in people.
plos-pone-0009580:
Kurt Pfannkuche and colleagues improved the picking of reprogrammed stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Adult cells can be pushed back to a stem cell state, called induced pluripotent stem cells. Workers usually pick the best colonies by their shape alone. Many colonies that look right are not fully reprogrammed, though. The team added a selection step based on a marker called UTF1.

Temporarily selecting for UTF1 greatly raised the share of truly reprogrammed colonies. Those colonies held their stem cell traits in later tests. A better filter saves time and raises the quality of cell lines. That matters for any use of these cells in research or medicine.
plos-pone-0009680:
Clinics treating HIV often track viral load, the amount of virus in a patient's blood. John Koethe and colleagues set out in 2010 to test whether routine viral load checks improve care in Zambia. Their PLOS ONE report covers the design of a cluster randomized trial. In this design, whole clinics, not single patients, were assigned to each approach.

The authors describe how the trial was put in place and who joined it at the start. Baseline details on the patients show what the two groups looked like before follow-up began. If routine checks prove useful, the trial could shape HIV care well beyond Zambia.
plos-pone-0009780:
Peter E. Larsen and co-authors published a genomics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study uses deep RNA sequencing to fix gene maps for Laccaria bicolor, a fungus that partners with tree roots. Gene maps drawn from DNA alone are often wrong, and RNA reads show the true shape of active genes.

The team focused on 1,501 gene models that differ between free-living and root-linked growth. For 96 percent of them, the method built clean corrected models with all error flags cleared. Most of the standard gene models, 69 percent, had in fact strayed from the RNA sequence. The authors offer the method for other species as well.
plos-pone-0009880:
Counting a pandemic's true toll takes more than counting confirmed cases. Fatimah Dawood and colleagues estimated the disease burden of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic in one Australian region. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many infections were mild and never reached a clinic.

The region was Hunter New England in northern New South Wales. Disease burden folds together cases, hospital stays, deaths, and strain on services. Estimates like this show how hard the pandemic hit one community in 2009. Planners use such numbers to prepare for the next pandemic. Local records grounded the estimate in real cases.
plos-pone-0009980:
Salmon engineered to grow fast may respond to warm water differently from wild fish. Mare Lõhmus and colleagues compared the two kinds across temperatures. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The fish were coho salmon, a Pacific species farmed and wild.

Genotype-temperature interaction means genes and warmth jointly shape the outcome. The team tracked development, growth, and morphometrics, body measurements, in both groups. Growth-hormone transgenic fish carry an added gene that speeds growth. How they fare as waters warm matters for farms and wild runs alike. Warm water speeds growth in most fish.
plos-pone-0010180:
The authors were Olga Matveeva, Yibin Kang, Alexey Spiridonov, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study improved design rules for RNA interference tools. RNA interference uses small RNA pieces, called shRNAs, to switch off chosen genes. Predicting which pieces will work well is a serious challenge, especially for genome-wide libraries used to test every gene.

The team optimized two features: how stable the RNA duplex is, and how uneven its two ends are. Better design rules mean fewer wasted pieces in large screens. That raises the odds that a screen points to the right gene the first time.
plos-pone-0010280:
Albert Wong modeled tiny fat bubbles used to carry drugs in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Liposomes can wrap a drug inside and deliver it in the body. For real use, they must behave well in the body and be made fast, at scale. Earlier work had not firmly established the general rules linking production choices to that in-body behavior.

Wong built a quantitative model covering both high-throughput production and in vivo kinetics. The model aims to pick design settings that give the wanted travel and release pattern. Better liposome rules can shorten the path from laboratory idea to a usable medicine carrier.
plos-pone-0010380:
Christiaan Masson, Jogchum Plat and Ronald Mensink mapped fat-handling proteins along the human gut in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gut absorbs cholesterol and long-chain fats from food. Transport proteins in the gut wall do that absorbing. Where along the tract each protein sits had rarely been charted. The team used samples from eleven people who had died, covering the tract from top to bottom.

Protein levels turned out to vary by location rather than staying even. That pattern matters for drugs that block fat uptake to lower cholesterol. A blocker works only where its target protein actually sits. The map also helps explain why some gut regions absorb more fat than others. It is basic anatomy with direct use in medicine.
plos-pone-0010480:
Brian Letzen and co-workers profiled tiny RNAs as stem cells became myelin-making cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oligodendrocytes wrap nerve fibers in myelin, speeding signals along them. They can be grown from human embryonic stem cells in the lab. That growth path could one day repair lost sensation or movement. The team tracked microRNAs, small RNAs that tune genes, along the differentiation path.

MicroRNA patterns shifted in an orderly way as cells matured. Those patterns can serve as signposts that the process is on track. They may also be levers to push cells toward the desired type. Demyelinating diseases, like multiple sclerosis, motivate this work. A reliable recipe for making oligodendrocytes is a long-sought goal.
plos-pone-0010580:
Rainer Strotmann and colleagues examined a calcium channel called TRPV4 in PLOS ONE in 2010. Channels like TRPV4 act as gates in the cell surface. When calcium passes through, the gate can become even more active for a while.

The team tested how parts of the channel protein interact with each other. They found that contacts between its inner regions control the calcium-driven boost. Changing those contact points changed how strongly the channel responded. The work clarifies how sensory channels tune their own sensitivity, a process that matters for touch, pressure sensing, and fluid balance.
plos-pone-0010680:
Alberto Diaz de Leon and colleagues linked chromosome caps to lung scarring, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The caps, called telomeres, shorten each time a cell divides. The enzyme telomerase can rebuild them. Rare faults in its gene TERT run in some families with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a stiffening of the lungs.

The team measured cap length and TERT faults in patients and families. Short caps appeared in many patients, even without a clear TERT fault. That points to cap wear as a shared thread in this disease. Checking cap length may help spot at-risk relatives before their lungs show damage.
plos-pone-0010780:
Keyan Zhao and colleagues read diversity across the rice genome, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Asian rice feeds more people than any other crop. Its two great groups, indica and japonica, split deeply long ago. Breeding since then has moved genes between groups in waves of crossing, a process called introgression.

Genome scans showed how much mixing each part of the genome carries. Some regions resisted mixing and hold the groups' core differences. Other regions crossed freely under breeding. Knowing which parts move easily guides breeders. Yield and toughness traits can be borrowed, while the traits that define each type stay intact.
plos-pone-0010880:
Sofia Caesar, Magnus Karlsson and Anders Forsman published this grasshopper study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pygmy grasshoppers come in many color patterns, and theory says a mix of types in a group can ease competition because different types use resources differently. But varied groups may also be less closely related, which could carry its own costs.

The authors set up groups whose founding mothers varied in number, then tracked survival at low and high density. Survival was better at low density, and at high density it peaked when color diversity sat in the middle range, not at the extremes. Family ties also shaped the outcome. Caesar and colleagues provide rare hard evidence that variety within a species can help or hinder survival depending on crowding, a nuance for how biodiversity is valued.
plos-pone-0010980:
Steven Schutzer, Tao Liu, Benjamin Natelson and co-authors published this cerebrospinal fluid study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The fluid bathing the brain and spine carries proteins that could reveal brain disease. Yet no one had listed its normal contents. Truly healthy samples are hard to obtain. The team applied high-sensitivity protein analysis to fluid from healthy volunteers.

They identified more than two and half thousand proteins in normal spinal fluid. Over half were specific to that fluid, absent from a much larger catalogue of blood plasma proteins the team built for comparison. Samples from symptomatic patients that labs had called normal still differed significantly. Schutzer and colleagues supply a reference proteome, the baseline that any spinal fluid biomarker for brain disease must be judged against.
plos-pone-0011080:
May, Bennett and Stevenson described a new lab tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was a mouse herpesvirus that can hide in the body and later wake up again. Studying that hiding and waking in living animals is slow and hard, so a dish based system was needed.

The team built a system in cell culture where the virus can be kept quiet and then switched back on. That setup lets researchers trigger each stage on demand in the lab. It should speed work on herpesviruses as a group. It also cuts the need for some animal tests.
plos-pone-0011180:
Kazembe and Mpeketula mapped newborn deaths in PLOS ONE in 2010. Where a baby is born can strongly affect its chance of survival. Using a structured model that accounts for place, the authors measured how newborn death rates vary across areas.

Their map shows clear spatial gaps, with some areas facing far higher risk than neighbors. National averages hide those pockets of danger. Aid aimed at the highest risk areas can save more of the most fragile newborns. The method gives health planners a tool to target clinics, staff and supplies where need is greatest.
plos-pone-0011280:
Teng, Chen, Lai and colleagues studied a beet virus in PLOS ONE in 2010. Beet severe curly top virus spreads through a plant by moving from cell to cell and through its veins. The team examined one small viral protein, called C4, for its part in that movement.

The protein proved involved in how the virus travels within the plant. Without effective movement, an infection stays local and mild. A movement factor is therefore a good target for crop protection. Resistant beet varieties or treatments that block this protein could limit a damaging disease of sugar beets and other crops.
plos-pone-0011380:
Bruce Hostager and colleagues identified in 2010 a new working part in the chain by which immune cells answer the CD40 signal. CD40 is a receptor that, when triggered, switches on a master controller of inflammation and immune defense genes. Mapping every link in that chain helps explain how B cells get activated during infection and vaccination.

The team showed that a protein called HOIP, which binds a partner protein, sits inside the CD40 signaling complex and helps tune the master switch. Placing HOIP in the chain gives immunologists a more complete wiring diagram of immune activation. That diagram matters for diseases where CD40 signaling runs too hot or too weak, and it names a fresh point where drugs might adjust the response with care.
plos-pone-0011480:
Lily Kahsai and co-authors reported in 2010 that a small group of brain cells in fruit flies steers how the whole body handles metabolic stress. When food runs out, the fly must ration energy and change behavior to survive. Neurosecretory cells in the brain release chemical messengers called neuropeptides, and these cells release several different ones at once rather than a single signal.

The team showed that this brain center modulates the fly's response to starvation through its cocktail of messengers. A compact control center that speaks in mixtures can fine-tune the response in ways one signal cannot. Fruit flies are a stand-in for broader biology here: human brains also govern hunger and energy with peptide signals. The study gives that shared system a detailed, testable address in a simple animal.
plos-pone-0011580:
Kalle Andreasson and colleagues reported this mouse cancer vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their vaccine used harmless virus-like particles carrying Her2/neu, a protein found on some tumours. Given ahead of time it blocked tumour growth, and it could also treat tumours when paired with an added booster.

The team asked which immune cells did the work. They found that CD4 helper cells and CD8 killer cells could each reject tumours on their own, without needing the other type present. That independence matters for vaccine design, since a useful vaccine may not need to trigger both arms at once.
plos-pone-0011680:
Frank Johansson, Baptiste Lederer and Martin Lind studied the common frog across its life stages, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Frogs begin as tadpoles in water and later transform into land-living adults. Because the two stages face different environments, a trait that helps a tadpole may not help the adult frog at all.

Working under stressful conditions, the authors measured how trait performance in youth relates to performance later. Their comparison shows when early promise carries through metamorphosis and when the link breaks. That knowledge helps biologists predict how environmental stress will affect frogs at the stage that matters most.
plos-pone-0011780:
Patrícia Pereira and co-authors measured natural variation in microRNAs in human cervical tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are short regulatory RNAs that control gene expression after a message is made. Their deregulation has been found in many tumours, and they clearly contribute to cancer development.

The team quantified how much microRNA levels vary between cervical samples from different donors. That background wobble is the baseline every cancer study must beat. Knowing the normal variability helps scientists tell true disease signals from person-to-person noise in the cervix and beyond.
plos-pone-0011880:
Neena Valecha and a large team ran in 2010 an open-label randomized trial in Asia comparing two combination treatments for falciparum malaria. One pairing joined dihydroartemisinin with piperaquine; the other joined artesunate with mefloquine, a standard option. The newer pairing had shown promise against malaria parasites that resist several older drugs.

Patients were assigned to one treatment or the other, and the goal was to show the newer pairing was not worse than the standard. Head-to-head trials like this decide what clinics across a region should stock first. A treatment that matches the standard while covering resistant parasites would give malaria programs a stronger first line where drug resistance keeps spreading.
plos-pone-0011980:
Michael Sinclair and co-workers found in 2010 that the hormone oxytocin also has a job in the tongue. Oxytocin acts in the brain to curb food intake, and mice lacking it over-consume salty and sweet solutions. The team asked whether oxytocin might act directly on taste buds through its receptor.

Testing mouse taste tissue, they detected the receptor there and explored oxytocin signaling in the buds. If the hormone tunes taste at the source, then flavor itself shifts with the body's state. That peripheral role could help explain why appetite and taste change together, and it adds taste buds to the list of places where this famous hormone works.
plos-pone-0012080:
Argyris Politis and co-workers joined in 2010 two ways of seeing to draw the true shape of cell machines made of many proteins at once. Such machines do most of the cell's heavy work, yet their shapes are hard to win: they are too big and loose for the usual tricks of the trade.
