Mike Groenhof and colleagues published a 2026 study of mating contact shapes in Choleva beetles. Male genitals often differ fast between close species, and the team asked whether a non-genital contact part follows the same pattern. They studied a small leg joint, the metatrochanter, in males.

The team built a family tree for 19 species-level groups from DNA, then scanned the leg parts with micro CT, a fine form of X-ray. Overall, joint shape changed in a smooth, steady way over time. Yet some shape traits jumped at points where new species split. A plain middle-leg joint showed jumps too, which may reflect linked growth of the middle and hind legs.
pmc-13264580:
Mina Botrous and a large team report a 2026 study of how often a pressure illness of the brain occurs in Victoria, Australia. The illness, called IIH for short, raises pressure inside the skull with no clear cause and links strongly to obesity. Data from the southern hemisphere and from children were scarce.

The team found 612 new cases from 2010 to 2023 at two major Melbourne hospitals, 504 adults and 108 children. Adults were mostly women, 94 percent, with a mean age of 28. Deng, Jiang, Yang, and co-authors present network methods for studying microbial communities. Learning how species in a community interact, and how they respond to change in nature, is a central goal in ecology. Defining network structure in a microbe community is very hard, though.

Microbial diversity is extremely high, and most interactions cannot be observed directly. Their analysis builds networks from survey data, linking species that rise and fall together. Such maps help predict how groups react to pollution, warming, or drugs, and which members hold a community together.
pmc-5076380:
Eldridge, Chan, Campbell, and their co-authors extended the CONSORT statement in 2016 to pilot and feasibility trials. CONSORT is a guideline that improves the transparency and quality of reporting for randomized controlled trials. Pilot and feasibility trials, which test whether a full trial can be run, were often reported poorly.

The extension adapts CONSORT items to these smaller, preparatory studies. It stresses aims such as testing recruitment and procedures, rather than judging treatment effects early. Clear reporting helps funders decide whether a full trial is worth its cost. It also stops weak pilot results from being oversold as evidence of benefit.
pmc-5708080:
Curtis Rueden, Johannes Schindelin, Mark Hiner, and many others described ImageJ2 in 2017. ImageJ is a long-running image analysis program used across biology and beyond. It is loved for its simple macros and the many plug-ins users share.

ImageJ2 rebuilds that base to handle modern image data, which can be huge and have many dimensions. It keeps the old interface and plug-ins working while adding a cleaner core for developers. Labs can keep trusted workflows and still handle new kinds of images. The paper explains the design choices that let old and new parts work together.
pmc-6941980:
Inmaculada Martínez-Reyes and Navdeep Chandel reviewed mitochondrial metabolites in health and disease in 2020. Mitochondria are signaling hubs that help set cell fate, not mere power plants. Their inner cycle, the TCA cycle, sits at the center of that signaling.

Metabolites from the cycle leak signals that steer gene activity, immune behavior, and growth. Broken cycle enzymes cause cancers and metabolic disease through those signals. The review connects classic biochemistry to new findings on cell communication. It reframes a textbook pathway as a control board for physiology. Worked disease examples include cancer, diabetes, and immune disorders driven by faulty cycle signals.
pmc-7299280:
Thomas Rogers and colleagues reported in 2020 that they had isolated powerful antibodies able to block SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. They reasoned that people who had recovered from the infection would carry antibodies shaped by real encounters with the virus. Finding the strongest of those antibodies was the first step toward turning them into a treatment.

The team screened blood from survivors, picked out the antibodies that stopped the virus most completely, and tested the best candidates in a small animal model. The leading antibodies protected the animals from disease. Published during the first year of the pandemic, the study showed that a survivor's own defenses could be copied into a drug, a path several treatments later followed.
pmc-8352980:
Sandra Lopez-Leon and colleagues pooled the evidence in 2021 on the lasting effects of COVID-19, counting more than fifty of them. Their systematic review and meta-analysis gathered studies that followed patients for weeks to months after they had supposedly recovered. They searched major medical literature collections to find every relevant follow up study available at the time.

Combining the results, the authors estimate how common each lingering problem was, from fatigue and breathlessness to hair loss and trouble concentrating. The sheer range of affected organs surprised many readers. The review gave clinicians and health systems an early map of the long tail of the disease, and it underlined the need for dedicated follow up care.
podcast-dannyjones-AziCjLnp780:
Dennis McKenna is a pharmacologist who has studied psychedelic plants for half a century, and the brother of the famed psychonaut Terence McKenna. With Danny Jones, he discusses the beings users of DMT report meeting in that drug's brief, intense state, and the ancient roots he traces for such encounters.

McKenna approaches the entities question as a scientist who has also had the experiences, which makes him an unusual witness. He separates what the chemistry does from what the visions mean, and refuses easy answers in both directions. Jones presses him on whether the beings are real. The episode preserves a serious researcher's fullest public thinking on a subject science mostly avoids, delivered with more honesty about uncertainty than either believers or skeptics usually allow.
podcast-dannyjones-EpW2lFqxx80:
Robert Salas was an Air Force officer stationed at a nuclear missile base in 1967 when, by his account, a glowing object hovered over the gate and his missiles went offline. On Danny Jones's podcast, the former nuclear warfare officer argues that something disturbing is still interfering with America's nuclear arsenal.

Salas has told his story to Congress and journalists for decades, and other veterans have reported similar shutdowns. The military's explanations differ, and no physical proof has settled the matter. What the episode offers is a trained officer's testimony, consistent over a lifetime, about the most sensitive weapons on earth. Jones questions him closely. Listeners must decide what such testimony is worth, which is exactly the problem the disclosure debate keeps circling.
podcast-dannyjones-LQZtTgA1N80:
Physicist Matthew Szydagis works on dark matter detection deep underground. He joins Danny Jones to discuss a startling extension of his field. It is evidence, as he presents it, that UFOs have been present on earth for a million years. His path runs from particle physics to the fossil and historical record of strange objects.

Szydagis applies a detector scientist's habits to fringe material, asking what would count as data and what is only story. Jones follows him from laboratory practice to ancient reports. The million-year claim is Szydagis's own reading, not his field's consensus, and the episode labels it by its framing. Listeners get something rare in this series: a working experimentalist explaining, carefully and on the record, why he thinks the UFO evidence deserves laboratory-grade attention.
podcast-joerogan-LeCpHugyI80:
Biogerontologist Aubrey de Grey joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 638, an early entry in the show's science run. De Grey argues that aging is a kind of damage the body can, in time, be repaired against. When this aired, the idea still sounded like science fiction to most ears.

He lays out the seven kinds of damage he wants medicine to fix, and his guess at the timeline. Rogan asks what a world without aging would do to work, family, and meaning. The episode preserves a bold claim at an early stage, from the man who made ending aging a public cause.
podcast-joerogan-RD-9Ghvt480:
Duncan Trussell's episode 1313 of the Joe Rogan Experience is another entry in the show's longest friendship. Trussell, comedian and host of a family-hour podcast of his own, treats Rogan's studio like a second home. Their talks need no news hook to get going.

The conversation drifts across psychedelic tales, the puzzle of the self, and the jokes Trussell builds from both. Rogan keeps one foot on the ground, telling his own stories between the flights. The episode is a pure example of the pair's chemistry, the blend of stand-up and soul talk that made Trussell a signature guest.
rochester-poems-1680: Rochester's 1680 Poems gather the Earl's obscene and brilliant verse. Court wit cut deep. The Tower library holds the full text. It mocked a king's court. Rhymes stung. Wit flashed. Scandal crowned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
scheele-air-and-fire-1780:
Carl Wilhelm Scheele was a Swedish apothecary who built a great lab life on a small wage. His work on air and fire came out in German in 1777, then in English in 1780. He did his best work in small towns, far from the great schools.

Scheele found the gas we now call oxygen on his own, and named it fire air. He printed his claim late, so the fame went to men who spoke first in public. The book is his own record, and it shows a fine hand at trials.
shabistari-gulshan-i-raz-whinfield-1880:
Mahmud Shabistari was a Persian poet of Tabriz. In 1317 he answered seventeen questions on Sufi doctrine in verse, and he called the poem Gulshan-i Raz, the Rose Garden of Mystery. E. H. Whinfield published his English version in 1880, with an introduction and notes drawn from the great commentary of Lahiji. The Persian text pages are left out of this copy; the English matter is complete.

Question by question, Shabistari treats the self, the heart, the beloved, wine, and the tavern of ruin as signs of the soul's road to God. His answers became the pocket summa of Persian Sufism. Students memorized the couplets for six centuries. Whinfield's version was the first door into the garden for English readers.
sixth-and-seventh-books-of-moses-1880:
The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses, in this 1880 English edition prepared under Johann Scheibel's name, is a German folk grimoire ascribed to Moses. A grimoire is a handbook of spells, seals, and conjurations for practical use. No book of spells traveled further in American folk practice.

Its pages give seals, psalms, and formulas for healing, finding treasure, binding enemies, and turning luck. German settlers carried it into Pennsylvania Dutch country, and from there it passed into African-American hoodoo practice. Conjure workers treated the book itself as a power object, kept wrapped and hidden like a weapon.
sixth-seventh-books-moses-1880:
The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses claim to print the lost magic books of Moses himself. This English edition of 1880 carried the German folk text to American readers. Packed with Solomonic seals, psalm charms, and conjurations, it became the most famous American grimoire of its kind.

In Pennsylvania Dutch country, the book became the backbone of pow-wow magic. Healers used its seals and words for cures, protection, and treasure. Copies passed through farm families as working tools, sometimes feared as much as valued. The 1880 printing fixed the text that spread through German America. Charms and cures from that world are still whispered where the book is kept.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume thirty of Casanova's memoirs: the conclusion. The great lover's farewell. The end of the 18th century's most famous life. Thirtieth volume: the farewell, the great lover bows out, the conclusion of a famous life.
tob-0144-56880:
After the sweeping systems of the first two volumes, volume three of The Secret Doctrine gathers looser material. Blavatsky left essays, fragments, and notes on occult history and symbolism, much of it unfinished at her death in 1891. Editors shaped the mass into a third volume.

Readers find teachings on hidden adepts, the inner meaning of symbols, and the secret history of religions. The tone shifts from chapter to chapter, since the pieces were written for different purposes. Fans prize the volume for hints dropped nowhere else. Newcomers fare better starting with volume one, then returning here.
tob-0180:
Cairo, 1904: Crowley said a voice named Aiwass dictated the Book of the Law to him over three days. The short, fierce text became the central scripture of Thelema, his new religion. Its best-known line lays down the law of the new age: do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law.

Three chapters speak in the voices of Egyptian gods, mixing command, prophecy, and riddling verse. Followers treat each line as charged with meaning; critics see a curiosity of occult history. Either way, few short texts have founded so much. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-9480:
Pindar, the leading lyric poet of ancient Greece, wrote odes to honor men who won at the Olympic Games. The Olympian Odes praise victors in running, wrestling, boxing, and chariot racing. Morice's English translation is the version named for this entry.

Each ode mixes praise of the winner with myths of gods and heroes linked to his city or family. Pindar warns winners to stay humble, since gods give success and can take it away. His grand, dense verse set the pattern for praise poetry in the West, and later poets from Horace onward studied him closely.
un-ga-res-a-69-80:
Peace around the Mediterranean Sea is the broad theme of Resolution A/69/80, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The lands that ring the sea, the text holds, bear the chief duty for its peace, safety, and joint work. It welcomes the steps of Euro-Mediterranean states to deepen their ties, above all in the fight against terror, through the joint code agreed at Barcelona in 2005.

Past pledges and meetings of the shore states are recalled in force. A fresh push came in 2008, when the Paris summit launched a stronger pact, the Union for the Mediterranean. The vote keeps the sea's peace framed as a shared task, from Gibraltar to the Levant.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Hosted under the Resolution 180 label, the text here is the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women. The General Assembly adopted the treaty on 18 December 1979, through resolution 34/180. An opening note explains the convention's background. It turns the earlier declaration against discrimination against women into a binding treaty. An expert committee watches over it.

The articles define discrimination against women. They then require states to ban it in law and in daily life. They cover voting and public office, nationality, and schooling. They also cover jobs and equal pay, and health care. They cover equality in marriage and family life. They call for an end to traffic in women.

Resolution 69/80 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns security and cooperation in the Mediterranean region. It treats Mediterranean security as closely tied to European and international security. It calls on states of the region to join disarmament and non-proliferation instruments. It calls on them to report military spending openly. It encourages joint action against terrorism, organized crime and drug trafficking. A further report is requested from the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-1380:
Western Sahara's referendum mission received a three-month renewal in late 2001. On 27 November 2001 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 28 February 2002. The Secretary-General had written to the Council that month. The Council recalled its backing of his envoy's search for a settlement. The dispute between Morocco and the Polisario Front remained unresolved.

The Secretary-General owed an interim report by 15 January 2002. A fuller assessment had to arrive by 18 February. The Council stayed seized of the matter. Short renewals like this one kept the ceasefire under watch. They also reflected how far the parties were from agreeing on a vote.
un-sc-res-1480:
Timor-Leste's support mission gained a final full year in May 2003. On 19 May 2003 the Security Council extended UNMISET until 20 May 2004. The Council praised the Timorese people and government. Their young state was building its institutions on democratic values. It also praised the mission's work under the Secretary-General's special representative. UNMISET was helping to train the national administration and police.

The extension kept United Nations backing in place for a second year of independence. The mission's name recalled its task, support for East Timor. Its staff worked beside Timorese officials rather than ruling directly. That marked a change from the earlier transitional administration. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter.
un-sc-res-1580: From 2004 comes Resolution 1580, a Security Council act preserved through an English Wikisource transcription of the official record. The document's authority rests on its form as much as its content: a single agreed text, voted once, binding in effect. The entry keeps that text complete, including the closing calls for follow-up reports.
un-sc-res-1680:
Lebanon's sovereignty resolution gained a progress check on 17 May 2006. The Secretary-General's third report on resolution 1559 (2004), dated 18 April 2006, noted real gains through the Lebanese national dialogue. Other parts lagged. Militias were not broken up or disarmed. State control did not run over all territory, and arms had moved into Lebanon for militias in the past six months. Beirut's prime minister had addressed the Council in April.

The Council repeated its call to apply resolution 1559 in full. All states and parties named in the report were told to cooperate at once. Syria was strongly encouraged to answer Lebanon's request for border talks and diplomatic ties. The Council praised Lebanon's steps against arms smuggling and welcomed the national dialogue's decision to disarm Palestinian militias outside the camps. It backed the Secretary-General and his envoy in their work.
un-sc-res-1780: In 2007 the Council voted Resolution 1780 into the record, and the text is preserved here via English Wikisource. The fifteen members' product is a single document with two voices: the preamble's measured assessment and the operative part's direct instructions. Readers who need to know what the Council required can go straight to those numbered lines.
un-sc-res-180:
African states brought a complaint to the Council. Thirty-two of them raised the case of lands under Portuguese rule. Resolution 180 was adopted on 31 July 1963. It recalls Assembly texts on those lands. The Assembly had called them Non-Self-Governing Territories. That status comes from the UN Charter. It points toward full freedom in time.

The Council confirms Assembly Resolution 1514. That text dates from 1960. It called for quick steps to hand power to local peoples. Their freely stated wishes were to guide the change. Race, creed, and colour were not to bar anyone. The Council also rejects Portugal's stance. Portugal called its colonies overseas parts of itself. The Council says that stance clashes with these principles.
un-sc-res-1880:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1880, adopted on 30 July 2009. A presidential election was set for 29 November 2009 under the Ouagadougou peace deal. Key reunification steps had to finish by September, two months before the vote. The peacekeeping mission and the French force backing it were near the end of their terms.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends both mandates until 31 January 2010. The mission must help the parties finish the remaining peace tasks. Disarmament of militias and former fighters continues. The electoral commission gets technical and logistical support for a safe vote. The mission also guards human rights work and helps restore police and courts across the country.
un-sc-res-280:
Lebanon brought the Council to Resolution 280, adopted on 19 May 1970 by eleven votes to none, with four abstentions. Israeli forces had struck deep into Lebanon on 12 May. The Council had already demanded a full pullout that same day. Earlier warnings after past raids had gone unheeded.

The Council calls the attack planned ahead and large in scale. It condemns Israel for breaking its duties under the Charter. It deplores Israel's failure to obey the earlier texts on Lebanon. Such armed attacks, the Council declares, can no longer be stood for. If they recur, the Council warns, it will weigh firm steps under the Charter to enforce its word.
un-sc-res-380:
Morocco's Green March entered Western Sahara in November 1975. Hundreds of thousands of civilians walked into the territory. The Council had twice told Morocco to call the march off. Its president had appealed directly to the king. The march went ahead anyway. On 6 November 1975 the Council deplored that it had taken place. The situation, it said, had seriously deteriorated.

Morocco had to withdraw all the marchers from the territory at once. All parties had to avoid acts that could raise tension further. They also had to cooperate with the Secretary-General. The Assembly's own review of the territory's status ran in parallel. Spain left within months, and Morocco took control of most of the territory.
un-sc-res-580:
South Africa's deadly raid into Lesotho was condemned on 30 December 1985. Lesotho's letter of 23 December told of unprovoked and premeditated killings. Six South African refugees and three Lesotho nationals lay dead in Maseru. The Council recalled resolution 527 (1982), passed after an earlier South African raid on the same city.

The Council strongly condemned the killings and the violence done against Lesotho, in flagrant breach of its sovereignty. South Africa had to pay full and adequate compensation for the loss of life and damage. Lesotho's right to give sanctuary to the victims of apartheid was reaffirmed. Member states were asked to give Lesotho urgent economic help to strengthen its power to receive and keep refugees. South Africa was called to settle its disputes by peaceful means. It also had to honor its pledge not to destabilize its neighbors or let its soil serve attacks on them.
un-sc-res-80:
Kashmir's demilitarization was pressed by the Security Council on 14 March 1950. The United Nations Commission for India and Pakistan had won agreement on a cease-fire, a cease-fire line from July 1949, and a plebiscite plan for the state's future. A Canadian general's talks on troop withdrawals had been reported to the Council. Both governments won praise for their statesmanlike steps so far.

The Council called on India and Pakistan to prepare and carry out a demilitarization programme within five months. It decided to appoint a United Nations Representative to push the process and help settle remaining disputes. The two governments were told to keep the cease-fire faithfully and guard law and order. The Council thanked the commission and the general for their work. It agreed the commission would be wound up one month after both sides reported the representative's appointment accepted.
un-sc-res-980: Judge Sir Robert Yewdall Jennings resigned from the International Court of Justice in 1995. His departure took effect on 10 July that year. On 22 March 1995 the Security Council set the date to fill the vacancy. The election would be held on 12 July 1995. It would take place at a Council meeting and at a General Assembly meeting. The Assembly was in its forty-ninth session. The short text performs only that scheduling task.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The Sahara envoy's compromise talks frame this extension of 2001. On 27 November, the Council adopted Resolution 1380 without dissent. It took note of the Secretary-General's letter of 12 November. The vote mission, MINURSO, was marking time that year. The envoy was testing if Morocco and the Polisario Front could take a deal instead of the stalled vote.

The text extends MINURSO's mandate to 28 February 2002. An interim report is due by 15 January. A full assessment must follow by 18 February. The Council stays seized of the matter in the meantime. Those February reports listed four paths for the territory. They set the agenda for debate through 2002 and 2003.

One year after Timor-Leste's independence, the Council kept its support mission there running. Resolution 1480 passed unanimously on 19 May 2003. The mission was called UNMISET. It was helping the young state build courts and police. It also supported administration and defense forces. Slowly, it was handing power to local officials.

The mandate now ran to 20 May 2004, the planned finish date. The text underlines police training as a top priority. It welcomes better ties between Timor-Leste and Indonesia. It also presses for border agreements. And it demands justice for serious crimes committed during the violence of 1999.

A military mutiny on 6 October 2004, in which senior officers were assassinated, shook Guinea-Bissau's fragile transition, and on 22 December 2004 its United Nations office is extended and reshaped. UNOGBIS, the Peace-Building Support Office, had watched over the transition. Legislative elections had been held that March, but the new institutions remained weak.

UNOGBIS is renewed as a special political mission with a revised mandate. The office is to help strengthen state institutions, support the rule of law and the fight against impunity, and assist the transition toward planned presidential elections. The Secretary-General is asked to review the office's work, and the National Assembly is urged to act on reforms, including in the security sector.

Resolution 1680, passed on 17 May 2006, pushes Lebanon and Syria on the loose ends of a 2004 text. That text, 1559, had told all armed groups in Lebanon to lay down their arms. It had told all foreign troops to leave. Talks among Lebanon's own leaders had moved some points on. But armed groups still held their guns. Fresh arms had crossed into Lebanon in the past six months.

The Council urged Syria to say yes to Lebanon's wish for two things. One was a clear line for their shared border. The other was full, normal ties, with envoys in each other's capitals. It also told all sides to carry out 1559 in full, and asked for fresh news on progress.

Haiti's stabilization mission, MINUSTAH, is extended until 15 October 2008 on 15 October 2007. Haiti had completed its local and municipal elections in April 2007, the final round of a long electoral cycle. Progress on security, the rule of law, and development are linked as gains that reinforce each other.

The Secretary-General's plan to reconfigure the mission, trimming its military side and strengthening its police, is endorsed. MINUSTAH is to keep backing the Haitian National Police, help reform the justice and prison systems, and support border management. It is also asked to give technical expertise to the government and to work with the United Nations country team on aid and recovery across the country.

Portugal's African territories are taken up on 31 July 1963, in a case brought by thirty-two African member states. The General Assembly had declared the territories Non-Self-Governing and had called for power to pass to their peoples at once. The Council's own Angola resolution of 1961 had gone unheeded by Lisbon.

The Assembly's declaration on ending colonial rule is confirmed, and Portugal's policies are affirmed to run against the Charter. Lisbon is called on to grant the territories' peoples their rights, including self-determination leading to independence. All states are asked to stop giving Portugal any help that lets it continue repression, and to block arms sales for that purpose. The Secretary-General is to report by 31 October 1963.

Côte d'Ivoire's election date is locked in as UNOCI is renewed in Resolution 1880, adopted on 30 July 2009. Under the Ouagadougou Political Agreement the first round of the presidential election was set for 29 November 2009. Voter registration was complete. But the provisional voters list was still unpublished. Human rights violations, including sexual violence, persisted.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews UNOCI's mandate until 31 January 2010, centred on supporting free, open, fair, and transparent elections. It insists the Ivorian actors respect the 29 November date. It says any postponement would break faith with the Ouagadougou Agreement. It demands the provisional voters list be published before the end of August 2009. The Secretary-General's Special Representative must certify the voters list and every electoral stage under the five-criteria framework. The Council warns it is ready to impose targeted sanctions on anyone threatening the electoral process.

Resolution 2580, adopted on 8 June 2021, is a single operative sentence from the Security Council. It decides who should lead the United Nations next. Having considered the question, the Council recommends to the General Assembly that António Guterres be appointed Secretary-General of the United Nations for a second term. The term runs from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2026. Under the UN Charter, the General Assembly makes the appointment on the Council's recommendation, so this brief text carries the full weight of the choice.

Israeli forces had struck deep into Lebanon in May 1970. Resolution 280, adopted on 19 May 1970, was the Council's angry response. Eleven members backed it. Colombia, Nicaragua, Sierra Leone, and the United States abstained. Both Lebanon and Israel had presented their cases.

The Council judged the attack planned and large in scale. It condemned Israel for striking in breach of the Charter. It repeated a solemn warning: further attacks would not be tolerated. If they came, members would consider firm steps to enforce their decisions. The text also mourns the deaths and damage caused by the fighting.

A vast march of Moroccan crowds crossed into Western Sahara in November 1975. King Hassan II had called the Green March to claim the land. Spain was set to quit the colony. The Council had begged the king to call the march off. He did not. Resolution 380 passed by common consent on 6 November 1975, the day the march crossed the line.

The Council voiced its grief that the march had gone ahead. Morocco had to pull all marchers out of the land at once. All sides had to work with the UN chief. His task came from two texts passed that fall. The vote did no good in the short run. Morocco held the land. A war with the Polisario Front ran for years. The file marks the start of a long, stuck fight.

Resolution 580, adopted on 30 December 1985, condemns a South African raid into Lesotho. The Council heard Lesotho's foreign minister describe unplanned, deliberate killings blamed on South Africa. Six South African refugees and three Lesotho nationals had been killed. Members said the attack broke Lesotho's sovereignty and was meant to punish the small kingdom for sheltering people fleeing apartheid.

The Council strongly condemns the killings and demands that South Africa pay full compensation for the lives lost and the damage done. It backs Lesotho's right to give shelter to victims of apartheid and asks member states to send urgent economic help so Lesotho can care for refugees. It demands steps to tear down apartheid and asks for a small UN presence in Maseru to watch the situation.

Resolution 80, adopted on 14 March 1950 by eight votes to none with two abstentions, restarts the UN effort on Kashmir. A UN commission for India and Pakistan had produced ceasefire and plebiscite agreements, and a Canadian general, A. G. L. McNaughton, had explored the remaining gaps in talks with both governments. Hostilities had stopped in January 1949 and a ceasefire line was drawn that July.

The Council praised both governments for the steps already taken, including agreeing that Fleet Admiral Chester Nimitz would serve as plebiscite administrator. It then moved to replace the commission with a single United Nations representative, who would press ahead with demilitarizing the state so the promised vote on Kashmir's future could be held.

Judge Sir Robert Yewdall Jennings, a British jurist on the International Court of Justice, resigned his seat effective 10 July 1995. Resolution 980, adopted on 22 March 1995, exists for one narrow reason: fixing the date on which his replacement on the world court would be elected.

The members chose 12 July 1995, two days after the resignation took hold. Voting would take place in parallel, at a Security Council meeting and during the General Assembly's forty-ninth session, because judges of the Court must be elected by both bodies. The text also records, in formal language, that Jennings's departure left a gap covering only the remainder of his original term.
wallace-island-life-1880:
In Island Life, published in 1880, Wallace asks why islands hold such strange mixes of plants and animals. He draws on his years in Malaysia and on reports from sailors and collectors worldwide. Islands, he argues, are natural test cases for how life spreads and changes. The book grew from the same travels as his Malay Archipelago.

Wallace weighs two answers: creatures rafted or flew across seas, or old land bridges once joined now-split lands. He uses ice ages, sea depth, and fossils to test each island case by case. His work founded island biogeography and still guides the study of island species.
willis-improved-chart-for-recording-a-de: Willis' Improved Chart, 1880. The character chart. This book preserves that chart. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
wood-order-zeuglodontia-nature-1880:
Searles Wood makes a bold claim for the sea serpent in his Nature note of 1880. Wood was a sage of old life forms. Ships oft told of a great long necked beast in far seas. He holds the beast could be a zeuglodon. Such whales of old ages had snake like frames. Thought long dead, one may yet live in deep seas men can't sweep.

His note is brief, grave, and writ for sages, not crowds. It gave the serpent a place in the tree of life. The row it sparked ran for years. It is a key text of that row.
yeates-affidavit-nsa-1980:
The National Security Agency fought in court to keep 156 UFO reports sealed, and its sworn word is this file. The in camera affidavit of Eugene Yeates, dated October 9, 1980, was sworn in the case of CAUS against the NSA. Yeates was chief of the agency's Office of Policy.

He tells the judge, in a closed filing, why each of the reports must stay dark. The papers were communications intelligence tied to foreign air and spy craft. Freed at last in 2009, with black bars still in place, the affidavit is the core file of NSA UFO secrecy. It shows the agency guarding its silence by law.
zola-attack-on-mill-1880:
Edmund Gosse translated The Attack on the Mill and its companion war sketches. Zola wrote the title tale in 1880, a decade after the Franco-Prussian War. The setting is a village mill on the day of a wedding feast.

Soldiers seize the mill in the midst of the joy, and the feast turns to slaughter. Few war stories in any language match its force and pity. The sketches around it extend the same bleak view of war's waste. Anger burns through every page at lives thrown away for pride and flags. Readers who know Zola only from the long novels will find his power in brief form here.
zollner-transcendental-physics-1880:
Johann Zollner claimed a fourth span of space in Transcendental Physics, his book in English from 1880. Zollner was a chief of star lore at Leipzig. He sat with Slade, a famed seer, and saw knots tied in sealed cords, rings passed through wood, and goods moved in ways no hand in our space could work, he swore.

A fourth span, with souls in it, is his bold key. Peers cried fraud and shame. Fans hailed a new age of science. The book is the row's most famed flash point. Its claims still spark heat.
